About the Author

Chris J. Mitchell received his BSc (1975) and PhD (1979) degrees in mathematics from Westfield College, University of London. Prior to his appointment as Professor of Computer Science at Royal Holloway in March 1990, he worked at Hewlett-Packard Labs in Bristol, UK, and before that at Racal-Comsec in Salisbury, UK. At Royal Holloway, he co-founded the internationally renowned Information Security Group with his PhD supervisor, Professor Fred Piper, along with Professors Dieter Gollmann and Peter Wild, and he continues to play a role in its ongoing development. His research interests lie at the intersection of discrete mathematics, computer science and digital engineering, focusing in particular on cryptography and its applications as well as on combinatorial mathematics. He has successfully supervised around 40 PhD students to completion. He has been an active participant in the international standardisation of cryptography and information security for over 30 years. He was born near the South Downs in Sussex and today lives in an old cottage in Wiltshire with his wife and Pluto, a rather eccentric Cavalier King Charles Spaniel, where he spends much of his time in a shed at the bottom of the garden.

Preface: Why This Book?

The good Christian should beware of mathematicians.

Mathematics is what mathematicians do.

Some are mathematicians; Some are carpenters’ wives. Don’t know how it all got started; I don’t know what they’re doin’ with their lives.

There are a vast number of books on mathematics, so why should you read this one? That is, of course, the million dollar question, which I will now try to answer. I should first say that I doubt that anything I say in this book has not been said many times before, and often in much greater detail. Indeed, in sketching historical and philosophical ideas relating to mathematics, I am very much aware that a huge amount could, and indeed has been, said already. If you find yourself interested in these topics, there are many excellent books on the history of mathematics, and also a host of discussions of a more philosophical nature on what mathematics is.

The main aim of this book is to provide a straightforward introduction to topics such as groups and finite fields to engineers and computer scientists who find themselves working with—and possibly implementing—some of the strange types of arithmetic involved. These arithmetics are fundamental to much modern information and communications technology.

Why is this book necessary? After all, there are plenty of excellent books that provide a grounding in mathematics for engineers and computer scientists. However, existing books cover what is commonly known as ‘traditional’ applied mathematics, that is very different to the topics that I cover in this book. While applied mathematics in the traditional sense is still of huge importance, modern digital systems increasingly build on very different types of mathematics, and these very different types of mathematics form the focus of this book.

I have attempted to make the book accessible to as large an audience as possible. I will provide some proofs (it wouldn’t be a mathematics book without proofs) but if you like you can skip them, although I think it would be a shame to avoid them altogether since they are such an integral part of mathematics. More importantly, in all the main chapters after the introductory material I provide case studies of how the mathematics I introduce underlies key modern digital technologies, in particular focussing on those relating to secure and reliable communications.

A somewhat subsidiary aim of the book is to introduce the general reader to some of the fascinating mathematics underlying the modern digital and information-centric world. In doing so, I am hoping to give non-mathematicians a taste of what mathematics is really about, at least as mathematicians see it. I should say that I first wanted to write this book at least ten years ago, but finding the time has been the main obstacle.

It seems rather ironic, to me at least, that much of the mathematics I will attempt to describe in this book was not developed with applications in mind. Instead it was developed, and is still largely taught, very much under the banner of Pure, as opposed to Applied, mathematics where—historically at least—pure mathematics means mathematics done without worrying about applications. The key area I will explore comes under the heading of what might be called ‘Abstract Algebra’ (or ‘Modern Algebra’).

So why do I say that this seems ironic? Well, traditionally, and perhaps surprisingly, some pure mathematicians have been a little sniffy about applied mathematics, regarding it as a lower form. Pure mathematics, at least as some see it, is somehow superior precisely because it isn’t related to applications but has been developed purely for its own sake. To some extent such a view seems nonsensical, since I suspect that the original roots of all of mathematics lie in applications, although in some cases mathematics has progressed a very long way from its origins. Of course mathematics is not unique; I suspect such views pervade other areas of human activity—for example, perhaps the art world is a little like this, where I get the impression that commercial art is sometimes thought of as being less worthy than fine art, or ‘art for art’s sake’.

Of course when I mention applied mathematics I mean mathematics applied to the physical sciences or to mechanical or electrical engineering. The term applied mathematics is often taken to mean just this, where other areas of mathematics which find real-world applications are not given the label. Anyway, while I’m sure not everyone would agree with this rather simple discussion of terminology, I hope it gives you a flavour of the rather strange way in which the terms pure and applied are used when referring to mathematics. My emphasis in this book is on mathematics which finds application in real-world systems relating to computing and communications, but is nonetheless often thought of as pure.

Anyway, back to algebra. The word algebra comes from the Arabic word al-jabr meaning ‘the reunion of broken parts’, used by the Persian mathematician and astronomer Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (in the 9th century CE) for naming a method of transforming equations. Interestingly, al-Khwarizmi also gives his name to the term algorithm, but that’s a story for another book.

I suspect most readers will think of algebra as relating to manipulating and solving equations involving symbols which represent numbers. Of course, using symbols in equations to solve problems is a hugely powerful technique that you were very probably taught at school. So we all know what algebra is; but what about ‘abstract’ algebra? Abstract algebra, as I will discuss in a little more detail in the first chapter, seeks to look at what happens when we think about some of the rules underpinning addition and multiplication of numbers, and look at what happens when we apply these rules to operations on more general objects—which might be thought of as new types of numbers. The implications turn out to be profoundly important for the modern world.

At this point I should also mention another branch of mathematics known as Number theory.

Until the second half of the twentieth century, number theory was thought of as the purest of pure mathematics. After all, what possible application could exist for investigating prime numbers, a subject of study by mathematicians for its own sake for at least two thousand years? Well, as I explore in this book, a hugely important method for encrypting data, which has been widely used in securing everyday financial transactions, is built on key results from number theory. So even number theory is not really ‘pure’ any more.

Another area of mathematics that forms a theme of this book is known as Discrete Mathematics. Discrete mathematics is the mathematics of discrete objects, such as the numbers 1, 2, 3, etc., as opposed to the world of continuous functions (such as the trigonometric functions sine or cosine). Why is discrete mathematics important here? Well, the numbers and objects processed by digital computers, including all the phones, tablets, PCs and servers we use on an everyday basis, are by definition discrete. These devices store and interchange information as zeros and ones, not as continuous values, and so it is inevitable that discrete mathematics is of key importance to the modern information age.

I have tried to give credit throughout this book to some of the great mathematicians of the past two or three thousand years who have developed the ideas I describe. However, I am a little ashamed to have to confess that the vast majority of the mathematicians I mention are men. There are many and varied reasons for this, not least because in many cultures women have been, and continue to be, denied access to mathematical education. More sinisterly, it seems that, as in many other walks of life, efforts have been made to hide contributions made by women, perhaps to try to maintain the fiction that women and mathematics do not go together.

Finally, given my claim about the importance of the mathematical ideas introduced here to the digital world, I will provide examples of how they are used throughout the book. I have to confess I haven’t chosen the applications I mention systematically—they simply happen to be the ones I know best. However, rest assured that there are many more that I don’t discuss here.

Chris J. Mitchell

Wiltshire

August 2025

Chapter 1
A Gentle Introduction

Mathematics is the language with which God wrote the universe.

Logic is the foundation of the certainty of all the knowledge we acquire.

Mathematicians are like Frenchmen: whatever you say to them they translate into their own language, and forthwith it is something entirely different.

1.1 What Is This Book About?

As I mentioned in the introduction, this is a book about numbers, but not just the numbers we are familiar with and use every day (such as 1, 2, 3, and fractions like and ). I want to introduce you to some rather less familiar types of numbers, which, whilst not something we as individuals use every day, nonetheless underlie much of the information and communications technology we take for granted. At the same time I hope to introduce you to mathematics as seen by mathematicians—which may be rather different, and perhaps more abstract, than what you thought of as mathematics at school. I am, of course, assuming that you would not call yourself a professional mathematician, but are nonetheless curious about the subject. If, for example, you have a degree in mathematics, you may find pretty much everything I have to say is routine, but I have nonetheless tried to stay on the right side of rigour; that is, I am hoping there are not too many errors!

Why is the title of this book Mathematics for the digital systems engineer? Well, as I just mentioned, although the numbers introduced in later chapters are not numbers as we are used to them, they are key to today’s information-centric world. I find the whole subject fascinating, as I have since I was introduced to them over 50 years ago as an undergraduate, and I hope to share some of that fascination with you, and give you the tools to engage with the mathematics involved when working with and developing new systems.

This is perhaps not a typical textbook. I have been rather self-indulgent and allowing myself to go down all sorts of rabbit holes. It has made writing this book more fun for me, and I hope you enjoy some of these diversions. Apart from its intended role as an introduction to the mathematics of many modern digital systems, I would also hope that it might be something of interest to anyone thinking of studying mathematics at university, as it attempts to give an introduction to one of the subjects forming a key part of any mathematics degree.

1.2 Mathematics as Mathematicians See It

I would like to start by saying that what professional mathematicians do, i.e. inventing (or perhaps discovering) new mathematics, is a creative activity. That is, a goal of mathematical research is to state and prove new theorems or conjectures, or to find examples which disprove conjectures or show that some set of conditions can actually be met. The hope of every working mathematician is always that in some way they can extend the body of mathematics.

At this point, I would like to have a quick gripe about the use of the word ‘creative’ in relation to certain endeavours, as if no other activities are creative. Indeed, the term creative is often used in connection with the so-called ‘creative arts’, as if to deliberately exclude any other pursuits, including science and mathematics. I would like to make the case that while undoubtedly painting a picture or composing a piece of music are creative acts, so is the development of a new piece of mathematics.

However, at this point I want to slightly contradict myself! Whilst mathematics is clearly something completely created by humanity, it is important to observe that many—if not most—mathematicians, consciously or unconsciously, talk about mathematics as if it has always existed. For example, they (and that includes me) will talk about ‘discovering’ a theorem rather than creating a theorem. Indeed, there is a widespread—often unarticulated—feeling that the ideas we develop and the theorems we prove always existed, and it was just up to us to discover them. This has been discussed at length by many previous authors, and platonism is the name usually given to this belief (although this is not the same as Platonism, the philosophy of Plato). Of course, when questioned about this seemingly bizarre belief, many mathematicians will row back somewhat and avow that mathematics is something created, but this doesn’t quite explain why talk of discovering a theorem or proof is so widespread in the mathematics community.

The fact that mathematics works, i.e. that it is not self-contradictory and is so effective when applied to a very wide range of activities, adds to the feeling that it is universal and has an existence beyond its human creators.

One of the great powers of mathematics comes from abstraction and generalisation. By abstraction I mean taking something concrete, for example addition over the whole numbers (the integers

This leads us to what I regard as the core of mathematics: theorems and proofs. Theorems and lemmas are simply statements about the properties of certain mathematical structures. To be a theorem, and not simply a conjecture, there must be an accompanying proof. The proof will establish the truth of the theorem in a logical way. Until a theorem has a complete proof, it will not be accepted as true by the mathematical community.

So why do we need proofs? Many of the theorems and lemmas I will state and prove in this book will seem obvious or intuitively true. However, while mathematical intuition is hugely important, it is also very unreliable, and ‘obvious’ results can turn out to be false. This is the main reason so much effort was made by mathematicians during the 18th and 19th centuries to put the mathematics of real and complex numbers on a firm foundation.

Of course, at this point I have to concede that we are all fallible; indeed, in the words of Alexander Pope ‘To err is human’.

The Four Colour Theorem (the ‘4CT’) is a famous case in point.

A ‘proof’ of this theorem was published by Alfred Kempe in 1879, which was accepted at the time. However, in 1890, a flaw was found by Percy Heawood. So, at that point, it became the ‘Four Colour Conjecture’, and it didn’t become the 4CT again until 1976, when Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken announced their computer-assisted proof. They needed the assistance of a computer to complete their proof to check through 1482 individual cases.

Generally speaking, we rely on other mathematicians checking proofs during the refereeing process for a paper when submitted for publication, although this is clearly not infallible. More generally, any major results are likely to be looked at and checked by many mathematicians. Interestingly, the fact that the 1976 proof of the 4CT was computer-assisted made human checking almost impossible, and this gave rise to a lot of controversy at the time, although the result is today well-accepted. Indeed, a second proof has since been published (or should I say discovered?)—requiring a substantially smaller number of cases to be checked by computer.

1.3 Theorems and Proofs

So if theorems are the bread and butter of mathematics, what do they look like? The statement of a theorem will typically start by saying what mathematical object (or objects) it applies to, such as the integers. It may also say what additional restrictions are in place—for example, a theorem about integers might only apply to certain specific integers, for example, prime numbers. The theorem will then list one or more statements which are true about the objects under consideration. This is all rather abstract, but the details of the statement of a theorem will vary a great deal depending on the subject matter.

A simple example is what is known as Pythagoras’ Theorem, although, as is often the case for named theorems, Pythagoras was not the first to know about it. Apparently, the Pythagorean rule was well-known over a 1000 years before Pythagoras was born. The theorem goes as follows.

Theorem 1.1 (Pythagoras’ Theorem)

For a planar right-angled triangle, with sides adjacent to the right angle having lengths and , and the other side (the hypotenuse) having length :

The statement of this theorem first mentions the objects it is dealing with, namely right-angled triangles (embedded in the plane), and then sets up some notation. The theorem ends up with the main statement, i.e. that the length of the hypotenuse squared is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides. Having said that every theorem has a proof, even for this example I feel obliged to give one (I have chosen one of the many ways that are known for proving this theorem).

Proof. Take four copies of the triangle and arrange them in a square shape with rotational symmetry, so that:

  • the right angles of the triangles form the corners of the square, and
  • part-way along each side of the square, two copies of the triangle meet in a point.

The arrangement is shown in Figure 1.1.

As shown in the figure, this results in a square whose sides have length . Moreover, there is a square in the middle with side length . The areas of the four triangles and the smaller square in the middle (with side length ), when added together, must have the same area as the large square. Now the area of the large square is and the area of the smaller square is . Each of the four triangles has area , since two such triangles can be joined together to make a rectangle with side lengths and .

Thus:

But , and so

and subtracting from both sides gives the desired result.

The little box at the end of the previous line (the symbol) marks the end of the proof,

So now we know what a theorem looks like, I should also try to explain the difference between a theorem and a lemma. At the most fundamental level there is no difference, since they both involve the statement of the truth of something and must both be accompanied by a proof. It is often a matter of authorial taste as to what gets labelled a lemma and what gets called a theorem. In general, a theorem is something that is worth stating for its own sake, whereas a lemma is typically something whose only purpose is to help prove other lemmas or theorems.

When stating a theorem, or indeed within a proof of a theorem, it is common practice to use the phrase ‘if and only if’ (sometimes abbreviated to ‘iff’) for a two-way implication. The usual context is something like ‘ is true if and only if is true’. The meaning is simply that if is true, then is true and also that if is true, then is true.

There are a number of ways a theorem can be proved; indeed, logicians interested in the underlying rules of mathematics have identified a range of different types of proof. Probably the most obvious method of proof is to give a logical progression of arguments starting from the assumptions of the theorem that lead to the desired result. The proof I gave of Pythagoras theorem is of this type.

Another very common type of argument is the reductio ad absurdum. This involves assuming the opposite of the result that is to be proved, and then following a series of logical deductions to result in something that cannot possibly be true—typically something that contradicts one of the assumptions underlying the theorem. As a result, the statement must be true (since, if it cannot be false, it must be true

A third form of argument, known as induction, only applies to theorems which assert the truth of a statement that is a function of the positive integer . This method of proof is explained in Chapter 3.

Finally, for theorems that state that a certain mathematical object exists, for example, a theorem stating that there exist Pythagorean triples, i.e. sets of three integers , and such that , a proof need only exhibit an example. For the case of the Pythagorean triples theorem, it is simply necessary to give an example of a suitable triple , e.g. (3, 4, 5).

There are other methods of proving theorems, for example, giving counterexamples to show that a claim is untrue, but the preceding list is good enough for this book.

Before moving on, I feel I should explain a little about how one might come up with a proof for a theorem. Often, when trying to prove a result, I might wrestle with the problem in my head until I think I have something—perhaps not a full proof, but maybe a step in the right direction. The acid test then comes when I try to write it down; sadly, often when I come to write down an idea, I find it doesn’t actually work because I missed some point that only came to light when I worked through the details. So writing things down is an absolutely key step; actually, I believe this principle applies in many areas of study, not just in mathematics.

When I have actually proved something, the first proof I come up with may be rather long and inelegant—indeed, it may still be wrong, as even writing things down doesn’t always catch subtle errors! The final proof that gets included in an academic paper or book is typically not the first proof that was found but a polished version, i.e. a version which is as succinct and neat as possible. Indeed, for well-known theorems, such as those included in this book, the mathematical community has often had hundreds, if not thousands, of years to come up with the cleverest, most elegant proof.

This is not something that is always discussed as much as it should be; you could even call it a slightly dirty secret of mathematicians. When you are presented with a proof as a student of mathematics, they always look so much better than any proof you might come up with when asked to devise one for ‘homework’ or as an exercise. But, of course, you shouldn’t feel bad about this—the same is true for most of us! So, when at various points in this book I ask you to try to prove a result, don’t be disheartened if your proof is rather less elegant or simple than the one I present at the end of the book; remember that I’ve cheated and used a wide variety of established sources to find the proof I like best. Also, don’t worry if your proof is different to mine; there are many different and equally valid ways to establish the same result.

In fact, finding a proof is often much simpler than working out what the theorem is that one should try to prove.

1.4 Abstract Algebra

I already briefly talked about the ideas of abstraction and generalisation. Abstract algebra, as its name suggests, is about investigating what happens when you throw away your preconceptions about what adding or multiplying together two objects means. The objects involved can be drawn from a finite or an infinite set, and the objects could be the familiar numbers, geometric objects, or more complex entities such as polynomials. As you proceed through the book, you will encounter a wide range of examples.

At the end of the next chapter, I will give some examples of abstract properties we might expect for our generalised notions of addition or multiplication (or operations as I call them). The list given there is by no means complete, and again later in the book, I will introduce other examples, notably one governing how two operations interact.

1.5 What Do You Need to Know to Make Sense of This Book?

This is, of course, a question of key importance. I am assuming a very basic familiarity with mathematics that you may have learnt at school, in particular elementary ideas about whole numbers, addition, multiplication, subtraction, and exponentiation (i.e. raising one number to the power of another).

However, in other respects, I have tried to make the book self-contained, and where I introduce new ideas I give examples which I hope you will find helpful. At times I suspect you may need to take a little time to play with a concept before proceeding, and I would recommend working out your own examples using pen and paper if you have trouble understanding something. Don’t worry, every mathematician (except perhaps those with planetary-sized intelligences) needs to scribble on a piece of paper every now and then to try to grasp a concept or check that something really does work.

1.6 Case Studies of Applications

I already mentioned in the preface that the main goal of this book is to provide an accessible introduction to topics such as groups and finite fields for the benefit of engineers and computer scientists who find themselves working on applications of these mathematical notions. Of course, I am hoping that the book will also be of interest to anyone interested in how key modern digital technologies actually work. The main emphasis is on the mathematics itself; however, in every chapter after the opening three introductory chapters, I provide case studies of applications of the mathematics that has been introduced. The main focus is on topics I am personally familiar with, in particular relating to the protection of digital communications, but I have tried to cover a range of application domains. The main case study topics are summarised as follows.

  • In Chapter 4, I introduce two quite different applications, both resting on modular arithmetic. The first is the notion of check digits, as used to protect the integrity of numerical data against accidental errors. Second, I introduce both the idea of public key cryptography and the RSA public key cryptosystem, whose security rests on the difficulty of finding the prime factors of very large numbers; RSA has been very widely used in many domains, notably in the protection of credit card transactions.
  • Chapter 5, which introduces groups, contains a description of a different type of public key cryptosystem, namely Diffie–Hellman key exchange, which has been widely implemented using a range of underlying groups.
  • In Chapter 6, where I introduce rings, I return to the problem of protecting data integrity and introduce a technology of huge practical importance over the last 60 years or so, namely block codes. I also introduce one key example of a class of block code, namely the Hamming codes.
  • Chapter 7 introduces the idea of polynomials as mathematical objects in their own right. The key application explored here is the linear feedback shift register and the sequences such registers generate. Shift register sequences have been widely used in a range of digital communication domains, including in cryptography and spread spectrum communications.
  • The summit of the mathematical mountain is reached in Chapter 8, where I introduce finite fields. The case study application described here again relates to cryptography, and in particular to what is known as elliptic curve cryptography.
  • The last main chapter, Chapter 9, is a little different from the rest of the book in that it consists of a compendium of topics I could not bear to leave out. Whilst some of the topics do not have immediate application, the introduction to difference sets and finite geometry touches on a range of topics of practical interest, including cryptography, although the applications are not explored here.

Chapter 2
Sets, Functions and Relations

A set is a Many that allows itself to be thought of as One.

2.1 Why Are Sets Important?

In this chapter, I will explore ideas that are fundamental for the mathematics in the rest of this book. I will use all these simple, but sometimes quite subtle, concepts throughout.

First I will introduce the idea of a set, which you can think of as a collection of objects of some kind; in principle these objects could be anything: people, animals, houses, planets or anything else, but here I will mainly be concerned with mathematical objects such as numbers. You may find the discussions in this chapter a little abstract in tone, but I will try to provide some examples to make the ideas more concrete.

So why am I going to the trouble of bothering you with all this? It turns out that sets are an absolutely fundamental tool for mathematics. This is perhaps surprising given that the notion of a set didn’t emerge until the late 19th century, notably in the work of Georg Cantor whose quote starts this chapter, but the idea of a set is so useful that today it pervades almost any discussion of mathematics. It gives us a convenient way of describing the objects we are dealing with.

I will also introduce the notion of a relation, where a relation is something that either holds or does not hold between any pair of elements in a set. For example, if a set consists of all the people living in a village, the relation ‘is married to’ probably applies to certain pairs of individuals in the village, but almost certainly not to every pair of individuals!

Following on from the introduction to relations, I will describe a particularly important type of relation known as an equivalence relation. Equivalence relations generalise the idea of equality, which is itself a special type of relation.

An equally important notion is that of a function. A function maps elements from one set (the domain of a function) to a second set (the function’s codomain). Of course the domain and codomain may be the same, but that is certainly not necessary. Examples of functions you will likely have already encountered are the trigonometric functions: sine, cosine and tangent (commonly known as sin, cos and tan), as well as numerical functions such as logarithm (usually abbreviated to log).

The chapter concludes with an introduction to operations, namely defined ways of combining pairs of elements from a set to give another element of the same set, just as addition or multiplication can be used to combine two numbers to give another number. Certain special types of operation will be key to just about all the rest of this book.

Indeed, one could say that all of mathematics is about investigating and proving properties of certain special types of sets, along with particular relations, functions and operations defined on elements of these sets. So in this chapter I am laying out the fundamental tools for just about all of mathematics. These fundamental tools of mathematics are simple and easy to state, but there seems to be no limit to what can be achieved using them—much as the few tens of thousands of words in the English language can be used to build an apparently unlimited number of pieces of literature, great and not so great.

2.2 Sets

So what is a set? As I already mentioned, a set can be thought of as a collection of things of some kind. There are no restrictions on what can be contained in a set; the key thing when defining a set is to ensure that there is an unambiguous rule enabling anyone to decide whether or not a particular object is a member of the set.

I will use some special notation to describe sets. First, I will always use curly brackets, {…}, to delimit the contents of a set. A simple example of a set might be

This set contains three objects, which happen to be the colours pink, blue and green. The members of the set are called its elements. I also use the special symbol to say that an object is a member of a set. Thus I could write

I could also write

where can be read as ‘not a member of’ or ‘not an element of’.

One important property of a set is its size, or cardinality, i.e. the number of elements in the set. For our simple example, the cardinality of is clearly 3. If I called this set , i.e.

then I use vertical bars to denote cardinality, that is, I can write

Two very important examples of sets are the Natural Numbers and the integers . The special symbols and are used very widely in mathematics. The natural numbers, as the name implies, consist of the everyday whole numbers we are all familiar with, i.e.

The set of integers contains all the natural numbers, and consists of all the whole numbers, positive and negative, as well as zero. That is

These two examples of sets contain an unbounded number of elements, so what is their cardinality? Well, informally they are said to have infinite cardinality, without necessarily wanting to define what infinity means. In fact, it is possible to formally define what infinite cardinality means—this is a subject I return to in the final main chapter of this book (see Section 9.2).

Often it is interesting to look at cases where one set is contained in another, meaning that all the elements in one set are contained in the other set. This is clearly the case for the examples I just gave, i.e. is contained in . I say is a subset of , and write

You should read the symbol as meaning ‘is contained in’ or ‘is a subset of’. Figure 2.1 depicts the subset relationship between and .

I also need one more piece of notation relating to sets. There is a (unique) set containing no elements at all. This is called the empty set and is written as .

I promised you proofs, so it is about time I gave you one apart from the example in Chapter 1. In formal mathematics we give statements that we want to show are true, and as I mentioned in Chapter 1, we label them theorems or lemmas (or lemmata if you’re being pedantic). For my first example of a proof (apart from that of Pythagoras’ theorem), I’ll start with a very simple result; I’ll call it a lemma rather than a theorem, as it is only a minor, albeit useful, result.

Lemma 2.1

Let and be sets. If and , then .

Proof. Suppose our lemma is wrong and , and thus there must be an element in one set that is not in the other; so I might as well suppose that but . Then , which contradicts our original assumption. Thus my supposition that must be wrong, and so I have proved the desired result that .

Note that in the proof I could equally well have supposed that but and used precisely the same argument—this is an example of an assumption made in a proof which is commonly said to apply ‘without loss of generality’.

I suspect you are a little puzzled (a) as to why I bothered to state this result, and (b) why I took the trouble to give a proof, since it seems as if it is blindingly obvious. The answer to (a) is simple: it gives us a simple way of proving two sets are equal—that is, if I can prove that and , then I immediately know that from Lemma 2.1. Indeed, that is often how we build mathematics: we develop a series of lemmas which we can then use together to prove whatever main result we wish to establish.

The answer to (b) is more complex. First and foremost I wanted to give you an example of a very simple proof, just to get you in the mood. Second, just because something seems obvious doesn’t mean it is true. Sadly the history of mathematics is littered with errors caused by blind acceptance of obvious claims which turn out to be false.

Third, I wanted to demonstrate the so-called reductio ad absurdum proof technique, in which I suppose that the result I am trying to prove is false, and then show that this results in a contradiction of something I assumed to be true—and hence the result must be true! Reductio ad absurdum is a hugely useful technique; indeed, as the great 20th-century British mathematician Godfrey Harold Hardy said

Reductio ad absurdum, which Euclid loved so much, is one of a mathematician’s finest weapons. It is a far finer gambit than any chess play: a chess player may offer the sacrifice of a pawn or even a piece, but a mathematician offers the game.

It is common to be dealing with cases where two sets have elements in common, and sometimes these common elements are of interest. To take a simple example, suppose is the set of colours conventionally associated with the rainbow, that is

and, as previously, suppose that

Then and have two elements in common: blue and green. I say that the intersection of and , i.e. the set of elements that and have in common, is , and I write

i.e. the symbol denotes set intersection. The relationship between the sets and is shown in Figure 2.2, where is the area where the two circles overlap. If the intersection of two sets and is empty, i.e. , then and are said to be disjoint.

In a similar way, I am also sometimes interested in the set of all elements which are contained in at least one of two sets. For two sets, the set of all elements in either one set or the other is called the union of the sets, and we use the symbol to indicate this. So I could write

meaning that the union of and is a set containing all the eight colours occurring as elements of either or . Looking again at Figure 2.2, is represented by the area inside one (or both) of the two circles. The figure is a simple example of a widely used way of depicting sets and their intersections, namely Venn diagrams, named after British mathematician, logician and philosopher John Venn, who was an advocate of their use back in the late 19th century. In a Venn diagram, a set is typically shown as a circle or ellipse, with the elements of the set placed inside the boundary.

Whilst the notion of a set is a relatively recent one compared to the long history of mathematics, during the 20th century sets came to be used as a fundamental and everyday tool by almost all mathematicians. However, those interested in the fundamentals of mathematics will tell you that sets need to be used with a little care, as became clear when Russell’s paradox was first formulated in 1901 by British logician and philosopher Bertrand Russell.

2.3 Cartesian Products of Sets

Then the set is the set of all pairs of elements, the first of the pair being from and the second of the pair from . This is known as the Cartesian Product of and . The name derives from the 17th-century French philosopher and mathematician René Descartes.

2.4 Relations

Sets on their own are not much use. I need to be able to say things about how elements of a set relate, or can be combined. As a first step in this direction I will define the notion of a relation on the members of a set. If is a set, then a relation holds for certain pairs of elements from the set. If and then I write ‘’ if is related to . (An alternative way of thinking about a relation is that it is a subset of the set , where if and only if .)

Consider the following simple example. Suppose is the set of numbers {1, 2, 3, 4}, and let be the relation ‘is less than or equals to’—normally written as ≤. Then 1 ≤ 1, 1 ≤ 2, 1 ≤ 3 and 1 ≤ 4, but the only number 4 is related to is itself (i.e. 4 ≤ 4). A complete listing of the relation is given in Table 2.1.

More strictly, I have defined a binary relation, since it applies to pairs of elements of a set. It is, of course, possible to define operations on groups of three or more elements, but that is outside the scope of what I am interested in here.

The example I have just given is a special type of relation called an ordering, and orderings have a theory of their own—I will give some basic properties of orderings in Chapter 3. However, next I want to define and give examples of another type of relation of key importance both in this book and for mathematics generally.

2.5 Equivalence Relations and Equivalence Classes

The notion of an equivalence relation is simple yet powerful. The idea behind the definition of an equivalence relation is to generalise the notion of equality, which is, after all, a special type of relation. To understand the motivation for the definition of an equivalence relation, it is important to think about the properties of equality.

The first key property of equality is that it is reflexive, that is, for any (whatever might be), it is always true that . The second important property of equality is that of symmetry, namely that if then it always follows that . The third fundamental property of equality is that it is transitive, that is, if and , then it follows that . These are, of course, trivial observations, but they motivate a very important idea.

Suppose a relation is defined on a set . Also suppose that has the following three properties:

  • for every (reflexivity),
  • if for some , then (symmetry), and
  • if and for some , then (transitivity).

Then is said to be an equivalence relation, meaning that is a relation that has some of the key properties of equality. It turns out that equivalence relations crop up in many branches of mathematics.

In particular, because equivalence relations have important properties, whenever I encounter an example of such a relation, I immediately know it has all these properties. This is an important idea in mathematics, namely that of proving properties of a general class of objects, and then applying it to specific examples. It shows the power of abstraction.

A simple, non-mathematical example involves people. Let the set be all the people in the United Kingdom, and suppose the relation is ‘living on the same street as’. It is not hard to see that is an equivalence relation. Every individual lives on the same street as themselves (reflexivity). If Jane lives on the same street as Mary, then Mary lives on the same street as Jane (symmetry). Finally, if John lives on the same street as Jim, and Jim lives on the same street as Mike, then clearly John lives on the same street as Mike (transitivity).

Of course, I’ve glossed over two issues with this example. First, there are people who don’t have a fixed street address, for whatever reason, so in such cases the relation is not defined. I could fix this by restricting the set to people with fixed street addresses—of course, this is often what governments do when wishing to ignore the problem of homelessness. Second, people are being born, moving house and also dying, all the time, and so the set and the relation are not fixed; nonetheless, the result holds as long as we consider and for a fixed point in time. Of course, that’s the trouble with real life—it is not as easy to deal with as the abstract world of mathematics!

I am particularly interested in one key property, namely that an equivalence relation partitions the set it is defined on, that is, it divides the set into discrete (non-overlapping) parts. To establish this important result, we first need another piece of notation. If is an equivalence relation defined on a set , then for any let denote the set of all elements that is related to; that is, in formal language:

The above can be read as ‘ equals the set of all in with the property that ’, i.e. when defining sets we use the colon as shorthand for ‘such that’ or ‘with the property that’. We call an equivalence class.

Armed with this notation we can now give (and prove) our key result. The theorem immediately below is expressed rather formally, but its implications are explained more informally below.

Theorem 2.1

If is an equivalence relation defined on a set , and , then either or .

Proof. Suppose that , and hence there exists an element with the property that and . If I can show that this means that then I have proved the theorem. As a first step, I will show that . Since , by definition we know that . Similarly, we know that . By symmetry of we know that , and hence by transitivity we have . I’m now halfway to our desired result.

I next want to show that . So how do I go about proving that one set is contained in another? The usual approach, and the one I follow in the next paragraph, is to choose an arbitrary element of the first set and then show it must be in the second set. It follows immediately from the definition that the first set must be a subset of the second.

Choose any . This means that . Since , by symmetry and transitivity it follows that , and so . Since I chose to be any element of , this means that any element that is in is also in , and I have shown that .

I can use exactly the same argument (interchanging and ) to show that . Finally, since and , Lemma 2.1 means that I have shown that .

So what does this theorem mean? If you think about it a little, it means that the equivalence classes partition the set on which the relation is defined, and all the members of an equivalence class are related to each other. Returning to our simple example where the relation means ‘living on the same street as’, then the equivalence classes are the sets of people living on a particular street—each street has its own equivalence class of people. So this relation partitions all the people in into street-subsets.

A simple equivalence relation defined on the set of words in English is ‘starts with the same letter as’. Some of the equivalence classes for this equivalence relation are shown in Figure 2.3.

In Section 2.6, I give a more detailed example of how this theorem works. However, before moving on to this example, I would like—as a bit of fun—to share a plausible (but false) argument with you. Suppose is a relation on the set which is symmetric and transitive. Choose any element , and let be any other element in for which . By symmetry we know that . Moreover, since and , by transitivity we know that , that is, must be reflexive. So it seems as if we can simplify our definition of an equivalence relation to be a relation which is just symmetric and transitive (and we don’t need to assume reflexivity).

So what is wrong with this argument? Please think about it. I discuss this further in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section at the end of the book (see page 222).

Of course, spotting errors in proofs is something mathematicians worry about a lot. It is sometimes easy to miss an implicit assumption, which is what has happened here.

2.6 Relations: A Detailed Example

I next want to give a rather more subtle example of a relation. The relation is again defined on people from a particular set. This time the set includes living and dead people—for the sake of argument I will define the set to be all the people alive in the United Kingdom since the beginning of 1800, but the arguments below would apply to any other defined set of people. The relation is then ‘is a blood relative of’. This is a rather woolly notion so, to make it more precise, I will say that two individuals and in are blood-related (i.e. ) if and only if and have a common ancestor in the set . So, for example, if Bob’s great-grandmother is Doris’s grandmother, then Bob and Doris are blood relatives (in fact they are first cousins once removed).

So what properties does this relation have? Well, it is clearly reflexive since any individual has two common ancestors with themselves, namely their mother and father.

So, this is not an equivalence relation, and it does not partition humanity into blood-related groups. Perhaps this is a good thing, as we hardly need another way for people to divide themselves into ‘us’ and ‘them’; after all, in recent years it seems to be increasingly popular for populist politicians to whip up prejudices against individuals who can be identified as ‘them’, with clearly highly undesirable results; after all, ‘us versus them’ is a well-established meme used by dictators. Nonetheless, is there any way we can restrict our definition to enable us to define an equivalence relation of this type? Well, it turns out that we can by looking only at one sex.

Let be the subset of containing all the women alive in the United Kingdom since 1800. Of course, without loss of generality we could do the same analysis for men. Then the relation , defined to be ‘have a common ancestor in the set ’, is an equivalence relation on . Why is this?

Well, is clearly reflexive and symmetric, just like . Why is it transitive as well? Suppose , and are all in , and that and , that is suppose and have a common female ancestor ( say), as do and ( say). We need to show that , i.e. that and have a common (female) ancestor. It is straightforward to verify that the female ancestors of form a chain, since had one mother, who had one mother (’s maternal grandmother), who had one mother, and so on. Then and must both lie somewhere in ’s ancestor chain of mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, etc., since they are both ancestors of . If then we are done since this means that is a common ancestor of and . So suppose that is lower down (more recent) in ’s ancestor chain than . Then is an ancestor of (which is an ancestor of ); that is, is an ancestor of both and and we are done since we could use exactly the same argument if is lower down (more recent) in ’s ancestor chain than .

So what does this mean when we look at the equivalence classes this family-based relation defines? Interestingly, all women in an equivalence class share the same mitochondrial DNA, since this is always inherited from an individual’s mother. Also, if we look at the corresponding relation for men ( say), then all men in the same equivalence class have the same Y chromosome, since this is always inherited from an individual’s father. Moreover, if I make the simplifying assumptions that men never change their surname and male children always take the surname of their father, then all men in an equivalence class will share the same surname.

This suggests two things to me. First that, unlike common practice in the United Kingdom and many other countries, perhaps women should take their surname from their mother not their father, so that females in the same equivalence class under would share the same surname,

Of course, there are certain problematic edge cases with our analysis of this relation. If the set was extended to all of humanity, living or dead, then all living humans would have a common ancestor, given that evolutionary biologists tell us that all of (today’s) humanity is descended from a single woman living in Africa two or three hundred thousand years ago—the so called Mitochondrial Eve. That is, would be rather uninteresting since everyone would be related to everyone else. This is one case where modern science agrees with the accounts in the Torah, the Quran and the Christian Old Testament, although the timescales are rather different!

More fundamentally, modern medical science enables babies to incorporate genetic material from more than two parents, which complicates matters. Also, DNA mutates over time, so it may not always be true that women in an equivalence class under will always share the same mitochondrial DNA, and similarly not all men in the same equivalence class under will share the same Y chromosome, although in both cases the differences within a class will almost certainly be very small. Indeed, if mutations didn’t happen, then we would all have the same mitochondrial DNA, given the (past) existence of Mitochondrial Eve.

To wrap things up, the above analysis suggests that proving that (or ) is an equivalence relation reveals some non-obvious facts about familial relationships. It turns out that equivalence relations crop up in most unexpected places, and Theorem 2.1 is therefore a very useful tool which tells us interesting things in many different contexts.

2.7 Functions

I suspect you already have an informal idea of what a function is, but I want to briefly put the idea into the more formal context of sets. For example, I’m sure you will have encountered examples of functions, such as the trigonometric functions sin and cos, but perhaps you have never seen a formal definition in terms of sets.

If and are sets, then a function that maps from to (written ) is a rule which, given any element , specifies a unique element , and we write . We call the image of under ; conversely, we call the pre-image of under . Also, if then we call the domain of and the codomain of . The range of is a subset of the codomain , defined to be all the elements of for which there is an such that . That is, the range is the set of elements in which are mapped to by at least one element in .

2.8 Operations

I will conclude this rather abstract chapter by introducing the key notion of an operation on pairs of elements of a set. In fact, we are all very familiar with some important operations on numbers, such as addition and multiplication. The abstract notion of an operation generalises these ideas.

Formally, I define an operation to be a process that takes any pair of elements of a set (not necessarily distinct) and gives as output an element of the set. So if is an operation on the set then, for any pair of elements and in (where may be the same as ), is an element of .

So what might be examples of operations, apart from addition and multiplication of course? The not so helpful answer is—almost anything! Two obvious examples applying to numbers are subtraction and division, and another is exponentiation, where the first number is raised to the power of the second number.

As I will discuss in later chapters, there are some key properties I would like an operation to satisfy in order for it to be ‘interesting’. These key properties are typically properties that some (or all) well-known operations have. We can then start to establish results about operations which satisfy certain key sets of properties, and these results will then apply no matter what the operation is, as long as it possesses the necessary set of properties. This is another example of the power of abstraction and generalisation.

Throughout the discussion below, I assume that is an operation on the set , that is, for every , there is a defined .

  1. The first example of a key property is that there is an element in the set called an identity element, often written as . An identity element has the property that if it is combined with any element of the set then the output is that element (i.e. it has no effect). Formally, is an identity element if and only if:

    Zero (0) is an obvious example of an identity element when the set is the integers, i.e. , and the operation is addition (+). Zero is an identity element in this case because for any integer . Another obvious example for the integers would be when the operation is multiplication; in this case 1 (one) is an identity element, because for any integer .

    If you think for a moment about the subtraction operation on the integers, then 0 only partly fits the definition of identity element. This is because while for every integer , as we would hope, , and unless . That is, for the subtraction operation on the integers, 0 is an example of a right identity, and an element is only a true identity element if it is a right identity and a left identity, where left identity is defined in the obvious way.

    What about division? Well, division is not an operation on the integers according to the definition we have given, because dividing an integer by any integer other than +1 or −1 does not result in an integer, so it doesn’t work (in this case the operation is said to be ‘not well-defined’). Remember that an operation must always give a result within the set it is defined on. Indeed there is another problem with division since, even when we work with fractions, dividing by 0 is undefined.

    Finally, it is important to note that an identity element, if it exists, will always be unique. This can be shown using the following simple argument. Suppose and are identity elements for an operation on a set . I need to show that this means that . Now since is an identity element . But since is also an identity element . So , and I have established uniqueness.

  2. A related property is the existence of an inverse for every element. Suppose is an identity element for the operation on . If is any element of , and then is called a right inverse of . Similarly, if then is called a left inverse of . We are typically interested in the case where every element has both a right and a left inverse and they are equal.

    An obvious example again involves addition and the integers. Every integer has an inverse under addition, namely the negative of the integer (recalling that the negative of a negative number is positive). So 3 + (− 3) = 0 and (−7) + (− (−7)) = (−7) + 7 = 0. However, when we look at the integers with the operation multiplication, no element has an inverse except for +1 and −1. Of course, if we allow fractions then the situation is different, but we are getting ahead of ourselves.

  3. The third important property is a little less obvious and is known as associativity. In essence, associativity means we can move or remove brackets without affecting the result. Formally, an operation on is said to be associative if and only if, for any elements , and in (not necessarily distinct):

    Yet again addition and multiplication over the integers have this property. However, subtraction does not, as (6 − 3) − 2 = 3 − 2 = 1 is not equal to 6 − (3 − 2) = 6 − 1 = 5.

  4. The final property we introduce here is known as commutativity. An operation is commutative if the order of the elements does not matter. That is, put formally, an operation on is said to be commutative if and only if, for any elements and in (not necessarily distinct):

    Unsurprisingly, addition and multiplication over the integers have this property, but again subtraction does not, as 3 − 2 = 1, which is not equal to 2 − 3 = − 1.

    You might be tempted to speculate that, since associativity and commutativity both deal with the ordering of operations, one might imply the other. However, this is most definitely not the case; that is, it is possible to define an operation that is associative but not commutative and also to define one that is commutative but not associative.

    There are many other possible properties of operations that I could have described, but the ones I have just introduced are some of the most important for the discussions in later chapters of this book. I will be particularly interested in the case where an operation has the first three of the four properties above, which will give an example of what is known as a group. Indeed, groups are so important that they are a topic for a chapter of their own (Chapter 5).

An opaque bag contains two balls, which may be white or black—each with a probability of 1/2 (or 50%). However, the obvious answer is wrong—the probability that the other ball is white is 1/2, i.e. 50%. Chapter 3
Numbers as We Know and Love Them

Die ganzen Zahlen hat der liebe Gott gemacht, alles andere ist Menschenwerk (God made the integers, all else is the work of man).

3.1 Where Does Mathematics Start?

The quote from Kronecker that starts this chapter is a surprisingly accurate summary of where mathematics starts. Over the last 200 years or so, and particularly during the 19th century, mathematicians have sought to rebuild all known mathematics from simple foundations in a rigorous way. That is, all of the mathematics you might remember from school, including the trigonometric functions like sine and cosine, logarithms, vectors, matrices, etc., have been rigorously developed from first principles. This means, in every case, starting from the fundamentals and proving that the functions exist and have the expected properties, without resorting to geometric arguments. This monumental effort gave a much firmer foundation to mathematics.

However, this rigorous development started from the integers. That is, the integers themselves form a fundamental building block on which rigorous mathematics has been built. Mathematicians would typically regard the definition of the integers as being part of the Foundations of Mathematics and not ‘regular mathematics’. Of course, there have also been efforts to build the integers from rigorous first principles, but such work is generally regarded by mathematicians as something that, while clearly important, constitutes a subject separate from ‘regular’ mathematics. Indeed, such work on the foundations of mathematics includes trying to analyse the very rules we use to build proofs and the various types of logic. By and large mathematicians take these concepts for granted. Of course, much more could be said about the nature of logic and mathematics, but doing so here would mean getting away from the main purpose of this book. I propose to follow the lead of other mathematicians and assume the integers are well-defined, as well as taking for granted certain fundamental properties of the integers.

At this point, you might reasonably ask, exactly what are the properties that I assume the integers possess? Well, to start, we assume that the integers have two associated operations: addition (+) and multiplication (×). Moreover, we assume that:

  • the addition operation satisfies all four of the properties listed in Section 2.8 (i.e. the existence of an identity (namely zero) and additive inverses, as well as the associative and commutative properties);
  • the multiplication operation satisfies three of the four properties listed in Section 2.8 (i.e. the existence of an identity (namely one), as well as the associative and commutative properties, but it does not possess multiplicative inverses except for +1 and −1);
  • multiplication distributes over addition, i.e. for any integers , and .

Of course, these are all properties we assume when doing any arithmetic on integers. We also assume that the integers are ordered, a topic we revisit in Section 3.4.

While the integers are not the main subject of this book, I nevertheless feel we need to start at the beginning and consider some of their key properties. The integers are also the basis of everything covered here, so it is worth spending a little while thinking about them. Given their importance as examples, at the end of the chapter I will also briefly introduce how we can build the rationals from the integers.

3.2 The Natural Numbers and the Integers

I really need to start with the natural numbers, that is, the whole numbers 1, 2, 3, …. The integers are simply the natural numbers extended to include negative numbers and zero, i.e. …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …. I already used the natural numbers and the integers as examples in Chapter 2. I should say at this point that some authors include zero in the natural numbers, but for the purposes of this book, I exclude zero from . Whilst discussing notation, I should also mention the sets and , the positive and negative integers, respectively. I’m sure you will immediately observe that and are the same set, at least as I have defined . Indeed, given the possible ambiguity regarding whether contains zero or not, I will mostly use from here on.

The idea of the natural numbers (or counting numbers) has been around for a very long time. At some point in prehistory, humans detached the idea of a number (three, say) from the existence of three objects of a particular kind. This involved recognising the idea of ‘three-ness’, so that three rabbits and three trees share this abstract notion of the number three. This fundamental idea was almost certainly reinvented many times, and no doubt it is something many of us rediscover for ourselves as infants. In any event, while much has been written about the development of the idea of counting numbers, in this book, I want to take them as something fundamental and immutable.

So what about the integers? Well, the idea that zero is a number (just like one, two, three, etc.), as opposed to simply being the absence of anything, is much more recent. Of course, using positional or place notation for numbers, i.e. writing 123 to mean one hundred plus two tens plus three, clearly requires some form of notation for zero, so that we can write 103 to mean one hundred, no tens and three; positional notation is discussed in a little more detail in Section 3.3. So does this mean that the invention of positional notation must have come after the idea of zero as a number?

Well, this is far from clear. Whilst various types of positional notation were invented in antiquity, it seems that the base 10 notation we use today originated in India, although other such systems were invented elsewhere, including in China. The positional notation came to Europe via the Arab world, who adopted position notation in Arabic numerals from around the 10th century c.e. This explains why—in English at least—the numerals we use today are known as Arabic numerals, even though they differ from the numerals used in Arabic!

So does this mean that zero was well-recognised as a number by the 10th century c.e.? Well, not necessarily, as early positional systems used a space or some other marker instead of the zero we would use today. I think it is fair to say that the adoption of zero as a number on an equal footing with 1, 2, 3, etc., is something that happened gradually.

Something similar appears to be true for the concept of negative numbers, i.e. −1, −2, −3, etc. That is, it is not unrealistic to say that in many cultures the natural numbers came first, then zero, and then the negative numbers. Of course, today we treat them all as part of the integers, and we call them all ‘numbers’, even though negative numbers can’t be used for counting things (despite the word number clearly originating in the notion of counting, as in the word ‘enumeration’).

Indeed, today we automatically use the word ‘number’ to cover many quantities which don’t directly relate to counting objects. For example, while I would call the fraction a number, it clearly isn’t useful for counting sheep—except perhaps in a butcher’s shop or in the meat section of a supermarket—but it is very useful for measuring things, for example, kg of butter. I intend to use the word ‘number’ in an even more general way to cover less familiar quantities, but nonetheless quantities which can be added or multiplied together and which may have an interpretation in real life. Indeed, this is the main purpose of this book.

Going back to the properties of operations we introduced in Chapter 2, zero has the benefit of providing an identity element for addition, and negative numbers provide inverses for the positive numbers under addition. That is to say that the operation of addition over the integers has all four of the properties we introduced, namely the existence of an identity element, the existence of inverses for all elements, associativity and commutativity.

3.3 Writing Down Numbers

In Section 3.2, I referred to the idea of positional or place notation. The version of place notation we all use is referred to as base 10 or decimal, since, working left from the rightmost digit of a number, the digits represent the number of ones, the number of tens, the number of hundreds, and so on. That is, successive digits represent multiples of successive powers of 10. So, for example, the number 4567 is equal to

Obviously the idea could be extended to work with any base, and not just 10. A particularly important alternative representation is base 2, or ‘binary’. In a binary representation of a number, successive digits represent multiples of 1, 2, 4, 8, …, i.e. successive powers of 2. The digits in a binary representation are either 0 or 1—and are referred to as bits as an abbreviation of binary digits. For example, the number 10110 in a binary representation is equal to 22 in the more familiar decimal representation. This follows since

Binary representations are fundamentally important in computing and digital electronics, since computer memory is made up of individual memory elements, each capable of storing a single bit, i.e. a single 0 or 1. As a result, computers store numbers using a binary representation. Analogously, digital communications typically involves sending sequences of zeros and ones.

Other widely used number bases include 8, where base 8 is referred to as octal, and 16, known as hexadecimal. In the latter case, we need six more digits to represent the numbers 10–15, and for this the letters a, b, c, d, e, f are almost always used, sometimes in upper case, where a = 10, b = 11, and so on. So, for example, the hexadecimal number fe equals in decimal. To avoid confusion, when using multiple bases, it is common practice to write the base as a subscript, so we could write .

3.4 Ordering the Integers

As I mentioned in Section 3.1, there are a number of properties of the integers that mathematicians take for granted in building mathematics. One is, of course, the fact discussed earlier that the addition operation has the four properties introduced in Chapter 2. Another key property is that the integers are totally ordered, i.e. given any two integers and , then either or (or both, in which case ). Moreover, if and , then . The ordering property also separates the integers into positive and negative values—the positive integers are those for which , and the negative integers are those for which (where simply means that and ). This ordering property is something we all take for granted; otherwise, how would we know which team was winning a football match?

The fact that the integers satisfy this ordering property underlies a widely used depiction of the integers on a ‘number line’, as shown in Figure 3.1. All the integers to the left of an integer are smaller than it, and all the integers to its right are larger.

A further assumed property of the integers is that both the sum and the product of two positive integers is also positive.

In fact, the ordering relationship between pairs of integers is just one example of a special type of relation called a partial ordering. If a set has a relation (usually written ) with the following three properties, then the pair is called a partially ordered set and is referred to as a partial ordering (on ):

  • for every (reflexivity);
  • if and for some , then (antisymmetry); and
  • if and for some , then (transitivity).

If you check back, you’ll see that the first and third properties are exactly the same as the first and third properties required of an equivalence relation. However, the second property has changed from symmetry to antisymmetry.

It should be clear that the integers and the relation, i.e. the pair (, ), form a partially ordered set. In fact, as I already mentioned, (, ) is an example of a totally ordered set, since for any two integers and , either or (or both, in which case ).

There are, of course, partial orderings which are not total orderings. A simple example is provided by the ordering on subsets of a set defined by the ‘subset’ relationship. It is not hard to see that this gives a partially ordered set. An example for the set is shown in Figure 3.2.

Another key property of the integers is that any subset of positive integers, i.e. , has a least element.

So, the property that every set of integers has a least element is perhaps not so obvious …. I should also say that I have glossed over one important point in these discussions. 3.5 Induction

This may seem like a digression from the topic of integers, but induction is a vital part of mathematics that depends on the least element property. Induction is a method for proving theorems. The principle of induction is simple to state.

Theorem 3.1

Suppose is a proposition (i.e. a claim of the truth of something) that is a function of the positive integer . If both:

  • is true for some positive integer , and
  • if is true, then this implies that is true for every ,

then is true for every .

Proof. I prove this important result by contradiction (i.e. using a reductio ad absurdum argument), so suppose is true for some positive integer and that is false for some . That is, suppose that , the set of all positive integers (with ) such that is false, is non-empty.

Now, is a set of positive integers and must therefore contain a least element, say, and since is in , it means that is false. Since is true (by the assumption of the theorem), it follows that . Next, observe that must be true, since and (the latter follows since and is the least element of ). But, since  is true, it follows that is true (by our second assumption), and hence we have a contradiction. Thus, is empty, and the theorem follows.

Sometimes the induction principle is stated in a slightly different way. That is, the statement of the second requirement is changed to:

if is true for every satisfying , then this implies that is true for every

The proof of the modified theorem works in exactly the same way.

For a very simple example of the use of induction, suppose the statement is:

We want to prove that is true for every .

From the principle of induction (i.e. Theorem 3.1), I need to show two things: (a) that is true and (b) that if is true, then is also true. To show (a), observe that is simply asserting that 1 = 12, and hence is clearly true. Now suppose is true, i.e. we know that:

So, we know that:

But and so we know that is true. So, from Theorem 3.1, we know that is true for every .

This is a rather trivial example, but induction can be used to prove much less obvious results, and it is an extremely useful tool in the mathematician’s locker. However, it must be used with care, as it is easy to go wrong. I will show this by giving a false proof of an obviously erroneous proposition.

Before doing so, I can’t resist mentioning that I don’t believe I am alone in feeling that proofs by induction are somehow aesthetically less pleasing than other types of proof. Why might this be? After all, isn’t a proof a proof, regardless of how it works? I am certainly not suggesting that proofs by induction are less valid than other types of proof; it is just that, in some cases at least, they do not shed much light on why the theorem is true. It is hard to justify this claim, and no doubt some mathematicians will think I am slightly crazy. However, I would certainly always prefer to prove something directly rather than by induction, I guess primarily for aesthetic reasons.

Anyway, back to the false proof. Suppose the statement is ‘Every group of people have the same name’. We want to prove that is true for every . We need to show that (a) is true, and (b) if is true, then is true. Now, is clearly true since one person clearly has the same name as themself. Now suppose is true, i.e. we know that any group of people always have the same name. Now consider any group of people, and suppose they line up in some order. We know that the first people have the same name (since is true) and also that the last people have the same name. Thus, all people must have the same name.

This is clearly a rather surprising result, and so there must be something wrong with the argument! See if you can spot the error. I have provided a short discussion of this in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section at the end of the book (see page 223).

I want to conclude this discussion of induction with a rather frivolous example—one that is well-known, at least in mathematical circles. But first, I want to mention an interesting piece of mathematical history. The number 1729 is sometimes known as the Ramanujan number (or the Hardy-Ramanujan number) because of a famous anecdote due to Godfrey Harold Hardy.

I remember once going to see him [Ramanujan] when he was ill at Putney. I had ridden in taxi cab No. 1729 and remarked that the number seemed to me rather a dull one, and that I hoped it was not an unfavourable omen. ‘No’, he replied, ‘it is a very interesting number; it is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways’.

This is often used as an example of the brilliance of Ramanujan. Whilst Ramanujan is not the subject of this chapter, I nevertheless want to explore the notion of a number being ‘interesting’, and contrariwise ‘not interesting’, a little further. I offer the following (somewhat tongue-in-cheek) proof that, in fact, all numbers are interesting, where by numbers I mean the positive integers. The proof relies on the fact that every set of positive integers has a least element, which is equivalent to the induction principle.

Let be the set of uninteresting numbers—we wish to show that is empty. Suppose the claim is not true, i.e. suppose there are some uninteresting numbers and so is non-empty. By the well-ordering principle, will contain a least element, say. That is, is the smallest uninteresting number. But this makes rather interesting, which is clearly a contradiction, and so must be empty.

Make of this what you will. Perhaps the most obvious problem with this argument is that I have not provided a rigorous definition of what ‘interesting’ means—without this the whole thing is rather meaningless. Nonetheless, this old chestnut has provoked much discussion over the last few decades—there is even a Wikipedia page devoted to it,

Before concluding, I can’t resist mentioning the Online Encyclopaedia of Integer Sequences

Why have I raised this here? Well, one way of deciding whether a number is interesting is whether it appears in an entry in the OEIS, and so we could define the smallest uninteresting number as the smallest integer not appearing in the OEIS. Of course, this is a moving target; as new sequences are added, so uninteresting numbers become interesting. Wikipedia
