3.7 Prime Numbers and Common Factors

I now want to spend a little time visiting a subject I hope you are all familiar with—the prime numbers (or just the primes). The prime numbers have been studied for thousands of years, as far as I am aware purely for reasons of curiosity, although mysticism and religion may also have been involved. However, before trying to define what a prime is, I need to introduce the notion of divisibility.

If and are positive integers and there is a positive integer with the property that , then we say that is a divisor or factor of (and is a multiple of ). We also sometimes write ‘ divides ’ and use the shorthand notation to mean that is a divisor of . So, for example, , so both 2 and 3 are divisors of 6, and we can write and .

We can now define what a prime number is. A prime number is a positive integer greater than one with the property that its only divisors are one and itself. Obviously, every positive integer has divisors 1 and since , and a prime number has no factors apart from these. The first few primes are:

You might be slightly surprised to see that I have excluded one from the list of primes. In the past, it was not uncommon to include one as a prime number but, because of its very special properties, the consensus over the last 100 years or so has been to exclude one from the list of primes. It is common practice to refer to any positive integer greater than 1 that is not prime as a composite.

Over the last 3000 years the study of prime numbers has given rise to a vast amount of new mathematics. However, it was not until the second half of the 20th century that prime numbers and their properties began to have an impact on the real world—apart, perhaps, via mysticism. I won’t spend a lot of time discussing the properties of prime numbers here, but I can’t resist mentioning one key fact known to the ancient Greeks (and written about by Euclid), namely that there are infinitely many primes. Proving this is actually quite straightforward, and I include a proof in Chapter 9.

3.8 Unique Factorisation

Having introduced prime numbers in Section 3.7, I feel obliged to introduce a result I suspect many of you know already, namely that any integer can be represented uniquely as a product of prime numbers, although the order of the prime numbers can vary. This result goes back to Euclid and is implicit in a result stated in Euclid’s ‘Elements’, written in the 3rd century B.C.E.

It can be stated as follows.

Theorem 3.3 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic)

Every positive integer (except the number 1) can be represented in exactly one way, apart from rearrangement, as a product of one or more primes.

This theorem is also known as the unique factorisation theorem.

3.9 The Euclidean Algorithm

I now want to introduce the first algorithm in this book. Before going into detail, I need to explain what an algorithm is. For my purposes, an algorithm can be thought of as a precisely defined sequence of steps to be followed to perform a particular calculation or to solve a problem. An entire major branch of Computer Science is dedicated to finding efficient algorithms to solve commonly occurring computational problems so that these algorithms can be coded up in computer software.

The Euclidean algorithm is, as its name suggests, an algorithm dating back to the ancient Greeks and was described by Euclid. It can be used to compute the greatest common divisor of any pair of positive integers in a very efficient way.

Fortunately, the Euclidean Algorithm is very efficient, and the number of iterations is bounded above by a constant factor times the number of digits in . This result was established independently in 1969/1970 by German mathematician Hans Arnold Heilbronn and Canadian mathematician John D Dixon. More recently, in 1998, French mathematician and computer scientist Brigitte Vallée formally established a comparable result for an efficient version of the algorithm known as the binary Euclidean algorithm. Just because an algorithm is ‘old’ doesn’t mean that there aren’t new things to discover about it!

Whilst they are not one of the main subjects of the book, one reason for discussing the rationals is that they are a very useful example of some of the algebraic structures I will introduce in later chapters. They are also a ‘natural’ extension of the integers. What do I mean by that?

As I have discussed, the integers under the addition operation satisfy all four of the properties introduced in Section 2.8, namely the existence of an identity element (zero), the existence of an inverse for every element ( is the inverse of ), associativity (moving brackets does not change the result), and commutativity . However, what about multiplication? It too has an identity element (1, since for every non-zero ), is associative (since for every , and ) and is commutative (since for every and ). However, apart from +1 and −1, no integers have an inverse under multiplication.

If I want to add multiplicative inverses to the integers, then I will end up with all the rationals. To see this, suppose is a set containing the integers, where is closed under multiplication (i.e. the product of two elements of is an element of ), and every element apart from zero has an inverse. But I required to be closed under multiplication, so must be an element of for every integer and every non-zero integer . That is, must contain .

So, the rationals have the nice property that the elements of have all four of the properties listed in Section 2.8 for both the addition and the multiplication operations.

It is sometimes helpful to think about the number line, a straight line on which all the integers and rationals are located. Figure 3.3 gives a very simple picture of the number line with the integers on it.

I could carry on indefinitely, showing figures like this for ever-decreasing sections of the number line, and in every case, I could still find as many fractions as I like to show in the figure. That is, the rationals are dense on the number line. If I choose any two fractions, no matter how close together, I can find another fraction, in fact, an infinite number of them, to fit between these two fractions.

So, given that the number line is densely packed with rationals, surely that’s it? Surely we can’t find any more numbers to fit in? This leads neatly to a discussion of the real numbers ….

So, 2 is a divisor of both and . But I assumed that was in its lowest terms, and this is a contradiction. So, I have shown that is not a rational. In fact, the same is true for for any integer that is not a square. But it seems reasonable that lies on the number line, because you can quickly work out roughly where it lies; it is approximately 1.4142, so it clearly lies between the fractions and —and it would be straightforward to continue to get better approximations. However, no matter how hard I try, and I can get as close as I like, I can never find a fraction that actually equals . As a result, is said to be irrational because it is not a rational.

Finding solutions to equations like or is not the only problem. You are probably familiar with the value known as , which equals the ratio between the length of the circumference and the diameter of a circle. The value is also irrational, although this was only shown in the 18th century by Swiss-French mathematician Johann Lambert. Indeed, finding a ratio equal to was a problem known to ancient Greek mathematicians, and it closely relates to the geometric problem of squaring the circle. To ‘square the circle’ would involve constructing a square with the same area as a particular circle, using only a finite number of steps involving a compass and a straight edge. Squaring the circle is impossible, although this hasn’t stopped people from trying!

The problem posed by the irrationals is solved by the so-called real numbers, commonly written as , which can best be thought of as including every possible value on the number line—including, of course, the rationals. Whilst the real numbers had been widely used for a long time, it wasn’t until the 19th century that mathematicians were able to formally define the reals using the rationals. This was a huge achievement, but sadly I would need the rest of this book to explain in full detail how it can be done. I can only refer you to a book on real analysis for an explanation—although, be warned, it is not at all straightforward.

The sets of integers, rationals and real numbers are clearly all infinite in cardinality (or size). However, it can be shown that the cardinality of the set of reals is somehow larger than the cardinality of the set of integers, so there is more than one kind of infinity. This surprising result is way beyond the main scope of this book, but I briefly explore it in Section 9.2.

Before concluding the chapter, I want to very briefly mention the complex numbers. I already mentioned that an obvious omission from the rationals are the solutions to quadratic equations such as , and this gap is solved by creating the reals which do contain solutions to this equation (there are actually two solutions, one positive and one negative). However, there remain equations of this type which do not have solutions in the reals. An obvious simple example is the equation . This clearly cannot have a solution in the reals since for any real number . The complex numbers are created by adding a new number to the reals, namely the solution to this equation. This number, usually labelled , has the property that . If is added to the reals, along with all the other numbers necessary to ensure that the result is closed under addition and multiplication, then this results in the complex numbers, usually written , and these complex numbers open up a whole new world of mathematical possibilities. However, I will leave it there, as I have other things to discuss!

Ultimately there is a lot more to ‘regular’ numbers than meets the eye! For the rest of this book, I want to look at different types of numbers which are in many ways much easier to handle than rationals, real and complex numbers, but have rather different properties. It also turns out that they have a host of important applications in the world of digital information communications and processing.

3.12 Applying Complex Numbers—An Everyday Example

Before moving on, I will briefly introduce an important application of complex numbers in electrical engineering. This sort of application very much falls into the category of ‘traditional applied mathematics’ and hence is not typical of the applications in the rest of this book. Nonetheless, it helps to illustrate why somewhat bizarre concepts, that seem only of interest to mathematicians, turn out to be vitally important for the real world.

Electrical circuits are very commonly built to make use of Alternating Current (AC); indeed, domestic electrical supplies all use AC. In an AC system, the polarity of the electrical current changes regularly; for example, in the United Kingdom and most of Europe, the electrical current switches polarity at 50 cycles per second. When analysing the behaviour of electrical systems using AC, it is most convenient to model current using complex numbers.

In particular, voltages and currents can be expressed as functions of complex numbers. If the voltage is written as a function of the time , then we have:

This representation can make circuit-related calculations much simpler.

More generally, complex numbers have applications in signal processing and control systems analysis, making a range of computational tasks simpler and more efficient.

Chapter 4
Modular Arithmetic on the Integers

Mathematics is the queen of the sciences.

4.1 Working Relative to a Modulus

The idea of modular arithmetic was first developed by Gauss, one of the all-time greats of mathematics, whose quote starts this chapter. I will start by giving a rather informal introduction to modular arithmetic, before giving a more formal version.

Modular arithmetic works on a subset of the integers, relative to a specific positive integer known as the modulus. When numbers reach the modulus they go back to the beginning. It is like the numbers on a clock—on a typical clock face you will find the numbers 1 up to 12. One hour after 12 o’clock is not 13 o’clock—instead it is one o’clock. That is, the hours on a clock face work modulo 12. Indeed, modular arithmetic is sometimes informally known as clock arithmetic. In modular arithmetic, instead of a number line there is a number circle, just like the face of a clock. The number circle when working modulo 6 is shown in Figure 4.1.

Apart from the hours in a (half) day, the other ways we measure time also use modular arithmetic (apart from years). Seconds and minutes run from 0 to 59, and then go back to 0, that is, they work modulo 60. Days of the week work modulo 7, although we use seven different names rather than numbers. Time is not the only example where we use modular arithmetic.

For example, degrees on a compass work modulo 360.

So if we are, for example, working modulo 6, we would count as follows:

Again working modulo 6, if we add 3 and 5 we get 2, and not 8 as we would if working in the integers!

It turns out that modular arithmetic has a very wide range of applications, as well as being interesting mathematically, as we will see.

4.3 Parity Checks: Using Modulo 2 Arithmetic

The first and perhaps simplest example of the application of modular arithmetic is in calculating check digits. What is a check digit, I hear you ask?

Check digits are used in many contexts, but in all cases it amounts to protecting against accidental errors when entering or managing numbers which have a special meaning. For example, I imagine that all of us, no matter where we are from, have a wide range of numbers that identify us, our possessions or other objects in some way. Obvious examples include credit card numbers, phone numbers, membership numbers, serial numbers, model numbers, postal codes or (in the United Kingdom) National Insurance numbers. Such identification numbers

When entering such numbers there is always the possibility of making an error, e.g. by entering an incorrect digit, and the consequences can potentially be very serious. The idea is to add one or more check digits to a number to enable the recipient of the number to check whether or not it is valid, and thereby reduce the chance of an incorrect number being accepted. If, for example, the number specifies a bank account that is to receive a large deposit, I’m sure you can see the importance of trying to ensure the number is right.

Perhaps the simplest example of a check digit applies to numbers consisting of purely zeros and ones, when we are working in . In , addition is simple:

For convenience we often simplify the notation and leave out the and write

Computers store data as sequences of zeros and ones (or bits), arranged in bytes (8-bit blocks) and words; the length of a word will vary depending on the computer, but is typically 64 bits. A modern computer can store vast numbers of words of data, and there is always the possibility of a bit being changed in error.

To enable such accidental errors to be detected, it has been common practice to add an extra parity check bit to a byte or word, the presence of which is purely to detect errors. That is, instead of allocating 8 bits to store a byte, 9 bits will be used. The parity check bit for a byte (or word) can be computed as the modulo 2 sum of all the bits in the byte (or word). So, for example, if the bits of a byte are , then the parity bit is defined as:

As a result, it will always be the case that the modulo 2 sum of all the nine bits making up a byte and its associated parity check bit will be zero. This is known as even parity. This means that if a single-bit error occurs anywhere in the byte, including in the parity bit, i.e. if a one is changed to a zero or vice versa, the modulo 2 sum of the nine bits will give a one, indicating that an error has occurred. Of course, if two errors occur then the parity check will not detect this, but in most cases this is much less likely than a single-bit error. This means we can greatly reduce the probability of an undetected error in calculations.

Clearly, to make this work, every time a byte is changed then the parity bit will need to be changed as well, and every time the value of a byte is used the parity bit should be checked. However, this should be simple to arrange and can be built into the memory hardware.

As a simple example, consider the byte (11011100). Summing the bits we have:

So the check bit is 1, and so the byte with its added check bit now looks like (11011100 1). If we add the bits together again we get , i.e. the byte with added check bit has even parity, as desired.

Observe that the system would work equally well if the default parity is odd parity, i.e. if

In such a case the modulo 2 sum of all nine bits will always be one, and if the sum is ever zero then an error must have occurred.

4.4 Check Digits: A More Complex Example

The parity check example is a very simple one, and much more complex check digit systems can be devised, typically using modular arithmetic. Indeed, there is an international standard for the calculation of check digits: ISO/IEC 7064, entitled Check character systems.

The method, known as MOD 11-2, is (not surprisingly given the name) based on arithmetic modulo 11. MOD 11-2 is a technique for computing a single check digit for numeric strings, i.e. where the value to be protected against errors consists of a sequence of digits between 0 and 9. More formally, if the sequence of digits to be protected against error is then the check digit is computed so that the following equation holds:

Observe that the value is equal to one more than the length of the string of digits to be protected, and the digits are numbered in reverse order. These slightly odd choices were made by the original authors of the standard, and so I have stuck with them here to avoid confusion.

This apparently rather complicated formula is actually easy to compute in practice by processing one digit at a time in the following way. You may have noticed that while, by definition, , , …, are all digits in the range 0–9, is computed modulo 11 and hence may be any one of 0, 1, …, 9, 10. So what if ? This is solved by replacing 10 by X (the Roman numeral for 10), so the check digit at the end may be any one of 0, 1, …, 9, X.

I’ll next work through a simple example to show how it works. Suppose we need to calculate the check digit for the number ‘0749’, i.e. , , , and ; we need to calculate . Following the recipe above, we first put . Since , we then need to perform the following steps.

So why do we go to all this trouble to compute the check digit? After all, analogously to the parity check, we could simply have added all the digits working modulo 10 to obtain a check digit, and this would have enabled us to detect any single error. However, doing this would not enable us to detect if we had written the digits in the wrong order, since they would add up to exactly the same value. Performing this slightly more complex calculation means that any single numerical error, as well as any transposition of adjacent digits (as well as transposition of digits separated by a small number of other digits) will be detected by the check digit. That is, if any of these types of error occur then the check digit calculation will give the wrong result, and hence the error will be detected. This is especially useful, as—at least from personal experience—accidentally getting digits the wrong way round is a common error when writing or typing a long number.

You might reasonably ask why the particular calculations involved in the MOD 11-2 check digit calculation give these desirable properties. Well, I can assure you that this is no accident. Please see if you can think of why the calculation works the way it does. I have included a discussion of the properties of the MOD 11-2 system in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section at the end of the book (see page 225).

Because of its relative simplicity and effectiveness in catching errors, a slight variant of this method was used in the original 10-digit version of the International Standard Book Number (ISBN), known as ISBN-10, that was in use until 2007.

ISBN-13 check digits are slightly less effective at detecting errors than their ISBN-10 counterparts, and can miss a pair of transposed digits if the two digits differ by 5.

Many other numbering systems use modular arithmetic to calculate check digits. For example, the International Bank Account Number (IBAN) contains two check digits calculated working modulo 97. The method is one of these specified in ISO 7064. Indeed, I would strongly recommend any new numbering system to incorporate at least one check digit using an appropriate method from ISO 7064.

This very important function is highly honoured to be associated with two such great mathematicians!

4.7 Cryptography Ancient and Modern

Before giving this example I need to explain a little about modern cryptography and its use of keys. The history of cryptography goes back over 2000 years, and until the 20th century cryptography was synonymous with the study of designing (and breaking) ciphers, i.e. methods for concealing the content of a message, so that a message could be sent via an untrusted channel without fear that its content would be divulged. The sender of a message (or plaintext) encrypts it using a procedure known only to the intended recipient to obtain the ciphertext; the recipient then decrypts the ciphertext to reveal the original plaintext. The encrypted message, i.e. the ciphertext, should not reveal anything about the plaintext message except, perhaps, its length.

In practice this meant, and still means, that although the underlying method of encryption might be well known—perhaps instantiated in a mechanical device—the sender and receiver share a secret value which is used with the method of encryption to define how the encryption procedure works. This secret value is known as a key. In today’s very widespread commercial use of cryptography, the methods of encryption, known as encryption algorithms, are public—indeed, they are typically standardised. So the security of the encryption process rests on just two things: the robustness of the encryption algorithm against cryptanalysis, and the secrecy of the key. By cryptanalysis I mean ways of trying to decrypt the data without knowing the key in advance—typically cryptanalysis works by analysing the ciphertext to find the key, and then using this key to decrypt all the encrypted data.

One rather trivial method of cryptanalysis involves trying every possible key, a bit like trying to unlock a combination lock by trying every possible sequence of digits. To resist this method it is sufficient to ensure that there are enough keys so this approach cannot succeed in a feasible amount of time—modern encryption methods typically involve keys that are at least 128 bits long, i.e. so that there are keys, i.e. 34 followed by 37 zeros; a very large number indeed! Of course, there are many more sophisticated methods of cryptanalysis, depending on the nature of the encryption algorithm. However, my main interest here is in the keys.

The encryption scenario I have just described remained essentially unchanged for 2000 years or more until the 1970s. All that changed during that very long period of time were the methods of encryption, which became increasingly sophisticated (and eventually mechanised) to resist increasingly clever methods of cryptanalysis. Before proceeding note that every method of encryption also needs an associated method of decryption. Typically they work in a very similar way; moreover, conventionally, the same secret key is used for both encryption and decryption.

So what changed in the 1970s? In 1976, American cryptographers Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published the truly ground-breaking paper ‘New Directions in Cryptography’.

Of course, so far there is nothing revolutionary in the idea. After all, this model works for conventional encryption (also known as symmetric encryption), where the decryption key happens to be the same as the encryption key. However, they then hypothesised that a system could be designed where (a) generating new key pairs is easy, and (b) finding the decryption key even if you know the corresponding encryption key is very difficult. If we could design such a system then everyone could choose their own key pair and could publish their encryption key (hence the term public key encryption). So if I want to send you a secret message, I first look up your public encryption key (e.g. on the Internet) and then use it to encrypt this message. I can then send you the encrypted message through an insecure channel (e.g. I could just post it on a social media page) and you would be the only one who could decrypt it, since only you know your personal decryption key.

Diffie and Hellman also described a linked idea, which is today known as Diffie–Hellman key exchange. This is a method designed to enable two parties to agree on a shared secret value, e.g. for use as a secret key with a conventional encryption scheme. This is described in Chapter 5.

While the Diffie–Hellman paper described the properties of a public key encryption algorithm, they did not have an example to give.

However, one proposed method not only survived careful scrutiny but became very widely used. This method, known as RSA after the names of its inventors American cryptographer and computer scientist Ronald Linn Rivest, Israeli cryptographer Adi Shamir and American computer scientist Leonard M. Adleman, was published in 1978,

It was revealed some years later that the idea of public key cryptography (also known as asymmetric cryptography), as well as the RSA algorithm, had been developed independently and in secret in the early 1970s by cryptographers working at the the UK’s Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ). James Ellis came up with the idea of public key cryptography, and his colleague Clifford Cocks later came up with the RSA algorithm (although of course it was not called that then). However, it seems that the GCHQ cryptographers had no conception of how their discovery could have such a major impact on the commercial world of security, perhaps because their role was to protect government secrets and not to make the wider commercial world secure. This is just one case of where a great idea is developed quite independently by different individuals, or groups of individuals, at roughly the same time. Sometimes the world is ready for an idea, and it gets invented independently multiple times.

The reason I am giving all this preamble is because RSA is based on modular arithmetic. Indeed, the fact that it works is based on theorems from number theory dating back hundreds of years. In the remainder of this chapter, I will explore how it works, how it is used and how implementation issues it presents can be overcome.

4.8 RSA: How Does It Work?

RSA works in the following way. Anyone wishing to receive encrypted messages must first generate their key pair, made up of an encrypting key (to be made public) and a decrypting key (to be kept secret). They proceed in the following way, noting that part of the key is the modulus, i.e. a positive integer used in modular arithmetic calculations.

  1. They first need to decide on the length of the modulus—the longer the modulus the greater the security, but also the more difficult the calculations involved in encryption and decryption. A typical length for the modulus might be 700–800 decimal digits. We are dealing with very large numbers here!
  2. Next, two large prime numbers, and , must be chosen, where they have a roughly similar number of decimal digits and where this number is equal to half the chosen modulus length.
  3. The modulus for the key pair is then .

  4. They must next choose a pair of positive integers with the property that

    observing that from Lemma 4.1. Such a pair exists by Lemma 4.2 (observing that and must be coprime to ). There are a variety of ways to choose such a pair—one possibility is simply to choose at random subject to the constraint that , and then work out what the corresponding must be. Note that, however we choose and , they must both be coprime to , and hence they must both be odd.

  5. Finally, set the encryption key to be the pair , and set the decryption key to be the pair . The encryption key can now be published. However, the decryption key and the primes and must be kept secret.

The idea underlying RSA is that, even if you know the public key, i.e. the pair , then finding the value of is computationally infeasible as long as is sufficiently large. This difficulty is, in turn, based on the difficulty of finding the prime factors of a very large composite number.

To illustrate the process, a simple example may help. This example uses very small primes, just to show how keys are generated. Suppose that the primes and are chosen, so the modulus . It also follows that .

Of course, this example would be hopelessly insecure, since it is trivially easy to factorise 187 (just by trying all possible prime factors until 11 is found); it is then straightforward to compute from . Very much larger numbers are required in practice to make factorisation infeasible.

It is important to explain why it is not easy to work out the decryption key from the encryption key. The piece of information the generator of the key pair has that a potential third party doesn’t, is knowledge of the primes and . If you know and , then calculating from is relatively straightforward, as I discuss in Section 4.9. Without knowledge of and , this is computationally infeasible as long as the primes are large enough.

Why is this? Well, it turns out that, although it is not difficult to multiply two numbers together, even when they have something like 400 decimal digits each, trying to find the prime divisors of a very large number (the integer factorisation problem) is a very difficult problem. Indeed, with current computers and the best available methods, trying to find and from an 800-decimal-digit is something that would take hundreds of years—at least using currently available techniques. The current record for factorising the largest number of RSA type (i.e. a number that is the product of two large primes) is around 250 decimal digits.

Clearly the security of RSA rests on the difficulty of factoring . That is, if it is possible to factorise the modulus making up part of a public key, then it is possible to determine the private key corresponding to that public key, and hence decrypt any intercepted encrypted messages. I also pointed out that learning from and is just as difficult as factorising . So does this mean that breaking RSA has the same difficulty as factoring large numbers? The simple answer is: no one knows.

The problem comes because it might conceivably be possible to decrypt an encrypted message without knowing . This may seem unlikely, but no one has been able to show that decryption is impossible without knowing . As other authors have observed, today this question seems rather less important than it used to given that, if a suitably large scale general purpose quantum computer is ever built, then factorising large integers becomes straightforward and RSA will be immediately rendered insecure. This issue is discussed further in Chapter 5.

4.9 Using RSA

So far I have described RSA purely in the context of encryption. Indeed, under the heading of cryptography I have only discussed encryption. However, today cryptography embraces a larger collection of important security-related functions.

Encryption provides one very important security service, namely the protection of sensitive information against disclosure to unauthorised parties. However, there are other very important security services relating to data, namely protecting data integrity and data origin authentication. Data integrity protects data against unauthorised modifications, and origin authentication enables the recipient of data to verify where it comes from. For example, if you send a message to a bank asking for a sum of money to be transferred to a specific recipient, you are relying on the integrity of the message being preserved, so that the bank doesn’t transfer the wrong amount or perhaps the right amount to the wrong recipient. The bank is also relying on origin authentication, since it wants to be sure that it is a genuine instruction from you and not from an impostor.

These services can be provided using cryptographic methods. Indeed, in many cases it would seem that protecting integrity and verifying origin are even more important than confidentiality. In today’s Internet, these services are provided automatically using cryptography-based protocols such as Transport Layer Security (TLS).

One way of providing integrity protection is by using something called a digital signature. A digital signature scheme is another type of public key cryptographic method, that enables the sender of a message to compute a value called a digital signature; this digital signature is computed as a function of a message, and if sent with a message can be used to verify its origin and integrity. The idea is that every party wishing to generate digital signatures creates a special pair of keys: a key that can be made public used for checking signatures, and a key used for creating signatures that needs to be kept secret.

As Rivest, Shamir and Adleman described in their 1978 paper, the RSA algorithm can be used as a way of creating and verifying digital signatures. This makes RSA especially valuable, as it can be used for both encryption and creating digital signatures. Anyone wishing to create digital signatures using RSA generates an RSA key pair, just as I have already described. However, in this case the key pair is made up of a signing key (which is kept secret) and a verification key which can be made public, so that everyone can verify generated signatures.

In order to create and verify digital signatures, a special type of function called a cryptographic hash function is needed. These functions are designed using cryptographic principles, but do not use a key. A cryptographic hash function takes as input a string of bits of arbitrary length and outputs a fixed length string of bits (e.g. a block of 256 bits). It must satisfy the following properties:

  • it must be simple and fast to calculate the output, even for long inputs;
  • given a possible output, i.e. a string of bits of the appropriate length, it must be computationally infeasible
  • for a given input, it must be computationally infeasible to find a second input which maps to the same output;
  • it shall be computationally infeasible to find two inputs which give the same output (this is known as the ‘collision-resistance property’).

There are a number of well-known, well-accepted and internationally standardised hash functions, including a very widely used function known as SHA-256, part of the SHA family of hash functions

Creating a digital signature for a message , which is assumed to be a sequence of bits, then involves the following steps:

  • Apply an agreed cryptographic hash function to to obtain .
  • If the RSA signing key for the sender is , compute , where the string of bits is converted to an integer, e.g. by regarding it as the binary representation of a number.
  • The signature on the message is then simply , and the originator sends the pair as the signed message.

Verifying a signed message works in the following way.

  • If the RSA verification key for the sender is , compute .
  • Apply the agreed cryptographic hash function to to obtain .
  • If then the signature should be accepted; otherwise it should be rejected as invalid.

The descriptions I have given of using RSA for encryption and for digital signatures have been a little naive. In both cases, some data formatting is required before computing the exponential. In the case of encryption, this formatting needs to include the addition of some random bits, which can be discarded after decryption. This formatting and use of randomness is necessary to address certain possible attacks.

Over the last 30 years, RSA has been very widely used, although we are almost certainly now past ‘peak RSA’ (a topic we address at the end of this chapter). For example, RSA has been used to underlie security for chipcard-based credit and debit card transactions, as well as being commonly used to help set up secure TLS sessions between web browsers and web servers. RSA is used both for encryption and for creating digital signatures.

RSA encryption is primarily used for encrypting keys for more conventional encryption algorithms. This is because performing an RSA encryption is computationally complex, and RSA encryption is several orders of magnitude slower than encryption using a modern conventional algorithm. So, instead of encrypting a message directly with RSA, a one-time key for a conventional encryption algorithm is randomly generated and used to encrypt the message. This one-time key is then encrypted using RSA with the public key of the intended recipient, and the encrypted one-time key is sent with the encrypted message. The recipient can first decrypt the RSA-encrypted one-time key, and then use the one-time key to decrypt the message.

The complete set of operations needed to encrypt a key, including the formatting and adding of randomness, forms what is known as a Key Encapsulation Mechanism or KEM. There are a variety of well-established and standardised KEMs involving the use of RSA.

There is, unsurprisingly, much more that could be said about the use of RSA, but I hope I have given you enough to whet your appetite and convince you that number theory and modular arithmetic are actually useful—as well as a source of mathematical interest for the last two or three thousand years.

4.10 Implementing RSA

There are a number of steps in the process of generating keys and using RSA which I have stated without any hint of how they might actually be implemented, and I suspect you have already been questioning the feasibility of certain calculations. The following three functions are necessary to use RSA, but it is perhaps less obvious how to implement them. I will round off this chapter by briefly explaining that the apparently infeasible is actually feasible after all.

4.10.1 Choosing the Primes p and q

This might appear to be the most challenging part of all. I suspect that for many readers, the only way of determining whether a number is prime is by finding its prime factors, and we are assuming that the numbers involved are so large that this is infeasible! So how do we decide whether a number is prime? We use what is known as a primality test. We know that primes have certain special properties, so if we have a ‘candidate prime’, i.e. a number which we hope might be prime, we can check whether it possesses this property. If it doesn’t, it is not prime, and so we can choose another candidate. If, on the other hand, it does have the property then it may be prime, ideally with high probability. If we repeat this process a sufficient number of times, and the candidate passes every test, then we know the candidate is prime with very high probability—which is good enough for our purposes.

So what might we test? Well, from Fermat’s little theorem (Theorem 4.4) we know that, if is a prime, then for any integer . So, if is a candidate prime, we can choose a random and compute —if the result is not congruent to modulo then is definitely not prime—otherwise is prime with probability greater than 1/2, i.e. the probability it is composite is less than 1/2. So if this test is repeated with random values of and it passes, say, 20 times, then the probability it is not prime is less than which is less than 1 in a million.

In practice, we can use other more efficient tests which weed out non-primes with a much higher probability, so far fewer tests are needed to be almost certain the candidate is a prime. Also, there is a small flaw in the use of Fermat’s little theorem as a primality test. Some composite numbers (the so-called Carmichael Numbers

4.11 RSA and the Future

I previously mentioned that we are probably beyond ‘peak RSA’. Why is this? There are two main reasons.

First, and perhaps most important, there are other schemes for both digital signatures and for encryption that are more efficient, i.e. that require less complex computations. In particular, schemes based on discrete logarithms in finite groups (a topic for Chapter 5) have rather taken over. With a careful choice of group, not only can operations be made more efficient, but keys can be made smaller.

Second, I think we can expect to see RSA and discrete logarithm based schemes gradually being phased out over the next 10–20 years, because of the threat posed by quantum computing. As far as RSA is concerned, if a sufficiently large-scale quantum computer is built, it could be used to factorise numbers much larger than can be factorised with today’s computers; this would mean that RSA would be insecure for any practical choices of modulus lengths. This issue is discussed in greater detail in Chapter 5.

Of course, improving methods of factorisation have always posed a threat to the security of RSA. Indeed, the advent of RSA suddenly meant that finding computationally efficient methods for factorisation, previously a rather niche area of computational number theory, suddenly became a mainstream topic. This meant many more academics working on the problem, as well as greatly increased funding!

Since the late 1970s, the lengths of numbers that can be readily factorised have increased very significantly. In the early days, it was deemed secure to use an RSA modulus containing 100 decimal digits. However, during the 1990s and 2000s a series of ‘challenge numbers’ of increasing sizes, i.e. RSA moduli promulgated to test the ability of research workers to factorise numbers, were gradually factorised. A 110-digit number was factorised in 1992, a 120-digit number in 1993, a 140-digit number in 1999, a 150-digit number in 2004 and so on. A history of this work up to around 2010 can be found in a short paper by American cryptographer Burt Kaliski

Progress has been achieved for three main reasons: improved algorithms, more powerful and greater numbers of computers and more effective implementations. It is difficult to untangle the precise contributions made by each of these advances, but my personal impression is that more efficient implementation has been the most effective tool. Certainly the fastest algorithm for integers not having a special form, known as the number field sieve, has been known for decades.

4.12 Other Applications of Modular Arithmetic

I already mentioned that computers store data as binary digits or bits (zeros and ones) arranged in words, where a typical word length is 64 bits. These words can be used to store a variety of types of information. If they are used to store whole numbers then, when two words are added together and the result stored in another word, this result will typically be computed modulo . This is necessary as is the largest number whose binary representation can be stored in 64 bits. That is, computers do not really do integer arithmetic—instead they do modular arithmetic. If you need to process numbers larger than , then special software will need to be employed so that multiple words can be used to store the numbers you are working with.

Further applications of modular arithmetic are discussed in Chapter 5. However, before concluding this chapter, I want to mention one simple application you may already be familiar with, but that you may not have realised relates to modular arithmetic. I already talked in Chapter 3 about divisibility of integers; on occasion it is of interest to know whether a given number is a multiple of a small value, such as 2, 3 or 5. The key principle here is that a number is divisible by if and only if . This is the basis of all the following simple checking methods.

Checking divisibility by 2 is simple, since a number is divisible by 2 only if it is even, i.e. if it ends with 2, 4, 6, 8 or 0. The fact that we only need to check the final digit follows because 10 is a multiple of 2, i.e. because . If, for example, a three-digit number has the form , where is the number of hundreds, is the number of tens and is the final digit, then , and so is divisible by 2 if and only if is divisible by 2. The same would be true for a value with an arbitrarily large number of digits.

Checking divisibility by 5 works in exactly the same way. We only need to check whether the final digit is divisible by 5 since .

Extending this idea, since , it is possible to check a number for divisibility by 4 simply by checking the last two digits. So, for example, 12364 is divisible by 4 because 64 is divisible by 4. Moreover, since , a number is divisible by 8 if and only if the value made up of the final three digits is divisible by 8.

Every digit in the usual decimal representation of a number represents a multiple of for some (for example, the number , where as always . But for every . So, working modulo 10, we have , and the same is true for any number; that is the sum of the digits of a number is congruent to the number itself modulo 3. So if the sum of the digits is divisible by 3, then so is the number. In the example I just mentioned, , which is divisible by 3, so 456 is also divisible by 3.

Exactly the same trick works for checking divisibility by 9, since we have . That is, if you sum all the digits of a number, then the sum will be divisible by 9 if and only if the original number is divisible by 9.

Finally, there is a slightly more complicated trick for checking divisibility by 11. This involves observing that , , and so on. So if we are given a number, for example 23456, to check for divisibility by 11, you add up the even digits and subtract the sum of the odd digits , and in this case get . Clearly is not divisible by 11 and so neither is 23456. However, for 93456 we get , which is divisible by 11, and so 93456 is divisible by 11 (in fact ).

To check divisibility by 6 we can simply check for divisibility by 2 and 3, and to check for divisibility by 12 we can check for divisibility by 3 and 4. Putting together all these methods, we have a simple way of checking for divisibility by every number less than 13 except for 7. Chapter 5
Groups

It appears to me that if one wants to make progress in mathematics, one should study the masters and not the pupils.

5.1 What Is a Group?

Groups are one of the most important, and also one of the simplest, structures in abstract algebra. A group is defined to be a set with an operation * defined on which has the following three properties:

  • contains an identity element , i.e. an element with the property that for every ;
  • every element has an inverse in , i.e. an element with the property that ;
  • the operation ∗ is associative, i.e. for any , .

These are, of course, the first three of the possible properties for an operation I introduced back in Section 2.8. Some authors would also add a requirement for closure, i.e. requiring that for any , but for the purposes of this book this is guaranteed by the definition of an operation.

It is worth pointing out at this point that the identity element in a group is always unique (I proved this in Section 2.8). In a group, it is also the case that inverse elements are unique. To show this suppose and are both inverses of in the group . Consider the expression (I can omit brackets since the associative law holds). First note that . But it also follows that , and hence . In fact, we only used the associative law to establish this result, so in any structure where there is an identity element and the associative law holds (i.e. in a monoid—see below), if an element has an inverse element, then it must be unique.

It seems that French mathematician Évariste Galois was the first to use the word group (actually ‘groupe’ in French) in this context in 1830. However, he used the term to mean what we would today call a particular example of a group of permutations. The term was next used in a more general context by British mathematician Arthur Cayley in 1854.

Mathematicians use the term Group Theory to describe the body of results covering the existence and properties of groups. Group Theory has become a major branch of mathematics, with a very wide range of applications not only in other areas of mathematics but in a wide range of sciences and the real world. A few of these applications are explored later in this chapter. It might seem surprising that such a simple object has such a deep and complex theory, but one might very well say the same about the integers—they seem deceptively simple creatures, but number theory is a very major part of mathematics and has been the subject of study for thousands of years.

One question that might spring to mind is: ‘Why this collection of properties, and not any other?’ I should first say that this is not because other possibilities have been ignored; many other possible structures have been studied—some of them also have a range of applications. Examples include the following:

  • A magma (or groupoid), is a set with a binary operation defined on that set. No additional properties are assumed of the operation. So, a group can be thought of as a magma with the three additional properties listed earlier.
  • A semigroup is a set with a binary operation that is associative, i.e. a semigroup is a magma with an associative operation.
  • A monoid is a set with a binary operation that is associative, and where the set contains an identity element. So a monoid is a semigroup with an identity element, and a group is a monoid where every element has an inverse.
  • Finally, I should mention abelian groups.

    The only reason I can offer as to why groups have been so extensively studied—much more than other possibilities—is because the three defining properties give just the right amount of structure to make them interesting. Too little structure, and there are simply too many possibilities, many of which may be uninteresting (in a mathematical sense); too much structure, and there are not enough examples to study.

    Whilst on the subject of the defining properties of a group, you may have noticed that I required the identity element to be simultaneously right and left identities, and I also required inverse elements to be both right and left inverses. In fact, I could have made a slightly weaker assumption. That is, I could just have assumed that there is a right identity, i.e. an element such that for every element , and also that every element has a right inverse, so that for every there is a with the property that . The left identity and left inverse properties can then be shown to be true. Please see if you can show this.

    Finally, in the remainder of this book, I will be particularly interested in finite groups, that is groups with the property that the set of elements is finite. You will have noticed that I am using the term ‘order’ in connection with both an element of a group and the group itself, but I hope this will not cause confusion as the meaning should be clear from the context.

5.2 A First Example: The Integers

I suspect I am well past the point at which I should have provided you with an example of a group, so I’ll start by giving you perhaps the most obvious example of all, the integers with the addition operation.

You may have already realised that the integers with the operation +, i.e. , form a group. Indeed, I already pointed out in Section 2.8 that the integers under addition satisfy the three required properties of a group, namely that they possess an identity element (0), every integer has an inverse (namely ), and the associative law holds. The fact that this last property holds is one of the properties of the integers we simply assume as a basic building block of mathematics (as discussed in Section 3.1).

The group is actually an abelian group, since, as I’m sure you know, addition over the integers is commutative, i.e. for any integers and . Clearly the order of this group is infinite, as there are an infinite number of integers. The order of every element apart from zero is also infinite.

But what about the integers with other operations? Well, neither subtraction nor multiplication give a group, albeit for different reasons. The integers with the operation subtraction, i.e. , fail to form a group because subtraction is not associative. Multiplication, i.e. , also doesn’t work because, although there is an identity element (one), and multiplication is associative, there isn’t an inverse element except for the elements +1 and −1.

In order to make a multiplicative group, we need to expand the integers to the rationals . The rationals form an abelian group with addition, and also the non-zero rationals form an abelian group with multiplication. That is both and are abelian groups, where denoted the non-zero rationals.

5.3 A Second Example: Modular Addition

Having said that I am particularly interested in finite groups, it may seem a little odd that the first examples I gave were of infinite groups. However, the integers are undeniably important so it seemed a good place to start. Anyway, I now want to give an example of a finite group.

In Chapter 4, I introduced , the integers modulo . I suspect it comes as no surprise to learn that the integers modulo with addition, that is , form a group for any positive integer . The identity element is and the inverse of any element is simply . The fact that the addition operation + is associative follows immediately from the fact that + is associative over the integers.

You can also check there is an inverse element for every element since 0 appears in every row and every column. Finally, you can see that + is commutative, i.e. is an abelian group, because the table is symmetric about the leading diagonal, i.e. the diagonal running from top left to bottom right.

However, as far as I know, there is no easy way of checking whether an operation is associative, just by looking at the table.

The simple answer is ‘No’, but I leave it to you to think about for which values of it is true that every non-zero element is a generator of the group under addition.

In fact, the same argument shows that the group , i.e. the integers with +, is also cyclic. In this case, only +1 and −1 are generators. So there are both finite and infinite cyclic groups.

5.7 Examples of Non-abelian Groups

So far, all the examples of groups I have given have been abelian. However, in this section, I describe two important classes of examples of non-abelian groups.

Indeed, as far as finite groups are concerned, in many ways, the non-abelian groups are far more interesting. Why do I say this? Well, it turns out that the abelian finite groups are relatively straightforward to classify. By contrast, the non-abelian finite groups are hugely varied and difficult to classify, and attempts to understand their existence and behaviour has given rise to one of the major mathematical achievements of the second half of the 20th century, namely the classification of all finite simple groups. This is not something I want to explore further in this chapter, as it would entail introducing a lot more terminology, including defining what a simple group is, and take us away from my main goal. However, in Chapter 9, I briefly return to this topic.

5.7.1 Groups of Symmetries

One very important class of groups is made up of the groups containing the symmetries of regular objects. By a symmetry, I mean a transformation, typically a rotation or a reflection, which maps a shape onto itself. The example I will use is two-dimensional, but the study of three-dimensional symmetries is an important topic within crystallography.

Suppose the shape is an equilateral triangle. One type of symmetry involves rotating the triangle by 120∘. This is shown in Figure 5.1.

Corner moves from the top to the right, corner moves from right to left and corner moves to the top. If I repeat this rotation, I end up with corner to the left, corner at the top and corner to the right. If I repeat this for a third time, then I get back to where I started. So if this symmetry is called , then , where is the identity symmetry (i.e. nothing changes), and where simply means performing three times.

But I am sure you are aware that there is another symmetry of the triangle, involving reflections. The effect of reflection about the vertical axis is shown in Figure 5.2.

Here corner stays where it is, and corners and reverse positions. If this reflection is repeated, then the triangle goes back to its original position. So if I call this symmetry , then . One remaining question is, how do these symmetries interact? The effect of rotation followed by reflection about the vertical axis is shown in Figure 5.3.

To see why this occurs, consider the effect of rotation shown in Figure 5.1, and then rotation simply switches corners and . The next obvious question is—do symmetries commute? That is, is the same result obtained by reflecting first and then rotating? The simple answer is ‘No’. This is shown in Figure 5.4, where the result is clearly different to that in Figure 5.3.

To see why this occurs, consider the effect of reflection shown in Figure 5.2. A subsequent rotation moves to the bottom right hand corner, to the bottom left hand corner and to the top.

The collection of all the symmetries forms a group, where the operation * is simply composition of symmetries, i.e. if and are two symmetries, then is the result of first performing and then . In the case of an equilateral triangle, this group has six elements; a Cayley table for this group is given in Table 5.8. It is a non-abelian group since, as I just observed, a reflection followed by a rotation does not give the same result as a rotation followed by a reflection.

Examining the table it is simple to see that every element has an inverse, since appears in every row and column, and also it is non-abelian since it is not symmetric about the main diagonal.

It is also straightforward to see that this group has two (cyclic) subgroups:

  • the subgroup consisting of the three possible rotations, i.e. , where , a subgroup of order 3; and
  • the subgroup consisting of the two possible reflections, i.e. , where , a subgroup of order 2.

Since they are cyclic these two subgroups are abelian (see page 258). Indeed, the top left hand corner of the table in Table 5.8, is the Cayley Table for the subgroup , and it is symmetric.

Of course, the group of triangle symmetries is just the first of an infinite family of examples of symmetry groups, namely the groups of symmetries of the regular polygons. In general, the symmetry group for a regular -gon will contain elements, made up of rotations and ‘reflected rotations’. So the symmetry group of the square contains elements, the group for the regular pentagon has 10 elements, and so on.

Three-dimensional objects can have more complex symmetry groups. So, for example, the symmetry group for the cube has a subgroup of 24 elements just for rotations. To see this, observe that the cube can sit on any one of its six faces, and can then be oriented in one of four directions. Thus there are possible rotations of the cube. But I have ignored reflections, which means that the symmetry group of the cube has order . Of course, things get even more complex for four or more dimensions, which I must admit I find impossible to visualise!

To complete this discussion of symmetry groups, observe that symmetries arise in a wide variety of mathematical objects, not just geometrical ones. These symmetries relate to the notions of isomorphisms and automorphisms, topics I explore further later in this chapter.

5.8 When Are Two Groups the Same Group?

There are many different groups, but some of them are the same. But what do I mean by this rather odd statement? Of course, it all depends on what I mean by the phrase ‘the same’.

In life we often attach a variety of different labels to the same thing. So, for example, if you speak French and want to refer to the first few positive whole numbers you might say ‘un, deux, trois, quatre’ instead of the ‘one, two, three, four’ that I would use as an English speaker; more generally, every language will have its own names for the whole numbers. Nonetheless, I think most people would agree that the numbers themselves are the same no matter what we choose to call them.

Equally, instead of the ‘arabic’ digits used in English and many other European languages, if you live in an Arabic-speaking nation you probably write numbers using the Arabic digits . Again, I think most people would agree that, despite the use of different symbols, the meaning is the same.

So how is this relevant to groups (or any other mathematical object, for that matter)? Well, consider the following three examples of groups, all of which have three elements (i.e. they all have order three).

To give this idea of ‘sameness’ a firm foundation I introduce the notion of an isomorphism between groups. An isomorphism is simply a mapping from one group to another that preserves the way group elements interact with one another. In essence, there is an isomorphism between two groups if and only if they have the same Cayley Table. A formal definition is as follows.

As above, I leave showing that satisfies the third condition for an isomorphism as an exercise.

Finally, I need to briefly mention the notion of an automorphism. An automorphism is simply an isomorphism that maps a group onto itself. A trivial example of an automorphism is, of course, the identity mapping. However, a group may well possess other automorphisms. For example, consider the group of the rotation symmetries of an equilateral triangle, with Cayley Table given in Table 5.10. Then the mapping defined as follows is an automorphism of :

To see why this holds, think about what and represent. The group element corresponds to a clockwise rotation of the triangle by 120∘, and is an anticlockwise rotation by 120∘. So if you imagine the triangle being written on a window then, depending on which side of the window you are looking at, and perform exactly the same operation. So it is hardly surprising that the groups and are in some sense the same.

Of course, in general the automorphisms of a group are not so easy to identify. However, the set of automorphisms of a group have a very important property—they themselves form a group! The group of automorphisms itself reveals properties of the underlying group; indeed, one way of showing that two groups are not isomorphic is by showing they have different automorphism groups.

It is helpful to think of automorphisms as being a kind of symmetry; indeed, the symmetries of a geometrical shape, such as the triangle used in examples earlier in this chapter, are essentially a type of automorphism. The rotations and reflections are ways of mapping the shape to itself which preserve all the properties of the shape.

5.9 Combining Groups

The basic method relies on the cartesian product of sets, introduced way back in Section 2.3.

5.10 Discrete Logarithms

I now want to introduce a key application of groups in the world of IT and secure communications. This application involves something called discrete logarithms, i.e. logarithms computed within a finite cyclic group.

I hope you can recall what a logarithm is, perhaps from mathematics at school. The underlying idea is that, given a real number called the base, every positive real number can be represented as a power of .

So, for example, if the base is 2, then there are the whole number powers, e.g. , , , , , and so on. It is also possible to use powers of 2 that are not whole numbers so that, for example, . Ultimately, every positive real number can be represented as for some real number .

The power that is needed to obtain a particular result is called the logarithm of to the base , and we write for this value. That is . Hence, for example, if then , and , because , and , respectively.

Before electronic calculators became ubiquitous, and they were in turn replaced by calculator apps on phones and PCs, tables of logarithms (so called log tables) were an invaluable aid when performing numerical calculations; these tables made it possible to quickly find for any number . Amongst other things, logarithms could be used to quickly evaluate the product of any two numbers. If I wanted to compute the product of and , I would use the tables to find and . I would then compute the sum of the two logarithms, i.e. —something easy to do with pen and paper. I would then use the tables again in reverse to find the number which had logarithm , i.e.

Then equals , since . Of course, I don’t suppose that today most people even know what log tables are, but they were extremely widely used, as were slide rules, which were a kind of physical analogue of log tables.

Anyway, discrete logarithms work in the same general way, but have a very different application. Suppose is a finite cyclic group of order . That is contains an element of order that generates , i.e. every element of is equal to for some . Then, if , the discrete logarithm of with respect to the generator , which is written as , is the unique positive integer with the properties that and (where, as previously, , the identity element of the group). The fact that exists and is unique follows from the arguments used in proving Lemma 5.3.

So, if you know the discrete logarithm of an element of , it is typically straightforward to calculate the element itself. This is because, if is the discrete logarithm of , i.e. , then by definition we know that . So as long as we can compute for group elements and reasonably efficiently, we can compute for very large values of using, for example, the square and multiply technique described in Section 4.10.3.

However, finding the discrete logarithm of a group element may be very much harder. How hard will very much depend on the representation of the group. I already said that is a finite cyclic group, so what else needs to be defined? After all, there is only one finite cyclic group of any particular order, since all cyclic groups of order are isomorphic.

Nonetheless, just because two groups are isomorphic does not mean that doing calculations within them is equally easy. This is, at first sight at least, a surprising claim, but it is nonetheless a claim on which the security of much of our Internet traffic depends! I will try to explain this using a simple example.

Let be the group of rotational symmetries of a regular polygon with sides (an -gon) for some very large —for argument’s sake suppose has 1000 decimal digits. There are rotational symmetries of an -gon. Let be a clockwise rotation by , and it is easy to see that is a generator of the cyclic group of order containing all the rotational symmetries. A group element consists of a clockwise rotation by . That is, for any group element it is easy to work out its discrete logarithm with respect to simply by dividing the angle of rotation by 360 and multiplying by , and the answer will be . So in this case computing discrete logarithms is very simple.

However, now consider the group where is a prime. As I described in Section 5.4, is cyclic when is a prime. Certain cyclic subgroups of this group are believed to have the property that exponentiating is straightforward but finding discrete logarithms is computationally infeasible, as long as we choose the prime to be large enough. Here, large enough means a number of approaching 1000 decimal digits.

Why is it hard? Consider the following small example. Suppose , a prime; then 3 is a generator of the group . That is, as ranges over the values from 1 up to 30, will cover every possible non-zero element modulo 31. For example, it happens that , and so the discrete logarithm of 17 to the base 3 (when working mod 31) is 7. Checking this is true is straightforward—you can just compute . But if I hadn’t told you the answer, how would you know what the discrete logarithm of 17 is? You could try computing successive powers of 3 until you obtain 17, which is possible in this small example, but you can see that this approach would rapidly become infeasibly time-consuming once the modulus gets large. In fact in this group there are more effective ways of computing discrete logarithms than just working through every possibility, but once the problem gets large enough even these more effective methods become infeasibly complex.

So, for some representations of a cyclic group, exponentiating is easy but computing a discrete logarithm is very difficult. Examples of such groups are of key importance for implementing cryptosystems, as I will describe in the remainder of this chapter.

5.11 Diffie–Hellman Key Agreement

The Diffie–Hellman key agreement scheme was originally described by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in their landmark 1976 paper ‘New Directions in Cryptography’, which also contained their description of the concept of public key cryptography (see Section 4.7). The scheme is designed to enable two parties to agree on a secret key value without revealing it to anyone else, and without the two parties having any pre-agreed secrets.

Before using the scheme, the two parties, and say, need to agree on a particular finite cyclic group and a generator for that group, which we suppose has order . This group and generator could be choices that are very widely used and agreed—or even standardised. and must possess two key properties:

  • it must be straightforward to compute for any integer ;
  • it must be computationally infeasible, given an arbitrary group element , to find an integer such that ; that is computing discrete logarithms with respect to must be very difficult.

Note that the term computationally infeasible is key. Given unlimited time and unlimited computing power it will always be possible to find the discrete logarithm of any group element. To see this, suppose it is desired to find the discrete logarithm of . Then, if the base for discrete logarithms is , you can compute , , and so on until the result is ; then, if , you immediately know that is the desired discrete logarithm. Thus, instead of requiring finding a discrete logarithm to be impossible, we require it to take an infeasibly large amount of time and computing resource. Indeed, this type of assumption about computational feasibility underlies almost all real world cryptography.

The scheme works in the following way.

  1. chooses a random positive integer , where , computes the group element , stores privately, and sends to .
  2. chooses a random positive integer , where , computes the group element , stores privately, and sends to . This step could take place after receives from or it could occur in parallel.
  3. uses the value received from along with its stored value of to compute .
  4. uses the value received from along with its stored value of to compute .

That is, at the end of the process both and have agreed on a group element , which was never sent between them. Indeed, neither party actually chose this element.

The protocol is shown diagrammatically in Figure 5.5.

The scheme is usable as long as computing an exponentiation in the group can be done efficiently. But what about security? Any party intercepting communications between and will learn and . The question is—can these two pieces of information be used to determine in a feasible way? Of course, if it’s possible to learn the discrete logarithm of a group element, then clearly the scheme is not secure, since it will be possible to learn from , and this can then be used to compute (from knowledge of ). However, we assumed that computing discrete logarithms is computationally infeasible. So the key question is: are there any other ways of determining from and .

The simple answer is that no-one knows. It is widely assumed that this problem, known as the Diffie–Hellman Problem or DHP, is about as hard as finding discrete logarithms, and for certain special cases it has been shown to be true. Using the language of computational complexity, a branch of computer science concerned with studying the difficulty of computational problems, we require that the Computational Diffie–Hellman (CDH) assumption holds for the group . The CDH assumption for a group simply asserts that determining from and is computationally difficult.

At this point, although not strictly relevant, I feel I must mention that the Diffie–Hellman key agreement scheme in some ways resembles an old idea for sending secret data between two parties that relies on padlocks. The idea goes as follows. Suppose wants to send a secret message. writes it down and inserts it into an (impregnable) briefcase which is then secured using a padlock to which only has the key. sends the briefcase to . now adds a second padlock to which only has the key and sends it back to . On receipt removes their padlock and sends the case back to . Finally, can remove their padlock, open the briefcase and read the message. At no time is the briefcase sent between and without at least one padlock attached. This is a very neat idea—sadly I have no idea where it originated. It’s not terribly practical as I don’t believe anyone has yet invented an impregnable briefcase. Additionally, the scheme suffers from the same authentication problem as Diffie–Hellman, something we discuss below.

Anyway, back to the main topic. So what group might we use to implement Diffie–Hellman? In practice we need to choose both the nature of the group and the size of the group (typically, the larger the group, the harder the computational problem becomes).

For many years the group of choice was a subgroup of the multiplicative group of the integers modulo a large prime number , i.e. a subgroup of , discussed in Section 5.4. Indeed, Theorem 5.1 given there states that is cyclic, so we could, in principle, choose a generator of this group. However, there are good security reasons for wanting the cyclic group we use for Diffie–Hellman to have prime order, and has order , which must be even and hence cannot be prime. So instead it is common practice to use a cyclic subgroup of with order a prime factor of .

One way of achieving this is to choose the prime to have the property that for another prime . Then will have order . Since is a divisor of the order of the group , by Cauchy’s theorem (Theorem 5.3) the group contains an element of order , say, and hence there is a cyclic subgroup of order . It has long been common practice to implement Diffie–Hellman schemes using a generator of this form, i.e. within a subgroup of order within the group , where is prime.

At this point I suspect a small worked example might help. Suppose (a prime), where and is also prime. We need to find an element of order in the group . For the purposes of this example I will choose , which has order 11 in (you can check that ). We suppose that and have previously agreed on the value of and the generator —in practice these could be agreed amongst a large group of users, albeit the real life values would be very much larger than those in this toy example.
