To discover the shared secret key, uses the value 13 received from together with the secret value to compute . Meanwhile uses its secret value along with the value 9 received from to compute . That is, both parties can recover the shared secret as the value 8.

Of course, when using the scheme ‘for real’ we need to ensure that (and hence ) are large enough to ensure that the CDH assumption holds for the group generated by . As briefly mentioned above, in practice this means choosing to be of the order of 1000 decimal digits long. Interestingly the recommended parameter sizes to ensure that the CDH assumption holds in the multiplicative group of are the same as the recommended parameter sizes for RSA. Indeed, there are interesting relationships between the integer factorisation problem and finding discrete logarithms in the multiplicative group of integers.

Over the last 10–15 years, a major trend has been to switch to a completely different representation of a finite cyclic group in which the discrete logarithm problem is believed to be much more complex for a given size of group. This has the great attraction of enabling computations to be made simpler since the values in the computations are much smaller. The group in question consists of the points on an elliptic curve computed over a finite field. An elliptic curve in this context simply means the set of solutions to an equation of the form , where is a cubic polynomial of a special type.

Since I have not yet defined what a field is, let alone a finite field, nor have I discussed polynomials, I will revisit these groups in Chapter 8, after introducing fields in the next chapter.

Before moving on to look at other applications of discrete logarithms I need to mention one fundamental shortcoming of Diffie–Hellman key exchange—namely that is not authenticated. That is, does not have a means of determining whether the received value really comes from , and similarly does not know that really comes from . As a result, although two parties agree on a secret key which is unavailable to any other party, neither nor know who they have actually agreed a key with.

In practice this problem is solved by using another security scheme to protect the integrity and guarantee the origin of the messages exchanged. One possibility is for the two parties to create digital signatures on the exchanges of the Diffie–Hellman protocols, thereby enabling and to know who they are establishing a key with. However, this is getting into a level of detail beyond the scope of this book.

5.12 Other Applications of Discrete Logarithms

The Diffie–Hellman protocol is by no means the only cryptographic scheme built on the Discrete Logarithm Problem. In 1985, the Egyptian cryptographer Taher Elgamal proposed two public key cryptographic schemes whose security rests on the discrete logarithm problem—a digital signature scheme and an encryption scheme.

Elgamal signatures have been very widely adopted. Of particular importance is a variant known as DSA (for Digital Signature Algorithm), which was adopted as a US Federal Standard in 1994.

However, the current version of the standard does not support the originally standardised scheme, and instead has adopted a closely related scheme known as EC-DSA (for Elliptic Curve DSA) in which the group is replaced by a group of points on an elliptic curve (see Chapter 8).

5.13 The Threat Posed by Quantum Computing

Over the last few years the impact of quantum computing on today’s cryptography has been widely discussed. Whilst there is still no general agreement that large-scale, general purpose, quantum computers will ever be built, huge efforts continue on developing them, and step by step progress is being made. Should such computers ever become available, the impact on the security of many of today’s cryptographic systems is considerable. In particular, a quantum algorithm, i.e. an algorithm which will run on a quantum computer, has been devised which seriously affects all of the public key cryptographic algorithms in wide use today, and in particular RSA and all schemes whose security is based on the difficulty of computing discrete logarithms.

This algorithm, devised by American mathematician Peter Shor and now known as Shor’s algorithm, was published in 1994. A key impact of this development is that, if a quantum computer becomes available capable of running this algorithm for appropriate parameter sizes, all public key cryptographic algorithms based on the difficulty of factoring large integers or computing discrete logarithms will be rendered insecure for currently used key lengths. Moreover, the (large) increase in key length needed to make currently used schemes secure would be so great as to render use of the algorithms infeasible in most cases.

Most commentators seem to agree that we are at least ten years away from the ‘quantum apocalypse’, when currently-used public key cryptography becomes vulnerable to attacks using quantum computers. However, the possibility means we need to think about the potential impact of cryptographic algorithms in current use being rendered insecure at some time in the future. For algorithms solely used for verifying the integrity of transmitted data, i.e. whose use has no long-term impact, there will no significant problems, as long as new ‘secure’ algorithms are introduced in time. However, the significance for encryption and key establishment algorithms in use today, years before this mooted apocalypse, is potentially catastrophic. Why is this?

Well, if ciphertext that is encrypted using an algorithm that becomes insecure at some future time is intercepted and stored, then it could be decrypted at the future point in time when the encryption algorithm is broken. That is, data whose secrecy has any kind of long-term significance is being made vulnerable right now through the use of algorithms which will become insecure if quantum computers are built.

Similarly, suppose a key establishment technique is employed which could be broken at some future time using data exchanged via an insecure link. If the key establishment exchanges are recorded, then any sensitive data encrypted generated using a key established using such a technique would be at risk of compromise as and when a quantum computer becomes available.

Given the potentially devastating consequences for the security of today’s cryptography, a number of agencies have been working for some years on developing new cryptography standards. The situation is very serious for public key cryptography, given that almost all current applications use algorithms which will become insecure. This has led to a number of standards organisations (including the US Federal Standards body the National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST), the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) in partnership with the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), to work on developing a suite of asymmetric cryptographic algorithms which will remain secure in a future ‘post-quantum’ world.

At the time of writing, NIST has recently published three standards

That is not to say that abstract algebra will stop being relevant to cryptography! The replacement schemes use a variety of mathematical structures, some of which we touch on in Chapters 8 and 9. The future of public key cryptography is still working itself out, although now that standards for replacement schemes are beginning to appear, at least from the US, the picture is starting to become clearer.

5.14 Other Applications of Groups

The main focus of this book is on applications of abstract algebra in the field of computing and digital communications, and in particular on cryptography. However, there are many other applications of groups in a wide range of domains. I will briefly mention a few.

One area in which groups play an important role is that of crystallography. According to Brittanica,

One important aspect of this work is looking for, and working with, symmetries of the objects under study. The set of symmetries of any crystal or molecule will form a group, and understanding of this group enables us to learn more about the structure of the object. Indeed, if two objects have different symmetry groups then we immediately know that their internal structure is different. However, there is much more to it than this.

Another area where groups play a vital role is in quantum mechanics.

During the earliest days of quantum mechanics, the mathematician Hermann Weyl quickly recognized that the mathematical structures being used were ones he was quite familiar with from his work in the field of representation theory.

I won’t even attempt to try to explain how group theory is actually used in quantum mechanics since, sadly, Richard Feynman’s quote applies to me.

This is by no means the end of the real world importance of groups. I should also add that groups crop up in many other areas of mathematics, making them an absolutely fundamental part of modern mathematical research. One obvious important application within mathematics is through automorphism groups. Although I only defined the notion of an automorphism for a group, an analogous notion can be defined for almost any conceivable mathematical structure, and the set of automorphisms of a structure will form a group. Studying these groups will not only reveal insights into the object having the group of automorphisms, but may also reveal interesting insights into group theory itself.

Chapter 6
Rings and Fields

My methods are really methods of working and thinking; this is why they have crept in everywhere anonymously.

6.1 Two Operations, Not Just One!

Having introduced groups in Chapter 5, I now want to describe a range of slightly more complex mathematical structures that build on the notion of a group. In particular, I will define what I mean by a ring and a field. I have to confess that this chapter is a little heavy on mathematical abstractions, and so I have tried to break up the formal expositions with examples. After all, it is hard to see the point of defining mathematical structures and proving theorems about them, if there are no known examples of these structures. It’s a bit like writing scientific volumes on the mating habits of unicorns, when there are actually no such things as unicorns.

The key property possessed by all the structures introduced in this chapter is that they involve two operations and not just one. Recall that a group is a set with a single operation defined on it. Here we are interested in structures which involve a set with two operations defined on it. More than this, we require the two operations to interact in a defined way.

Of course, I’m sure you can think of examples of sets with two defined operations, including the integers , the rationals , the real numbers , and , the integers modulo . I will mention all of these examples at various points in this chapter, as they are all examples of the mathematical structures I am interested in.

Before going any further I want to explain the notation I will use for the pair of operations within the structures covered here. Throughout this chapter I will use the same two symbols for the two operations defined on a structure, namely + and × (sometimes referred to as addition and multiplication, respectively). An operation defined on a set can, of course, be represented by any symbol, but we already use these two symbols for operations in very familiar contexts, including the integers, rationals and reals. Whilst I am concerned here with structures other  than the more familiar ones, in all cases the two operations will have properties analogous to the properties we expect of the more familiar uses of these symbols.

Again in line with familiar examples, I will also use the symbol 0 for the identity element for the + operation, and if the identity element for the × operation exists, I will denote it by the symbol 1. The inverse of an element under the + operation will always be written as , and the inverse of an element under the × operation will be written as (if it exists). I will use two pieces of shorthand for an operation repeated multiple times on the same element:

  • I will write for added to itself times, i.e.

    and

  • analogously, I will put for multiplied by itself times, i.e.

Finally, as is common practice, I will usually write or even instead of .

6.2 So What Is a Ring?

The simplest structure I will define is called a ring. Informally, a ring is a set with two operations + and × defined on where is an abelian group, × is associative on , and + and × obey the distributive law. This latter requirement governs how the two operations interact.

The roots of the theory of rings go back at least to the 19th century, where the work of Richard Dedekind and Leopold Kronecker can be seen as laying some of the foundations for the theory. Rings were only formally defined in the 1920s by Emmy Noether and Wolfgang Krull.

Some authors require a ring to possess an identity element 1 for , where here, as throughout, denotes with zero omitted. However, for the purposes of this book I don’t make this requirement. Authors requiring a ring to contain a multiplicative identity would use the term ‘rng’ to describe what I call a ring (where, of course, ‘rng’ is ‘ring’ with the 1 removed).

More formally, a ring can be defined as follows. The triple , where is a non-empty set, and + and × are operations defined on , is said to be a ring if:

  • is an abelian group;
  • × is an associative operation on ;
  • for any (the left distributive law).
  • for any (the right distributive law).

The left and right distributive laws are referred to jointly as just the distributive law.

A motivating example is provided by the integers where, as I discussed previously, is an abelian group, is associative on , and the distributive law holds for multiplication over addition. Another obvious example is provided by for any integer . For those of you familiar with matrices, the set of 2 by 2 matrices with real elements along with the usual addition and multiplication operations for matrices form a ring.

Some basic properties of rings are captured in the following trivial lemma. The lemma describes two important ways in which the two operations and interact.

6.3 Types of Rings

There are a range of types of ring, i.e. rings with various additional properties. The algebraic structures I will examine in the remainder of this book, in particular the polynomials rings and the fields, are special types of ring. It is therefore important to review some of the key examples of types of ring, along with some of their most important properties.

  • A ring with one is simply a ring which possesses an identity element 1 for the multiplication operation (which must be both a right and a left identity), i.e. for every . As I noted above, many authors would call a ring with one simply a ring. To avoid the trivial case where the ring contains just one element , as is common practice I require that , and hence a ring with one contains at least two elements.

    If is a ring with one, then some of the elements in (where, as always, denotes the set of non-zero elements of ) may have a multiplicative inverse. That is, for some elements there exists an such that . If is such an element then it is known as a unit. Every ring with one will have at least one unit, namely 1 itself, which helps to explain the term unit. Another way of thinking about units is that an element is a unit if and only if it is a divisor of 1.

    As above, both and (for any positive integer ) are rings with one. But which elements of these rings are units? In the case of , only and are units, the latter being a unit since . The situation for is a little more complicated. If is prime then every element of is a unit—this follows from Lemma 4.2 stated in Section 4.6. However, more generally, again from Lemma 4.2, an element is a unit if and only if , and as discussed in Section 5.4, the set of units in form a group under multiplication called the reduced residue system. In fact, the collection of units form a multiplicative group in any ring with one, so, in particular, the product of two units is always a unit.

  • Commutative rings as their name suggests, are rings for which the multiplication operation is commutative. A commutative ring need not be a ring with one, and a ring with one need not be commutative. As I’m sure you will have observed, both and are commutative rings with one. However, the ring of two by two matrices with real number entries has a one (namely the matrix with ones in the diagonal and zeros off the diagonal) but is not commutative. From here on I will mainly be discussing commutative rings with one.

  • Finally, before defining a special type of ring known as an integral domain, I need to explain the notion of a zero divisor. A zero divisor in a ring is an element for which for some non-zero element ; i.e. as you might expect, it is an element which is a divisor of zero.

    Clearly, zero itself is a zero divisor in any ring. Other examples arise in if is not a prime. So, for example, if , then, as is evident from Table 5.3 in Section 5.4, the values 2, 3 and 4 are all zero divisors. More generally, it holds that any element in that is not coprime to , i.e. for which , is a zero divisor. That is, will possess non-zero zero divisors if and only if is not a prime.

    Having explained what a zero divisor is, I can now give the definition: an integral domain is a commutative ring with one having no non-zero zero divisors. Interestingly, many key properties of the integers also hold for any integral domain, as we explore later in this chapter.

    So, since contains non-zero zero divisors if is not a prime, in this case is a commutative ring with one, but is not an integral domain. However, for prime is an integral domain, as of course are the integers .

There are many other special types of ring, but these are some of the most important. How some of the most significant types of rings relate to each other are shown in Venn Diagram form in Figure 6.1.

6.5 Integral Domains—Some Key Properties

In this rather abstract section I state and prove some key properties of integral domains. Whilst you may want to skip the proofs, I would encourage you to at least briefly look at the results I give, as they are important for ideas I develop later. These results trivially hold for the integers, and highlight how an integral domain has many of the properties of the integers.

6.6 Unique Factorisation Domains—Key Properties

It turns out that integral domains in which the unique factorisation property holds are of particular interest. Integral domains in which this property holds are known as Unique Factorisation Domains. That is, if the irreducible factors of every non-zero non-unit element are uniquely defined, up to multiplication by a unit, then an integral domain is called a unique factorisation domain (or UFD for short). As we just showed, not every integral domain is a UFD.

In a UFD, the converse to Lemma 6.4 holds; that is, every irreducible element is prime. Just like for the integers, any two elements of a UFD have a greatest common divisor,

I can now give the following lemma, which shows that the greatest common divisor of any two elements of a UFD is unique, up to multiplication by a unit.

Lemma 6.5

Suppose is a UFD. If and are both greatest common divisors of and , then and are associates.

Proof. Suppose is any element of that is a divisor of both and , i.e. for which and . Then by definition and . But is a divisor of both and and hence (so for some ). Similarly we know that (and so for some ). That is, , and hence, by the cancellation law, , i.e. is a unit, and hence both and are units. The result follows.

More generally, UFDs possess many of the properties of the integers. However, in general, a UFD will not possess an analogue of the division theorem (Theorem 3.2), as this requires there to be some kind of ordering of elements, which a UFD won’t necessarily possess. Of course, we can go on adding extra properties to define rings which have even more of the properties of the integers, including Principal Ideal Domains and Euclidean Domains, and in the latter the division theorem will hold. In particular every Euclidean Domain is a Principal Ideal Domain, and every Principal Ideal Domain is a UFD. However, defining and exploring the properties of these specialised types of integral domain is way beyond the scope of this book.

6.7 When Are Two Rings the Same Ring?

Just as was the case for groups, there are many different rings, but some of them are the same. That is, if we look at the Cayley Tables for two rings, (and a ring will have two such tables, one for addition and one for multiplication), and if we find that they are identical except for the labels and ordering of elements, then the rings are essentially the same.

So I need to introduce the idea of an isomorphism between rings to formalise this idea, just as I did for groups. Suppose and are rings. A mapping from to is a ring isomorphism from to if the following three conditions hold:

  • is one-to-one and onto;
  • for every , in ; and
  • for every , in .

It should be clear that the first two conditions are precisely the same as the conditions for an isomorphism between groups, and, as was the case for groups, the idea is that the mapping conserves exactly how the ring operations work.

If there exists an isomorphism between two rings then they are said to be isomorphic. Just as was the case for group isomorphisms, ring isomorphism is an equivalence relation on the set of all rings. The argument to establish this is essentially the same as the corresponding argument for groups.

6.8 Fields

The final type of structure I want to introduce here is the field. A field is a commutative ring with one for which every element in is a unit, i.e. for which every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse. In particular, this means that is an abelian group, and all the elements of are units. A field is by definition an integral domain, since the cancellation law holds (because there are always multiplicative inverses), and hence a field has no non-zero zero divisors.

Perhaps the most obvious motivating examples of fields are provided by the rationals , the real numbers and the complex numbers . However, another example of a field I have already looked at quite closely is provided by the integers modulo a prime , i.e. . In fact, I already showed that is a field in Section 5.4.

By introducing the notion of a field, as with any of the algebraic structures we consider in this book, any theorem we can prove about a field applies to all examples. So, instead of having to prove separate theorems about , , , and , any theorem that can be proved for an arbitrary field will automatically apply to all of them.

Just as with groups and subgroups, we can define the notion of a subfield of a field. Suppose is a field, and also suppose that is a subset of (i.e. ). If:

  • is closed under the two field operations + and ⋅,
  • is a subgroup of , and
  • is a subgroup of ,

then is a subfield of .

Obvious examples of subfields build on those just mentioned, namely is a subfield of , and is a subfield of .

I also need to introduce isomorphisms of fields, just as I did for groups and rings. In fact, since a field is simply a special type of ring I don’t need to redefine isomorphism, as the definition of ring isomorphism applies equally to fields. As previously, if there exists an isomorphism between two fields then they are said to be isomorphic.

The fields are an important special case of the finite fields, i.e. fields with a finite number of elements. Finite fields form the main focus of Chapter 8.

Before moving on to looking in more detail at finite fields, I need to introduce an important characteristic of any field, namely its characteristic. Suppose 1 is the multiplicative identity of a field . Then, if it exists, the smallest positive integer such that

for every , then the field is said to have characteristic zero or infinite characteristic. Note that the characteristic of a field is equal to the order of 1 when considered as an element of the additive group . Also observe that if the field has a finite number of elements then it necessarily has finite characteristic, but the converse does not hold—that is there are examples of fields with finite characteristic containing an infinite number of elements.

Unfortunately I am not aware of any examples of infinite fields with finite characteristic that I can describe without using concepts that I have not yet introduced. Nonetheless, I feel I should at least mention one example; so if this description makes no sense don’t worry! I hope it will make more sense once you have read Chapter 7, where I introduce polynomials. The set of all polynomials with coefficients from forms an integral domain. If you then add to this integral domain the reciprocals of all polynomials (to give multiplicative inverses), you obtain a field. This field contains an unbounded number of elements, i.e. it is infinite, since the polynomials can have arbitrary degree; however, it has finite characteristic, since the polynomial coefficients are from .

6.9 Coding Theory

6.9.1 Coding and Block Codes

One of the most important domains for practical applications of rings is in coding theory, which is the theory of how to encode data for transmission through channels which may be unreliable, i.e. that may introduce errors. Perhaps the simplest way of distinguishing coding theory from cryptography is that coding theory involves methods for protecting against accidental errors, whereas cryptography is concerned with deliberate (malign) manipulation and interception of communications channels.

How can coding theory protect against errors? Well, I am assuming that data is to be sent from one place to another (for example from one computer to another) in the form of a sequence of symbols via an unreliable channel. There are three words in this sentence that merit explanation!

  • What are the symbols? Typically, the symbols sent are zeros and ones, but they could also be numbers or indeed any elements of an algebraic structure, such as a ring. Of course, zeros and ones are the elements of , which is not only a ring but also a field.
  • What is a communications channel? Well, for the purposes of this discussion I simply mean a way of sending data from one place to another, with an identified sender and receiver. If two devices are connected via a cable capable of supporting data transmission, then the channel is very simple—however, in practice a channel between computers connected via the Internet will involve a wide range of different data links.
  • What is an unreliable channel? As I mentioned above, this means that the channel may introduce errors, i.e. so that the data received is not quite the same as the data sent. Various types of error might occur, depending on the nature of the communications channel. For example, symbols may be accidentally changed (e.g. a one may be transmitted but a zero received), and symbols may either be omitted or extra symbols inserted. Different techniques are typically required to deal with differing types of error. For the purposes of this discussion I will focus on the case where symbols might accidentally be changed. It is important to observe that all the techniques I will mention are intended to deal with accidental errors; if the errors are deliberately introduced, then typically the methods I describe will not work, as the malicious party introducing the errors can contrive to create them in such a way that they won’t be detected. To address deliberately introduced errors requires other methods, typically involving cryptography.

The block codes are a key component of coding theory. The idea of a block code is to divide the data to be transmitted, which consists of a sequence of symbols from a fixed alphabet, into data blocks of a fixed size. You then add additional check symbols to each block, computed according to a specified formula. The data blocks and the check symbols together form what is known as codeword.

So what happens next? If an error is detected, then the receiver can discard the received data as suspect and request it to be sent again. If the block code is capable of correcting errors, then the receiver can use the corrected version of the data symbols.

A simple example of such an arrangement is provided by the parity checks described in Section 4.3. In this case the symbols are 0 and 1, and the data block can be of any length. There is just one check bit for every block, computed so that the codeword, i.e. the sequence of data symbols with the check bit appended, has even parity. That is, the modulo 2 sum of the data bits and the check bit is zero.

In general, a particular block code will have two associated algorithms:

  • an encoding algorithm, which is used to compute the check symbols for a given sequence of data symbols;
  • a decoding algorithm, used for processing the received word and using the check bits to either detect errors and/or correct errors.

For the parity check example, encoding simply consists of adding together all the data bits to compute the parity check bit, and decoding involves adding together all the bits in a received word and checking whether the result is 0 (even parity) or 1 (odd parity). If the result has even parity then no errors have been detected; alternatively, if odd parity is found then the word contains an error and this can be reported for further action.

Of course, just like any block code, the parity check method is not foolproof. It will only detect an odd number of errors in a codeword. For example, if a codeword is subject to two errors, i.e a zero is changed to a one (or vice versa) in two positions within a codeword, then the parity of the erroneous received word will be even, and no error will be detected. This simply means you need to choose a code appropriate to the expected probability of errors in a particular communications channel (and your tolerance to occasional errors going undetected). As always, in practice it is a trade-off.

The efficiency, or rate, of a block code can be measured by computing the ratio of the number of information-bearing symbols (the data symbols) to the number of symbols in a codeword. So if a block code involves information symbols and check symbols, then the rate is simply

since a codeword will contain symbols. If a parity check scheme is used to compute a parity bit on a block of 8 data bits, then the codewords will have length 9, and the rate of the code will be . Obviously, in general, the higher the rate, the better. However, the more protection capability the code provides, the lower the rate will be.

Finally, I need to introduce the notion of distance for words. Suppose we are considering words containing symbols for some . In the example immediately above, . Then, given any two words and , the Hamming distance between them

then the Hamming distance between them is three, since they differ in three places (you can easily check this).

This means that, every code has a minimum distance, namely the minimum distance between any two codewords. For the parity check example, the minimum distance is two. Why is this? Well if is a codeword, then it has even parity. Now consider all the words at distance one from —they will all have odd parity, and hence they cannot be codewords. So two codewords cannot have distance one, and we have shown that the minimum distance is two.

Conversely, any code which has minimum distance two, i.e. for which every pair of codewords has distance at least two, will be able to detect a single error. More generally, if a code has minimum distance for some positive integer , then it will be able to detect errors, since changes to a codeword will never result in another codeword.

Finally, I want to briefly discuss the possibility of correcting errors. Suppose the code has minimum distance three, i.e. any two codewords have Hamming distance at least three. In such a case, one error in a received word can be corrected. Why is this? Well, if a codeword is subject to a single error in transmission, then the received word will still be Hamming distance at least two from every codeword other than the correct one. So, the receiver can pick the ‘closest’ codeword to the received word, which will be the correct codeword as long as at most one error has occurred. More generally, if the minimum distance is at least , then errors can be corrected. I will next show how to construct a code that has minimum distance three, and hence can be used to either detect and correct single errors, or detect at most two errors.

6.9.2 Hamming Codes via a Party Trick

I will now give an example of a block code which can not just detect but also correct errors. The code is known as the Hamming Code after its inventor the 20th-century American mathematician Richard Wesley Hamming.

There are a wide range of ways of describing this code, many of which use mathematics I have not introduced here. To avoid over-complicating things, and perhaps make life a bit more fun, I will use a rather simple description based on an age-old party trick you may be familiar with. A set of five cards for a rather small version of the trick is shown in Figure 6.2. I believe the usual versions involve a slightly larger set of cards (perhaps six or seven) with rather more numbers on each card, but the principle is identical. The party trick is so well-known that a few years ago I got a miniature set in a Christmas cracker!

So what do you do with the cards? As you will see, each card has 16 numbers on it, all in the range 1 to 31.

The victim is first invited by the magician to choose a number between 1 and 31, but not to reveal it. The trick involves working out the victim’s number with almost no information. The victim is given the set of five cards, and invited to select all those which contain their secret number, and to return just these to the magician who barely glances at the cards and can instantly tell the victim what their secret number is.

How does the magician do this? Well, they simply add together the numbers appearing at the top left hand corner of the selected cards. So, for example, if the victim’s secret number is 26, then they return the second, fourth and fifth cards, which have the numbers 2, 8 and 16 at their top left hand corner, and you can immediately check that indeed .

Perhaps you have already worked out how the trick works. The cards themselves give it away. It is all to do with binary representations of the numbers between 1 and 31. The first card contains all the odd numbers, i.e. all the numbers with a 1 in the rightmost position in their binary representation. To put it another way, it contains all the numbers which are congruent to 1 when working modulo 2. The second card contains all the numbers with a one in the next to rightmost position in their binary representation, and so on. So by picking out the cards which contain a given number, the victim is revealing in which positions the secret number has a one in its binary representation, and the rest is history.

Going back to the example of 26, first observe that 26 has binary representation 11010, i.e. . So, by being given the second, fourth and fifth cards, the magician immediately knows that the secret number has binary representation 11010, and adding together the numbers in the top left hand corner of the chosen cards gives a simple way of converting from a binary representation to a decimal one.

A similar trick works for a mystery number in the range for any positive integer , where there are cards. The example I just gave was for , where the mystery number was in the range and there are five cards.

So now you know how the trick works—but, you might well ask, how does this relate to coding theory and block codes? The Hamming Code, which is a binary code, i.e. it has symbols 0 and 1, works on exactly the same principle as the party trick. In a Hamming Code, the codewords have length for any positive integer , and of the bits in a codeword, are check bits and the other are data bits. It has minimum distance three, and hence can be used to correct a single error.

Suppose the bits in a codeword are labelled . Then the check bits are , and all the other bits in a codeword are the data bits. So how are the check bits computed?

Each check bit is computed as a (modulo 2) sum of a selection of data bits. Check bit is computed as the modulo 2 sum of all the data bits for which the binary representation of has a 1 in the rightmost position. Check bit is computed as the modulo 2 sum of all the data bits for which the binary representation of has a 1 in the next to rightmost position, and so on.

I hope this sounds familiar because this is exactly the way in which the cards for the party trick work. So if (as in the set of cards shown in Figure 6.2), then check bit is computed as the modulo 2 sum of all the data bits for which appears on the first card in Figure 6.2. Check bit is computed as the modulo 2 sum of all the data bits for which appears on the second card, is computed as the modulo 2 sum of all the data bits for which appears on the third card, is computed as the modulo 2 sum of all the data bits for which appears on the fourth card, and is computed as the modulo 2 sum of all the data bits for which appears on the fifth card.

So that’s how encoding works, i.e. that’s how to compute the check bits for any set of data bits. Two questions remain. First, what is the capability of this code in terms of detecting and/or correcting errors? Second, how does decoding work, i.e. what does a receiver do with the received word to check and possibly correct errors?

The first question is simple to answer—the minimum distance is three, i.e. any two codewords will always differ in at least three positions. See if you can prove this is true. A possible way of proving this relies on looking at the binary representation of for any data bit , and considering how many ones it might contain. I give a brief proof in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section at the end of the book (see page 257).

The answer to the second question relies on the party trick cards again. Suppose a word (i.e. what was sent as a codeword but may now contain an error) is received. The receiver first recomputes the check bits using the received data bits, and in each case compares the newly computed check bit with the value of that check bit that was received. If they all agree then there are no errors, and the data is accepted as it stands. However, if some disagree, then we need to use the party trick cards to work out where the error is.

Simply take the indices for all the check bits which disagree and add them together to get a number . The error will then be in bit . This is just like the way we identified the secret number in the party trick by adding together the numbers at the top left hand corner of the cards containing the secret number. Why does this work? Well, there are two cases to consider.

  • If there is an error in a check bit, say, then this will be the only place where a discrepancy shows up, since all the other check bits will compute correctly. So we have and we have successfully identified where the error is.
  • Now if there is an error in a data bit, say, then all the recomputed check bits which depend on will differ from their received values. These will be precisely the check bits for which has a one in its binary representation, and these check bits correspond to the cards which have written on them.

I will next give a simple example of how this all works for the case , i.e. where there are bits in a codeword, of which are check bits (bits , and , and the other four bits are data bits. In Figure 6.3, I show the three party trick cards for this case, which I’ll use to illustrate both encoding and decoding.

First, encoding. Suppose the four data bits are 1101, so the complete codeword will look like , where the check bits are marked with an . The three check bits are computed as follows.

  • The first check bit is computed as the sum of the for the values of on the first card in Figure 6.3, namely , and . So, working modulo 2, .
  • Similarly, is equal to the sum of the for the values of on the second card, namely , and , and so .
  • Finally, is the sum of the for on the third card, namely , and , and so .

So the codeword is 1010101.

So how does decoding work? If there are no errors then 1010101 will be received, and when the check bits are recalculated using the received data bits they will agree with the received values of the check bits. Next suppose there is a single error.

  • First, suppose the error is in a check bit, say . For example, suppose is received as a one instead of a zero, i.e. the received word is 1110101. The other two check bits ( and ) are independent of , and so the only difference between the received check bits and the recomputed check bits will be for , meaning that the receiver can determine that is the erroneous bit.
  • Second, suppose the error affects a data bit. Suppose as an example that is received as a zero instead of a one, so the received word is 1010001. Checking with the three cards in Figure 6.3, both cards 1 and 3 have 5 on them, and so and are functions of . That is, the recomputed versions of both these check bits will differ from the received versions, meaning that the erroneous bit is number .

The Hamming Codes are an example of a very important class of codes known as linear codes. A linear code over a finite field is one in which all symbols are chosen from , and the check bits are linear functions of the code bits (computed in ). What do I mean by a linear function? Well, if the data symbols are , say, then a linear function of the data symbols is of the form

where the (the coefficients) and the data symbols are all elements of the field . Of course, in the case of the Hamming Code, the coefficients are all either zero or one, as we are working in the field .

It should also be clear that the parity check case is also an example of a linear code over a finite field, since in this case the parity bit is the sum of all the data bits. In this case, as with the Hamming Code, the underlying finite field is . There are many other important examples of codes that are linear over a finite field, including the Reed–Muller Codes, one example of which was used to deliver error-corrected photographs of the surface of Mars sent by the Mariner 9 probe in 1971.

6.9.3 Codes via Rings

Historically, the most discussed block codes have an algebraic structure, with their elements drawn from a finite field. Indeed, the linear codes over a finite field play a central role in coding theory, at least historically. However, important examples of highly efficient block codes (i.e. codes with a high data rate relative to their minimum distance) have long been known which are not linear over a finite field.

However, unexpectedly, a paper published in 1994 by A Roger Hammons, P Vijay Kumar, A R Calderbank, N J A Sloane

This discovery sparked a huge interest in codes that are linear over a wide range of rings, and such codes have become an established part of coding theory. So whilst going into the details of these codes is way beyond the scope of this book, I hope I have convinced you that, for coding theory at least, rings are of genuine practical importance as well as playing a fundamental role in abstract algebra.

Polynomials and Polynomial Rings

I, who do not profess to be a mathematician, but who, whenever there is leisure, delight in mathematical studies . . . .

7.1 What Do I Mean by Polynomials?

I now want to introduce something you may already feel you are familiar with, namely polynomials. However, I will define and use them in a way that may not be so familiar.

The underlying idea here is to treat mathematical expressions, e.g. ‘’ or ‘’ as mathematical objects in themselves. I am interested here in expressions involving a single unknown or indeterminate, which I label . I suspect you are more used to handling these expressions as part of an equation, e.g. ‘’ or ‘’, which you are invited to solve. Assuming that arithmetic is done in the integers, in the former case is the unique solution, and in the latter case and are two possible solutions. However, I am not interested here in polynomial equations, just the expressions involving . I will treat these expressions as elements in an algebraic structure, and look at how expressions can be combined. That is, the expressions themselves are a kind of number, and it turns out they have many of the properties we expect from more ‘regular’ numbers, such as the integers.

If is an expression involving elements of , a commutative ring with one, and a single indeterminate (and possibly arbitrary powers of ), then we call a polynomial in , and we refer to the elements of multiplying powers of in the polynomial as coefficients.

So, for example, is a polynomial over the integers , and the values 3, 5 and 7 are the coefficients of , and respectively. The zero polynomial is simply the ring element 0, i.e. the additive identity in the ring .

If is a polynomial and is the largest power of in with a non-zero coefficient, then is known as the degree of . Also, the term of involving , where is the degree, is known as the leading term of the polynomial, and the coefficient of the leading term is known as the leading coefficient. So, for example, the polynomial has degree 5, the leading term is , and the leading coefficient is 6; also, the polynomial 7 has degree zero (since the largest power of appearing in the polynomial is ), and the leading coefficient is 7. The polynomials with degree zero, which correspond to individual ring elements, are called constant polynomials; two constant polynomials of particular importance are 0 and 1 (the additive and multiplicative identities in ).

Two polynomials are said to be equal if they have the same degree and their corresponding coefficients are equal. If the leading coefficient of a polynomial is equal to 1 (the multiplicative identity in the ring ) then we call the polynomial monic.

I should at this point say that, although it is possible to define polynomials over an arbitrary number of indeterminates, we are only interested here in polynomials with a single indeterminate —so called univariate polynomials.

7.2 Doing Arithmetic with Polynomials

I have already defined how addition and multiplication work for polynomials. I then showed that if the underlying ring is a commutative ring with one, then the set of polynomials with the defined addition and multiplication operations is also a commutative ring with one. Also, if the underlying ring is an integral domain, then so is the ring of polynomials.

In this section, I will further explore the arithmetic properties of polynomials over a ring, and in particular show how they have a key property of the integers. That is, we have an algebraic structure made up of objects very different from the whole numbers, that yet share many properties with them.

7.3 Polynomials over a Field

I will next look at what happens when the coefficients for a polynomial are chosen from a field. That is, I am interested here in polynomials in when is a field. Since a field is more ‘special’ than a commutative ring with one, notably all of its non-zero elements are units, the ring of polynomials also has special properties.

First, observe that since a field is an integral domain, as I observed at the beginning of Section 6.8, it follows from Corollary 7.2 that is an integral domain. I already defined the notion of associates for elements of an integral domain (see Section 6.5), but to make life simpler, I will repeat it here for the special case of for a field .

If and are polynomials in , then and are associates if there exists a unit in such that . So what do units in look like? Well, any element of is a unit (i.e. it has a multiplicative inverse), since, by definition of a field, is an abelian group. So the units of include all the elements with degree zero, i.e. the ‘constant polynomials’. I claim that no other elements of can be units, since the degree of the product of two non-zero polynomials is the sum of the degree of these polynomials (from Lemma 7.1), and hence no polynomial of degree greater than zero can be a unit. That is, the units in are precisely the elements with degree 0. 7.4 Shift Register Sequences

7.4.1 What Do Shift Registers Do?

Polynomials have a very wide range of applications, both in other areas of mathematics and in uses of mathematics in communications and computing. The application domain I briefly introduce here, namely linear feedback shift registers (LFSRs), has links to cryptography, but also many other applications in engineering and computing.

However, before showing how polynomials are useful for analysing shift registers, I need to explain what a shift register is. I will explain the idea of a shift register as if it is something implemented in hardware (typically electronics), but a shift register can equally well be implemented in software.

The simplest example of a type of shift register is shown in Figure 7.1. The ‘boxes’ represent storage elements, or stages, i.e. locations where a single symbol can be stored. The state of a shift register at any point in time is the sequence of symbols stored in the stages. For my purposes here, I am only interested in the case where the symbols are in a finite field, and of particular interest is the case where the field is , where addition and multiplication work modulo 2, and there are only two symbols (0 and 1).

The state of a shift register changes at regular intervals (or time slots), which involves the contents of a stage being moved into the stage to its left, as the arrows indicate. A new symbol is moved into the right-most stage (the input to the shift register) and the output of the register is whatever was in the leftmost stage. We number the time slots , so the initial state of the register is the state at time , the state at time is the state for time moved left one place, and so on.

If you consider the register shown in Figure 7.1, and suppose it has stages for some positive integer , then the input at time is the output at time . Of course, whilst such shift registers may have applications in simple digital circuits, mathematically they are not very interesting.

A second simple type of shift register, namely a feedback shift register, is shown in Figure 7.2. Here, the input is simply the same as the output. The contents of the register will simply rotate.

Suppose there are stages in the register. I label the stages , as shown in the figure. Also, suppose that the contents of stage at time is denoted by . So at time , when the register is in its initial state, the contents of the stages of the shift register are

Now, since the feedback just recirculates, the state of the register at time will be the same as the state at time , , and so on. Again, feedback registers as I’ve described them here are not very interesting mathematically, but they exhibit one important behaviour, namely periodicity, which is also true for the next and more important example. What do I mean by periodicity?

Well, the sequence output by a feedback shift register will repeat itself after terms. That is, if the initial state of the register is , then the sequence output by the register will be

This is an example of a periodic sequence. More generally, a sequence

is said to be periodic if for some for every . If is the smallest positive integer for which the sequence has this property, then the sequence is said to have period . So, for example, the all-one sequence has period one, and the sequence 010101… has period two. I will refer to a period of such a sequence as being consecutive symbols, so a period of the sequence 010101… is simply [01].

So, going back to the feedback shift register case, what is the period of the sequence it outputs? It could be , but it might be less than . If, for example, the initial state is all ones, then the sequence output will be 1111…, i.e. a sequence with period one. The only thing we can say for certain is that the period will be a divisor of —what the precise period is will depend on the initial state of the shift register.

7.4.2 Linear Feedback Shift Registers

The next diagram, Figure 7.3, shows the type of shift register I am particularly interested in here, namely the linear feedback shift register, or simply an LFSR.

In this diagram, between every pair of stages there is a tap, with the output of the tap being added to the outputs of the other taps, after multiplication by a fixed value (which must be in the finite field). This means that the value fed back into stage at time is equal to:

In the case of particular interest here, namely the binary case where we are working over , every value is either zero or one, and so the value fed back is the sum of a selection of the values currently in the register. Normally, we always take to be non-zero, or else we can get exactly the same output sequence by deleting and working with a shorter register.

From now on, I will mainly focus on the binary case, i.e. where the field is . However, pretty much everything I have to say can be generalised to the case where the symbols are drawn from an arbitrary finite field.

To make things clearer, I next give a simple example of a binary LFSR with , as shown in Figure 7.4.

There are two taps, so the feedback is the sum of two of the stages. That is,

Suppose the initial state is 00111, i.e.

The successive states of the shift register for are shown in Table 7.1.

I next want to make an important, albeit rather simple, observation. The state of an LFSR at time depends only on the state at time . That is, if the state of an LFSR ever equals the state at some previous time, then the sequence of states thereafter will be exactly the same as the sequence of states after the previous occurrence of the repeated state. So the sequence of states of an LFSR will always, eventually, be periodic.

So what about the example I have just given? It is simple to see that the state at time is the same as the state at time , and hence the sequence of states has period dividing 31. However, since 31 is prime, the period is exactly 31. You can check the table to see that no state recurs before .

So how long can the periodic sequence be? Well, this will clearly depend on the number of possible states of the shift register. That is, since if the same state recurs, the sequence will also recur from that point, then the period of any sequence of states must be at most the number of states. Thus, if the symbols that fill the stages of the register are taken from a set of size , then the maximum period for an -stage shift register must be . In fact, we can do slightly better than this.

Suppose the initial state of the register is all zeros. Then the feedback bit will be a linear function of all zeros, and hence will be zero. That is, if a shift register is ever in the all-zero state, then it will stay in this state for ever. So a maximum length sequence cannot contain the all-zero state, and so the maximum period of the sequence of states of an LFSR is .

7.4.3 LFSR Sequences and Polynomials

As I just mentioned, I am particularly interested here in the sequences output by a LFSR, and specifically the maximum period sequences, i.e. those with period . These are known as m-sequences (where the ‘m’ stands for maximum period), and they have a range of interesting properties which make them useful in a wide range of practical applications, which are explored a little further below.

Perhaps the key question is how to choose the feedback taps to ensure that the LFSR generates a maximum period sequence. This is where I need to use polynomials. However, before explaining the theory, I will give another example to illustrate that not all feedback tap settings generate maximum period sequences. The sequences generated by the LFSR shown in Figure 7.5 do not have the maximum possible period.

7.4.4 Properties of m-sequences

The m-sequences, i.e. the maximal period LFSR sequences, have a wide range of interesting properties. One obvious property, of course, is that a very simple circuit involving just a few storage elements can generate a sequence with a long period. For example, a 20-stage binary LFSR can generate a sequence with period over a million.

They also have the very nice property that if any two shifts of the same sequence are added together, then the result is another shift of the same sequence (or the all-zero sequence). Why is this? By a shift of a sequence, I simply mean starting in a different place. For example, if we consider the periodic sequence

then the shift of this sequence one place to the left is simply the periodic sequence

Why does this property hold? Well it is a consequence of the fact that both shifts of the sequence satisfy the same linear recurrence relation. The sum of two sequences satisfying a linear recurrence relation must satisfy the same recurrence, so this means that the sum of two shifts of the same m-sequence must be another shift of this sequence.

Apart from this, they exhibit a number of other properties which means the sequence looks rather like a random sequence (while, of course, it is very far from actually being random)! Sequences which are generated by a deterministic process, like m-sequences, and which, to some extent at least, resemble random sequences

The eminent American mathematician and engineer Solomon Wolf Golomb

  • R1: In any period of the sequence, the number of ones differs from the number of zeros by at most one.
  • R2: In any period of the sequence, approximately half the runs
  • R3: If the sequence is compared to a shift of itself, then over a period of the sequence the number of agreements minus the number of disagreements is a constant for all shifts (apart from the zero shift). Using more mathematical terminology, the out-of-phase autocorrelation of the sequence is a constant.

The m-sequences satisfy all of R1–R3. As an example, consider the m-sequence of period 15 generated by the LFSR shown in Figure 7.6, namely the sequence:

I have given exactly one period of the sequence here. It is simply to verify that a period of the sequence contains eight ones and seven zeros, so R1 holds. There are four runs of zeros—a half of them (i.e. two of them) have length one, and a quarter (one) have length two. There are four runs of ones, and again half have length one and a quarter have length two. So R2 holds.

R3 holds as an immediate corollary of the property that the sum of two shifts of an m-sequence will yield another shift of the same sequence. When computing the sum of two bits, if the two bits being summed are the same then a zero will result, and if they are different then the outcome will be a one. But an m-sequence generated by an LFSR with stages will always contain exactly ones and zeros, and so the number of agreements between any two shifts of an m-sequence with be , and the number of disagreements will be . Hence, the number of agreements minus the number of disagreements will always be .

Of course, any sequence which satisfies R1–R3 will clearly not be random. Indeed, these properties mean that the sequence over a full period will be ‘too regular’, but if we are using just part of a m-sequence then it will be suitable for applications requiring random-looking properties.

7.4.5 Applications of m-sequences

As I already mentioned, there are innumerable real-world applications of m-sequences. In particular, their pseudorandomness properties, large period and simplicity of generation make them useful for any case requiring large volumes of ‘random-like’ sequences of bits. Two examples of applications are as follows.

  • In spread spectrum communications, m-sequences are used to ‘spread’ radio signals across a broad band of frequencies as part of Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) systems. Each transmitting entity is assigned its own m-sequence code, enabling multiple signals to be transmitted simultaneously over the same set of frequencies, minimising interference. The m-sequences are important for spreading signals because of their autocorrelation properties, which minimises interference between two signals. Their balance and run properties also enable reliable synchronisation between transmitters and receivers.
  • It is possible to derive codes for error detection and correction using m-sequences. The set of shifts of an m-sequence form what is the known as the Simplex Code, which is very closely related to first order Reed–Muller Codes.

    There is one further application I will explore in a little more detail, namely their use as a component in a type of encryption technique called a stream cipher. The high level operation of stream cipher encryption is shown in Figure 7.7.

    Encryption works in a very simple way. The plaintext needs to be converted to a sequence of zeros and ones, although typically this is how data is stored anyway. The key component is the sequence generator. The sequence generator takes as input a secret key (which must be shared with the entity authorised to decrypt) and gives as output a sequence of zeros and ones, often referred to as the keystream. This keystream sequence is then combined bit by bit with the plaintext to give the ciphertext. This combination simply involves modulo 2 addition.

    The sequence generator needs to have a number of important properties if the stream cipher is to be secure. These include the following.

    • The keystream sequence needs to have a large period (it must be periodic since like an LFSR it will have a finite number of possible internal states).
    • The keystream sequence needs to have pseudorandomness properties, i.e. it must resemble a random sequence.
    • Perhaps most importantly, it should not be computationally feasible to use knowledge of part of the keystream sequence to deduce other parts of the keystream sequence.

    Why these properties? First, if the period of the keystream sequence is not sufficiently large, then the same sequence of keystream bits may end up being used to encrypt two different pieces of plaintext. If this became known to a cryptanalyst, then this could be used to reveal information about some of the plaintext.

    If the keystream has non-random properties, e.g. if ones are much more likely to occur than zeros in the sequence, then statistical properties of the plaintext will ‘leak’ into the ciphertext, i.e. purely by doing statistical analysis of the ciphertext it might be possible to deduce information about the plaintext.

    The need for the final property is perhaps a little less obvious. The reason for requiring this is that it may be possible for the cryptanalyst who has access to the ciphertext to somehow know what part of the corresponding plaintext is. This could be for any number of reasons. It might simply be that the plaintext is highly formatted, and always starts in the same way. This is true for many popular file formats. The history of cryptography and cryptanalysis has many examples of where so called ‘known plaintext’ attacks have been possible.

    If a cryptanalyst knows a ciphertext bit and the corresponding plaintext bit, then their sum will be the keystream bit (this is just how modulo 2 addition works). So, knowledge of, say, a couple of hundred consecutive plaintext bits, and the corresponding ciphertext bits, will immediately yield 200 known keystream bits; it is therefore vital that this cannot be used to deduce more keystream bits (or, worst of all, work back to the secret key).

    So how does all this relate to LFSRs? I hope you will have already noticed that m-sequences satisfy the first two of the three desirable properties for a keystream sequence. Moreover, they are easy to generate at very high data rates with very simple electronics (or software). However, they dismally fail to meet the third requirement. Given consecutive bits of an m-sequence, it is possible to easily work out any other bit of the sequence even if you don’t know the feedback tap positions. Indeed, it is hard to imagine a sequence which failed to meet the third property more disastrously!

    Nonetheless, LFSRs have a key role to play in many designs for stream cipher sequence generators. By combining two or more LFSRs using non-linear logic, pseudorandom sequences with large periods can be generated which, as far as we know, also possess the third property. The ease of implementation of LFSRs and their periodicity and pseudorandomness properties make them very attractive components in stream cipher designs.

    Before wrapping up this topic, I can’t resist mentioning a historically important family of stream ciphers, namely the Lorenz SZ40, SZ42a and SZ42b systems used by Germany during the latter part of the Second World War. They were used for high level traffic and were believed to be immune to cryptanalysis. However, thanks to the brilliance of British–Canadian mathematician William Thomas (Bill) Tutte

    Despite not knowing how the Lorenz sequence generator worked, he was able to deduce its operation given only a portion of keystream. This keystream was obtained from an accidental misuse of the system by its operators, where two versions of the same message were sent encrypted using the same keystream sequence. This allowed John Tiltman, a senior Bletchley Park cryptanalyst, to deduce that the encryption system in use was a stream cipher. Tiltman was then able to deduce the two messages and hence obtain a portion of the keystream sequence. This was then given to Bill Tutte to work on as a seemingly lost cause. To be able to deduce the operation of a complex sequence generator given only a portion of the output sequence was an incredible feat, one I still find hard to believe was possible, especially in the absence of any automated data processing.

    Once the operation of the Lorenz system was known, it became possible to work on methods of cryptanalysis. Eventually, it became clear that it was necessary to mechanise the process, which led to the design and construction of the Colossus, one of the world’s first digital computers. Colossus was designed by the Post Office engineer Tommy Flowers, and of course, as is well known, Alan Turing was also involved in the work. However, it should be made clear that, despite popular misconceptions, Colossus was built to help break the Lorenz stream cipher and not the Enigma machine.

    Colossus remained top secret for many years after the war, and, sadly, eventually all surviving instances of the device were securely destroyed. However, the good news is that enough information, and original creators, survived to enable a working replica to be built at Bletchley Park, and it can be viewed at the Bletchley Park Museum.

    7.4.6 Non-linear Feedback Shift Registers

    So far, I have only looked at the case where the feedback function of the shift register is a linear function of the values stored in the stages of the register. That is, as shown in Figure 7.3, where the value of stage at time is a linear function of the contents of stages at time . However, it is also of interest to consider the case where the feedback function is not restricted, i.e. where the value of stage at time is an arbitrary function of the contents of stages at time , as shown in Figure 7.8.

    Shift registers with a non-linear feedback function are known as non-linear feedback shift registers (NFSRs). Such shift registers have been extensively studied and have a range of real-world applications, including in the design of stream cipher keystream sequence generators.

Chapter 8
Finite Fields

An author never does more damage to his readers than when he hides a difficulty.

8.1 The Core of the Book

It took me a while to get here, but I am now ready to describe the properties of finite fields, as well as a small selection of their many practical applications. As mentioned previously, the applications I have highlighted here reflect my interests; there are many that I don’t mention here. It turns out that finite fields are of key importance in modern information and communications technology, although I am sure that the mathematicians who developed the basic theory well over 100 years ago had no conception that this would be true.

The finite fields are known as Galois Fields after Évariste Galois, a quote from whom is given at the beginning of this chapter. Indeed, the Galois Fields form part of an area of mathematics known as Galois Theory. In his brief and turbulent life, Galois laid the foundations for a major branch of algebra, although, of course, the terminology we use today was developed a long time after he died in 1832. Although Galois is often credited with developing fundamental ideas underlying group theory and Galois Theory, the Italian mathematician Paolo Ruffini came up with many of the ideas first, although his work was ignored by the mathematical community at the time.

8.2 The Prime Fields

I already introduced the notion of a field in Chapter 6, where I observed that is a field for every prime . Moreover, as I showed in Lemma 6.7 every field with elements is isomorphic to .

These fields, known as the prime fields, are of key importance both to the rest of mathematics and in a wide range of practical applications, some of which I have already described. In particular, as Theorem 6.1 shows, they are the foundation on which all fields with finite characteristic are built. That is, since finite fields must have finite characteristic, all finite fields must contain a copy of for some prime , where is the characteristic of the field. As an example of a prime field, I gave Cayley tables for the field with five elements, , in Tables 5.1 and 5.2.

However, the prime fields are not the only finite fields; in Section 8.3, I consider how many elements a finite field might have, and subsequently I show how to construct a ‘non-prime’ finite field for every possible number of elements. This then leads naturally to a consideration of applications for finite fields, in addition to those I have already mentioned.

8.4 Prime Power Fields

8.5 Uniqueness and Representation of Finite Fields

A fundamental result in the study of finite fields is that, for any and , the finite field with elements, denoted by where GF stands for Galois Field, is unique up to isomorphism. I regret to say that I haven’t managed to find a proof of this result that does not involve setting up quite a bit more mathematical machinery. So, unfortunately, you will need to look elsewhere for a proof, although any standard text on the subject will provide one. It is also the case that the multiplicative group of the non-zero elements of any finite field is cyclic.

From now on, I will assume this result and refer to as the finite field with elements, where for some prime and positive integer . In particular, of course, we know that for every prime .

I suspect that if your instinct is to implement things, you may be wondering what the best way of handling the elements of might be. In fact, performing computations with finite fields is more straightforward than you might think.

To remind you, the elements of for ( prime) are residue classes of polynomials, where each class contains a unique polynomial of degree less than that can be used to ‘represent’ that class. A polynomial of degree less than can be represented as an -tuple of coefficients, where each coefficient is from the prime field . That is, if the residue class is

where the values are from , then we can represent the residue class by the -tuple

For example, in the above example for , we can represent the nine residue classes by the nine 2-tuples:

which correspond to

respectively. Thus, the field elements can be represented as elements from an array of dimension .

Moreover, addition is simply addition of the corresponding digits in the -tuple, e.g. for the above example: , corresponds to the polynomial addition . So computing additions in the finite field is no more difficult than performing additions in the prime field . In fact, addition works just like addition in the product ring , as defined in Section 6.4. However, multiplication is not so simple.

If the finite field is small then probably the easiest way to implement multiplication is using a pre-computed table—much like the Cayley table shown in Table 8.2. For larger fields, where a table would be prohibitively expensive in storage, a process akin to long division can be used to find the remainder when the product polynomial is divided by the irreducible polynomial defining the finite field. For computations involving large degree polynomials (i.e. when is large), other tricks are available to simplify computations.

8.6 Elliptic Curve Cryptography

I now want to describe an important application of finite fields in cryptography. In Chapter 5, I described the notion of discrete logarithms, which are defined for any finite cyclic group. As I described there, discrete logarithms are the basis of some very widely used cryptographic techniques. I also described how discrete logarithms work for one particular instance of a cyclic group, namely the group for any prime . In fact, standard practice is to use a large cyclic subgroup of this group.

This particular instance of a cyclic group is used because:

  • computing for any positive integer is straightforward (where is a generator of the cyclic group), even for large values of , whereas
  • if is an arbitrary element of the group, then finding the value of for which (i.e. computing the discrete logarithm of ) is believed to be computationally infeasible, at least as long as the group is large enough.

However, any instance of a cyclic group that has the aforementioned properties would work equally well in a wide range of cryptographic methods. In particular, it would be desirable to find instances of large cyclic groups where computing remains straightforward, but computing discrete logarithms is significantly more difficult than for for given sizes of group. In such a case, the desired level of security could be achieved using smaller groups, which would potentially make computations faster (and keys smaller). This is precisely the motivation for the development of elliptic curve cryptography.

In essence, using elliptic curves enables us to define cyclic groups for which solving the discrete logarithm problem is much more computationally demanding than the discrete logarithm problem for for a given size of group. As a result, over the last decade or more there has been a major switch from using cryptography based on discrete logarithms in a subgroup of to cryptography using discrete logarithms in an elliptic curve group.

So what is an elliptic curve, and what is an elliptic curve group? I want to start by introducing the notion of a curve. For my purposes here, a curve is simply a set of solutions to a particular equation defined over a field . So, for example, if the field is the real numbers , then the equation defines a very simple curve—in fact, if we plot all the solutions on a graph we get a diagonal straight line that goes through the point and heads from south-west to north-east. A graph of the curve (kindly created by ChatGPT) is shown in Figure 8.1.

A slightly more interesting curve, again for the field , is obtained if we consider the equation . In this case we get the curve known as a parabola shown in Figure 8.2 (again provided courtesy of ChatGPT).

Although the two examples of curves that I have just given can be plotted as lines on a graph, as one might expect from the name curve, in general this will not be true. That is, for my purposes, a curve is simply the set of solutions to an equation involving and , and does not necessarily have a nice geometric interpretation.

In general, an elliptic curve is simply a set of solutions to an equation of a particular form defined over a field . We will typically denote the set of points on the curve, i.e. the set of pairs that satisfy the defining equation, by , where is the underlying field—or just by if the field is obvious from the context. A general elliptic curve equation looks like:

where are all elements

The reason they are called elliptic curves is that they originally arose as part of efforts to study the length of an arc in an ellipse. This in turn led to the study of certain functions called elliptic integrals over the real and complex numbers. So the relation to the term ellipse is not so straightforward—it certainly doesn’t mean that the curves are in the form of an ellipse, although they have ellipsoid features.

Fortunately it is possible to simplify the general equation defining an elliptic curve by changing the variables and this essentially involves choosing an elliptic curve with simple parameters from amongst a set of isomorphic curves, where curve isomorphism maps between two essentially equivalent curves, analogously to group or field isomorphisms. Unfortunately, the precise form of the simplified equations depends on the characteristic of the field, where, as discussed in Section 6.8, the characteristic of a field is either infinite or equal to a prime number.

The following cases arise:

So, how many points will there be on a curve over in general? Well, since there are at most two solutions to the equation for any value of , and there are possible values for , there will be at most solutions to the curve equation, i.e. there will be at most points on the curve. Hence there will be at most elements in the group (since we add the extra element ). However, the actual number will always be significantly less than this. In fact, a result proved in 1931 by the German mathematician Helmut Hasse states that the number of points on an elliptic curve over a finite field is always in the range

The next result tells us that the group on a curve is in most cases either cyclic or possesses a large cyclic subgroup.

Theorem 8.3
