If then clearly is cyclic. For the example of a curve given earlier  over GF(29), the order of the group is 37, which is prime, and hence in this case the group is cyclic. In fact, the point is a generator of the group. The successive powers of are shown in Table 8.4.

So by choosing the curve appropriately, we can obtain a cyclic group. That is, given a generator of the cyclic group, we can define discrete logarithms with respect to this generator. It turns out that, as far as we know and as long as the parameters are chosen carefully, computing discrete logarithms in an appropriate elliptic curve group is much more computationally complex than computing discrete logarithms in the group of non-zero integers modulo , i.e. (as discussed in Chapter 5). As a result it is possible to use significantly smaller group sizes when implementing discrete logarithm-based cryptographic schemes, such as the Diffie–Hellman key establishment scheme described in Section 5.11. This has significant practical advantages, and as a result elliptic curve-based schemes have become very widely used over the last 10–20 years.

As I just mentioned, the curve to be used needs to be chosen carefully to avoid certain cryptanalytic attacks, i.e. cases where computing discrete logarithms turns out to be much easier. Indeed there are widely recognised standards both for generating curves, such as ISO/IEC 15946-5

Individual curves have also been standardised, since there is no known risk in the same curve being used by multiple users.

Computations in an elliptic curve group are, on the face of it, rather more complex than in the group of . If you look at the equations given above for computing when the curve is , you will see that:

  • computing involves four finite field additions (or subtractions), one division operation, and one squaring operation; and
  • computing involves four finite field additions (or subtractions), one division operation, and one multiplication operation.

Observing that division is simply multiplication by an inverse element, and the inverse of is , this means that computing involves three finite field multiplications, one squaring operation (which may be a little cheaper than a multiplication) and eight addition operations. While the addition operations will be much simpler than multiplication, this is still a considerable amount of computation if the field is large, as will be necessary to ensure that computing discrete logarithms is computationally infeasible.

Fortunately there are a number of well-documented optimisations which can reduce the computational load. For example, it is possible to choose the curve in such a way that the computations are less taxing.

Finally, as I have mentioned previously, what really makes use of the elliptic curve group in cryptography so attractive is that computing discrete logarithms is, as far as we know, significantly more complex in this group than in the group . The gains through the choice of significantly smaller parameters far outweigh the slightly increased computational cost of performing the group operation.

8.7 Quantum Computing—What Comes Next?

Unfortunately, as was discussed in Section 5.13, the security of discrete logarithm-based cryptosystems is threatened by the possible advent of large-scale general-purpose quantum computers. That is, a suitable quantum computer can make computing discrete logarithms feasible for large groups pretty much regardless of the representation of the cyclic group in which discrete logarithms are calculated. So, within the next few years we need to move away from all cryptosystems using discrete logarithms.

As I mentioned previously, a variety of new cryptographic methods have been proposed which are believed to be secure even in a world containing large-scale quantum computers. To date, the proposals taken most seriously are based on three mathematical problems, briefly summarised as follows, and all of which relate to themes already explored in this book. So just because there is a move away from (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) RSA and discrete logarithm-based cryptosystems does not mean that cryptography is moving away from abstract algebra. Far from it! Indeed, in recent years—mainly because of the threat posed by quantum computers—cryptographers have been ransacking much of abstract algebra looking for problems which could be used as the basis for new, and hopefully quantum-computing-resistant, methods for encryption and digital signature.

  • The first is the problem of decoding large block codes. In Section 6.9, I introduced block codes and gave a simple example of a block code, namely the Hamming Code. I also introduced the idea of encoding and decoding for a block code, where encoding involves using data bits to compute the check bits, and decoding involves processing a received word to detect errors and/or correct errors in that word. More generally, encoding can be thought of as transforming a sequence of data bits into a codeword. Computing check bits and combining these with the data bits to obtain a codeword is just one type of transformation, but in general it may not be so simple.

    I also mentioned that if the minimum distance between codewords is at least then it is possible to correct up to errors in a received word. The purpose of a decoding algorithm in such a case is to work out the codeword with least Hamming Distance from the received word. In a general case, there may not be an efficient decoding algorithm, and so finding the ‘closest’ codeword to a received word may be computationally difficult, at least if the codeword is very long. One of the first ever proposed public key cryptosystems is built on this difficult computational problem. It was published by the distinguished American engineer Robert J McEliece way back in 1978.

    It has never been widely used, primarily because encryption and decryption are complex, and keys are very large. Nonetheless, in recent years it has gained significant interest because there are no known attacks, even using a quantum computer. Indeed, it is one of the ‘post-quantum’ encryption algorithms at an advanced stage of international standardisation (as a forthcoming amendment to ISO/IEC 18033-2

  • The second, and most widely discussed, computational problem used as a basis for new cryptographic algorithms is the learning with errors (LWE) problem. It refers to the computational problem of inferring a linear function over a finite ring (typically , the ring of integers modulo for some ) from given samples , some of which may be erroneous. The LWE problem is believed to be hard to solve, even in the presence of a quantum computer.

    More precisely, the unknown function maps from -tuples of elements of to . The function is linear, so if then where are the secret coefficients (from ) and all the operations are computed in . The input to the problem is a set of pairs where for each pair with high probability. The problem is then to deduce . Of course, if all the inputs are correct, then finding is very simple given a sufficient number of pairs. However, if some of them are wrong, then the problem becomes much harder.

    The LWE problem, and variants of it, has been used as the basis for a wide variety of public key cryptosystems, including methods for encryption, digital signatures and secret key establishment. Techniques using LWE have been, and are being, formally standardised by a wide range of bodies.

  • The third problem relates to a special class of functions between groups known as group isogenies. More specifically, an isogeny is a special kind of function between elliptic curves that preserves the group structure. Recently proposed public key cryptosystems based on isogenies have been attractive because they offer significantly smaller key lengths than other methods. However, designing systems which are secure against subtle attacks has proved difficult.

    Indeed, one very prominent scheme, known as SIDH or SIKE (for Supersingular Isogeny Diffie–Hellman Key Exchange) came quite close to adoption as a standardised scheme. SIDH is analogous to the Diffie–Hellman scheme described in Section 5.11. However, it was shown to be completely insecure in 2022 by methods not involving a quantum computer.

    8.8 Other Applications of Finite Fields

    Over the last 75 years or so, a wide variety of practical applications for finite fields have emerged. I have just described one, namely in elliptic curve cryptography. However, there are many others, and I will next briefly introduce just two, namely Reed–Solomon Codes, and bilinear pairings as used in cryptography.

    Indeed, such is the richness of the application domain for finite fields that there are academic journals devoted entirely to this topic, including Finite Fields and their Applications.

    8.8.1 Reed–Solomon Codes

    The Reed–Solomon codes were invented by American mathematicians and engineers Irving S Reed and Gustave Solomon. Details were first published in 1960. They are block codes, where the individual codeword symbols are from a finite field. They are very widely used, for example, in protecting data stored in CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray media, as well as protecting transmitted data in many systems, including Digital Video Broadcast (DVB). Perhaps most famously, a Reed–Solomon code over the field GF(256) was used in conjunction with other coding techniques to protect data sent back to earth by the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes to the outer solar system.

    Like the Hamming Codes, they are systematic codes, i.e. where the data symbols are separate from the check symbols. Codewords contain symbols, of which are data symbols and the other are check symbols. If the symbols in a codeword are taken from the finite field then , the length of a codeword, must satisfy . Whilst the codes exist for any finite field, in typical applications the symbols are drawn from a field of the form for some positive integer , and so symbols consist of binary -tuples (i.e. binary vectors of length ).

    The Reed–Solomon codes are examples of Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) codes. MDS codes have the highly desirable property that the distance between codewords is as large as possible for a given data rate. To explain this, I first need to introduce something known as the Singleton bound, named after American mathematical statistician Richard Collom Singleton, who published it in 1964. In fact, the bound had been published twice previously, by Indian statistician D D Joshi in 1958 and even earlier in 1953 by the Japanese mathematician Y Komiyama. So this is one of those cases where the bound is incorrectly named—perhaps it should be renamed the Komiyama–Joshi–Singleton bound, to reflect the fact that it was independently derived on at least three occasions. The bound is summarised in the following theorem.

    Theorem 8.4

    (The Singleton Bound) If a block code with symbols from a set of size has codewords of length and minimum Hamming distance , then the number of codewords satisfies:

    Any code which meets this bound, i.e. which has codewords, is called Maximum Distance Separable.

    Proof. Suppose we have a block code containing codewords of length , with symbols from a set of size and with minimum Hamming distance . Now suppose we shorten every codeword by deleting the first symbols. Every codeword now has length . Most importantly, all the shortened codewords are distinct, since in the original code every pair of codewords differed in at least places, and hence every pair of shortened codewords must differ in at least one place. So we have a set of shortened codewords of length . But there are exactly possible words of length , and so:

    as desired.

    Since it is an MDS code, a Reed–Solomon code with minimum distance must contain precisely codewords. Alternatively, if the codewords have symbols from a set of size , and there are data symbols, then there are codewords, and the minimum distance is . But how do Reed–Solomon Codes work?

    There are various ways of describing these codes, and I will choose an approach that is a little different from that originally used by Reed and Solomon, but simpler. I assume that the data symbols are taken from a finite field with elements, for some prime power . A specially chosen polynomial , called the generator polynomial, is used to compute the check symbols from the data symbols. This polynomial has coefficients from the chosen finite field and has degree . It is always possible to construct an appropriate polynomial, although I omit the details.

    Suppose that the data symbols for a block are . From this we define the data polynomial of degree . The codeword to be sent now corresponds to the coefficients of the polynomial ; that is, to ‘encode’ the data simply involves multiplying the data polynomial by the generator polynomial. Observe that will have degree , and so there will be coefficients. Because of the way in which is chosen, the resulting code is guaranteed to have minimum distance .

    The procedure I have just described can be modified in a simple way to give a systematic encoding procedure, where each codeword contains the data symbols as the first symbols and the check symbols as the last symbols. I leave you to think about this as an exercise; I have described how it works in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section—see page 247.

    Finally, there are also efficient decoding procedures, where a received word can be efficiently processed to correct up to errors, where is the minimum distance of the code.

    8.8.2 Bilinear Pairings

    The final application of finite fields that I want to describe relates to cryptography (again)! It involves a special type of function between groups called a bilinear pairing. While the notion of a pairing is quite general, and can be defined over any commutative ring with one, I am interested in the following ‘special’ type of pairing.

    Let and be finite groups of order , for some prime (and hence they are both abelian and cyclic—see Theorem 5.1). A bilinear pairing is a mapping from to that satisfies the following two properties.

    1. Bilinearity: and for every in .
    2. Non-degeneracy: for every in , where I write 1 for the identity element in both and .

    To be useful in a cryptographic application it is also necessary that the function can be evaluated easily, and I assume this from here on. Lemma 8.1 gives additional properties of a bilinear pairing.

    Lemma 8.1

    Suppose is a bilinear pairing mapping from to .

    1. .

    The proof of this lemma is elementary, and I leave it as an exercise for the reader. Full details are given on page 248 in the ‘Answers to Questions for the Reader’ section.

    An interesting implication of the bilinearity property is that an instance of the discrete logarithm problem in can be reduced to an instance of the problem in in an efficient way. So that if a pairing exists between and , and there is an efficient means of computing discrete logarithms in , then there will also be an efficient way of computing discrete logarithms in (since we assumed that is easily computable).

    So, how does this reduction work? Suppose is a generator of , and suppose for some positive integer and . Computing from (and ) is straightforward (as long as we have an efficient method for computing products of elements), but computing from and involves computing a discrete logarithm. From bilinearity (and Lemma 8.1) it follows that

    To be useful as the basis of a cryptographic algorithm we need to have an intractable computational problem. In the case of bilinear pairings the key problem is known as the Bilinear Diffie–Hellman Problem (BDHP), and is as follows. Suppose is an element of and are positive integers. The BDHP requires you to compute given four values: , , and .

    If solving the BDHP is computationally infeasible then this implies that the Diffie–Hellman Problem (DHP) (see Section 5.11) is hard in both and . Put another way, if we can solve the DHP in either or , then we can solve the BDHP for a pairing mapping to . This is straightforward to check. However, no other ways have been found for solving the problem. Unfortunately, since a sufficiently capable quantum computer can find discrete logarithms in even very large groups, this means that the BDHP can also be solved by a quantum computer; thus, long term, all cryptographic schemes based on the difficulty of BDHP will need to be replaced.

    At this point you might reasonable ask why I am discussing bilinear pairings under the heading of applications of fields when only groups are involved. Well, the two most widely discussed bilinear pairings both involve finite fields; in fact, they involve elliptic curve groups defined over a finite field. These pairings are known as the Weil and Tate pairings after their respective inventors French mathematician André Abraham Weil

    Anyway, let’s suppose we have a bilinear pairing where the BDHP is hard to solve. A wide variety of cryptographic schemes have been devised based on the difficulty of the BDHP. I will briefly describe one that enables three parties to agree on a secret key; it is analogous to the Diffie–Hellman key agreement scheme I introduced in Chapter 5 except that it involves three parties and not two. The scheme was published by French cryptographer Antoine Joux in 2000; the version I describe is the original scheme as modified in 2001 by Dutch cryptographer Eric Verheul.

    Suppose the three parties are , and , and that they have agreed on a suitable pair of groups and (of prime order ), a bilinear pairing between them for which BDHP is hard, and a generator of . The main steps are as follows:

    1. chooses a random integer satisfying , computes in , and sends (broadcasts) to and .
    2. Similarly, and respectively, choose random integers and , (respectively), and compute and broadcast and .
    3. can now compute the shared secret key as . and can perform the corresponding calculations on the values they receive to obtain the same shared secret key.

    The Verheul protocol is shown diagrammatically in Figure 8.3.

    Note that the three parties keep the values , and secret, as knowledge of any one of them, together with the broadcast values, can be used to reveal the secret key. An eavesdropper who obtains the three broadcast values , and , and who can be assumed to know , must solve an instance of the BDHP to obtain the secret key.

    There are many other cryptographic schemes that can be built on bilinear pairings, but the Joux scheme is particularly elegant in its simplicity (much like Diffie–Hellman key exchange). More generally, there are a host of other real-world applications of finite fields that I have not even touched on. Anyway, I hope I have convinced you in these few pages that the rather weird arithmetic of finite fields, where the ‘numbers’ are actually polynomials and multiplication involves working modulo a polynomial, is something that should be more generally known and thought about.

Of course, for cryptographers and quantum physicists this whole business has been a bonanza—so every cloud has a silver lining.

    12. 12 The definition I give here is actually for a special case of a bilinear pairing known as a symmetric bilinear pairing—however it is sufficiently general for my purposes here.
    13. 13 Some of Weil’s greatest achievements were made when he was in prison in France in the early years of the Second World War. Whilst initially the conditions were hard, it seems that things improved for him over time. Indeed, he wrote the following to his wife from the prison: ‘My mathematics work is proceeding beyond my wildest hopes, and I am even a bit worried—if it’s only in prison that I work so well, will I have to arrange to spend 2 or 3 months locked up every year? In the meantime, I am contemplating writing a report to the proper authorities, as follows: “To the Director of Scientific Research: Having recently been in a position to discover through personal experience the considerable advantages afforded to pure and disinterested research by a stay in the establishments of the Penitentiary System, I take the liberty of, etc. etc.”’.

Chapter 9
Why Stop Now?

If I have seen further than others, it is by standing upon the shoulders of giants.

9.1 Some Edited Highlights

This is a sort of bonus chapter. My main goal in writing this book was to get as far as finite fields and their applications and, assuming you have read the previous chapters, you will have seen how I needed to build up to it in stages. This is how mathematics works—as mathematicians, major and minor (and I am very much in the latter category), we take the work that has been done by our predecessors and build on top of it. Unlike in the sciences where old theories or models eventually give way to new theories or better models, ‘old mathematics’ doesn’t fade away or become irrelevant. Instead it forms the foundations on which we build. This is captured by the very well-known Isaac Newton quote which starts this chapter.

So now we have reached the end of our quest, I would like to encourage you to continue to develop your knowledge of mathematics—so please don’t stop now! To encourage you I thought I would include brief introductions to a few topics which I find particularly interesting. This might be relating to applications or just because of the beauty of the results.

The topics I have chosen are quite a mixture, and I can’t claim there is any great logic to the selection I have made or any relationship between them. They are simply my personal edited highlights. I hope you like them.

9.2 Sizes of Infinity

When I was introduced to this first topic as an undergraduate, I remember thinking it is both really surprising and rather wonderful. Certainly, in the 1870s when Georg Cantor first published the ideas I will briefly explore here, he got an extremely negative reaction from his contemporaries, including some of the leading mathematicians of the day. Leopold Kronecker accused him of being a ‘corrupter of youth’ by promoting his ideas, and also reportedly said that ‘I don’t know what predominates in Cantor’s theory—philosophy or theology, but I am sure that there is no mathematics there’. Pretty strong stuff, I think you’ll agree, but it goes to show that mathematicians care deeply about mathematics—perhaps Kronecker more than most.

So what are these radical ideas (which, by the way, are today an established part of mathematical thought)? Well, his really radical ideas

Cardinality for finite sets is something we discussed previously, and is simply the number of elements in the set. However, what does cardinality mean for sets where the number of elements is not finite? Well we can start by giving a simple way for deciding whether two sets have the same cardinality—this definition applies regardless of whether the two sets have finite or infinite cardinality.

If and are sets, then we say that their cardinality is equal, i.e. , if and only if there is a one-to-one and onto function mapping from to . In such a case we say that there is a one-to-one correspondence between and . This makes obvious sense for finite sets since if a set has elements then we can define a one-to-one correspondence between and the set , and both sets clearly have cardinality . It is possible to show that this notion of cardinality-equality is an equivalence relation.

I next give our first infinite cardinal number. Define the cardinality of the natural numbers to be (where , to be read as ‘aleph’, is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet). That is, any set which can be put into one-to-one correspondence with has cardinality . However, unlike the rationals, the real numbers are not countable, i.e. . The proof of this result is extremely elegant and simple, and is due to Cantor; it is known as Cantor’s diagonal argument.

The proof actually shows that the real numbers between 0 and 1 (including 0 but excluding 1) are uncountable, and goes as follows. The proof is by contradiction, so we start by supposing that the real numbers satisfying are countable, and hence can be put into a one-to-one correspondence with the positive integers 1, 2, 3, ….

The real numbers in this range can all be represented as infinite decimal expansions of the form , e.g. , , , and so on. So suppose we use the one-to-one correspondence to put all the real numbers in the range in a numbered list, e.g. something like:

So the real numbers in the range zero to one are uncountable, and so clearly all the real numbers are uncountable.

There is much more that can be said about infinite cardinals, and I mention just two more things. The algebraic numbers are all the real numbers that are solutions to equations with rational coefficients. So numbers like are algebraic, although they are not rational. However, clearly all rational numbers are algebraic. So if denotes the set of algebraic numbers then

So all the weird and wonderful real numbers like (which is not algebraic) are really much more numerous than all the algebraic numbers. That is, the transcendental numbers, i.e. all the real numbers that are not algebraic, are uncountable. If you find this hard to get your head around, don’t worry; when the results were first published they caused a major shift in thinking about sets and the nature of infinity.

Finally, you might wonder whether there are even ‘larger’ infinities than the cardinality of the real numbers. Well, this is not immediately obvious, since it is fairly straightforward to show that . So there are ‘the same number’ of complex numbers as there are real numbers.

There is a ‘smallest’ infinity, however, and that is the cardinality of —which we write as . You might also reasonably ask whether there is an infinity larger than but smaller than . The simple answer is that no one knows! It is one of the great unsolved problems of mathematics. The Continuum Hypothesis due to Georg Cantor, states that there is no set with cardinality greater than but less than . It turns out that the question of the truth or falsehood of the Continuum Hypothesis cannot be decided with ‘standard’ set theory, and it is possible to build two versions of mathematics—one with the hypothesis true and one with it false; this was established by American mathematician Paul Joseph Cohen, and the result was published in 1965. Intuitively this is beyond weird, but so much for intuition! I should conclude by saying that this is an ongoing area for work by logicians and set theorists, so there is still a lot to be said on this subject, although it’s way beyond my pay grade.

9.3 How Many Prime Numbers Are There?

I now want to revisit integers and prime numbers. I hope you are all familiar with primes, and the series of primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, …. One obvious question about the primes is whether they ever ‘run out’, i.e. is there a largest prime, or are there more primes no matter how large you get? This problem was resolved in antiquity, and a proof was provided by Euclid in his ‘Elements’.

Theorem 9.1

(Euclid’s Theorem) There are an infinite number of prime numbers.

Proof. The proof is by contradiction. That is, to start with I will assume that the theorem is false, i.e. I suppose that there are only a finite number of prime numbers. Suppose the complete list of prime numbers is:

I want you to consider the number

Now is clearly larger than all of the primes, and so cannot be prime. It must therefore be a equal to a product of prime numbers, say for primes . However, none of are divisors of , since for every prime . So the primes are not in the set . But we assumed this set contained all the prime numbers, and we have just found some prime numbers not in the set, and so we have a contradiction.

This proof is very simple and elegant and is one of many beautiful proofs included in the volume Proofs from the Book by Austrian mathematician Martin Aigner and German mathematician Günter M Ziegler.

The study of prime numbers and their distribution has fascinated mathematicians for millennia, and remains a key part of mathematics today. There are, it seems, endless questions that can be asked, many of which are hard to resolve. One of the most famous results concerns the approximate number of prime numbers less than any given positive integer. Let be the number of primes less than or equal to the positive integer . By the end of the 18th century mathematicians were already looking at the behaviour of the function for increasing values of , and conjecturing how it might behave. In 1798, French mathematician Adrien-Marie Legendre was the first to conjecture what became known as the Prime Number Theorem (when it was eventually proved a 100 years later).

Building on work by many mathematicians, notably including the renowned German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, in 1896 two French mathematicians independently arrived at a proof for this theorem: Jacques-Salomon Hadamard and Charles de la Valée Poussin. The proofs they came up with involve the theory of complex numbers and are long and difficult. Other proofs have been devised since, but none can be described as simple. There are a number of reasons why difference sets are of interest. I will briefly describe two of them. The first relates to finite geometry. I should first explain what I mean by the term. For my purposes here, a finite geometry is simply a pair of finite sets called points and lines and a relation between them called incidence. That is, a point is either incident with a line or it isn’t. So a finite geometry can be defined as a triple , where is the set of points, is the set of lines and is the incidence relation between and . I will use the common geometric terminology and refer to a point being on a line or a line going through a point if the point and line are incident.

Perhaps surprisingly, such a simple definition gives rise to a wealth of possibilities. A particularly important class of finite geometries consists of what are known as the finite projective planes. A finite projective plane is a finite geometry with the following three key properties:

  • the number of lines is the same as the number of points (and the sets have cardinality at least two);
  • every line has the same number of points incident with it;
  • for every pair of points there is a unique line that is incident with them both.

The following simple result follows without difficulty.

9.5 Finite Simple Groups

The very final topic I want to briefly explore relates to finite groups, and is one of the greatest mathematical achievements of the second half of the 20th century. This achievement is the classification of all finite simple groups.

To explain what this means I first need to tell you want a simple group is, although to get there I first need to introduce some other ideas. As I explained in Section 5.5, if is a group, then is a subgroup of if and the elements of form a group under the operation *. I also defined the notion of a coset, where if is a subgroup of , then the coset is the set of all elements of of the form , where . I need to go a little further here and introduce the notion of right and left cosets. What I have just defined is a right coset of . A left coset, written is simply the set of all elements of of the form , where .

Of course, if is abelian, i.e. a group for which the operation is commutative, then a left coset is exactly the same as a right coset, but in general this won’t be true.

I can now make a key definition. Suppose is a subgroup of ; is said to be a normal subgroup of if for every . That is, is a normal subgroup if all the left cosets of are the same as the right cosets of . It is common to write to indicate that is a normal subgroup of .

Of course, if is abelian then, as I just noted, left cosets and right cosets are automatically the same, so all subgroups of an abelian group are normal. However, the definition becomes more interesting for non-abelian groups.

A simple example is provided by the group of permutations of the set , described back in Section 5.7.2. This group, usually referred to as , has six elements and is non-abelian. The six elements are

where the first element in the list is the identity element in the group (it maps 1 to 1, 2 to 2 and 3 to 3). Three of the elements, namely

form a subgroup known as , which is a normal subgroup of , i.e. . It is simple to check it forms a subgroup since the two non-identity elements are inverses of each other. One way of showing it is a normal subgroup is to observe that is half the size of , i.e. . Now, since a (left or right) coset of will always have the same number of elements as (see Section 5.5), there are only two possible right cosets and two possible left cosets of . One of the two will be itself, and so the other left coset and the other right coset must be the same, consisting of all the elements of not in ! This argument immediately gives us the more general result that if is a subgroup of and , it follows that will always be a normal subgroup of .

The subgroup of consists of all the even permutations in . Odd and even permutations can be defined in the following way. First define the identity permutation to be an even permutation. Next, consider the ‘simplest’ possible permutations, namely those that interchange two elements but otherwise leave everything unchanged—these are known as transpositions. For example, in the following three permutations are transpositions:

All transpositions are defined to be ‘odd’ permutations.

Working on from there, the product of two transpositions is, as you might expect, an even permutation; the product of three transpositions is an odd permutation; and so on. We can define when every permutation is odd or even in this way, since every permutation can be expressed as a product of transpositions. When expressing a permutation in terms of transpositions, oddness and evenness is preserved, no matter how you might express it.

As I described in Section 5.7.2, the set of all permutations on is known as the symmetric group and is denoted by ; the order of this group is . The set of all even permutations in always forms a subgroup known as the alternating group, and is denoted by . There are always the same number of odd and even permutations, and so for every . Since , this means that, as above, is always a normal subgroup of , i.e. .

I can now define the key term for this discussion. A group is said to be simple if the only normal subgroups are itself and the trivial subgroup containing just the identity element. It turns out that simple groups are fundamental to understanding the possible structure of finite groups.

So which groups are simple? Well, any group which has no non-trivial subgroups must be simple, and hence the cyclic groups of prime order (often written as for prime) must be simple. This follows since the order of a subgroup divides the order of a group (see Theorem 5.2), and if the order is prime then a subgroup can only have order the prime itself or one.

A more interesting family of simple groups is provided by the alternating groups . It can be shown (although the details are well beyond the scope of this book) that is simple for . The fact that is simple was first shown by Évariste Galois, although the full importance of simple groups in the understanding of finite groups only emerged in the 20th century.

I need one further definition before I can give the key results establishing the fundamental role of simple groups, namely that of a quotient group. Suppose is a normal subgroup of . Then we define the set to consist of all the right cosets of (which will be the same as the set of left cosets, since ). The set will contain elements, since every coset will contain elements of . We can now define an operation ⋅ on the set in the following way.

Suppose and are two elements of . Then define

I claim that this operation on satisfies the axioms of a group, i.e. is a group.

First observe that

But is a group, and hence * satisfies the associative law. Hence and so ⋅ is associative.

The identity element is , since

I can now explain why simple groups play such a central role in the study of groups. The key facts that make simple groups so important are encapsulated in the following two theorems, which I give without proof.

Theorem 9.4

If is a finite group then it has a composition series of the form

where every is a group and the series cannot be further refined.

This is complemented by the following fundamentally important theorem due to French mathematician Marie Ennemond Camille Jordan and German mathematician Ludwig Otto Hölder.

Theorem 9.5

(Jordan–Hölder Theorem) If and the subgroups are as in Theorem 9.4, then the set of composition factors is unique and independent of the choice of composition series.

It is important to observe that although a group can have two different composition series, and two different groups can have the same composition series, the Jordan–Hölder Theorem means that any two composition series are equivalent up to the ordering of the composition factors.

The above results mean that the finite simple groups are in a sense the ‘atoms’ or building blocks of all finite groups, a little like prime numbers for the integers or irreducible polynomials for polynomials. So, if you understand all the possible finite simple groups, you have a handle on understanding all the finite groups. As a result, during much of the 20th century the most high profile problem in finite group theory has been to classify all the finite simple groups. The problem was finally solved only in the last few decades of the 20th century. So what are the finite simple groups?

I already mentioned two infinite families of simple groups which have long been known, namely the cyclic groups of prime order and the alternating groups for . There are two further infinite classes of finite simple groups. These are the ‘classical groups’, i.e. matrix groups over a range of fields, and the exceptional groups of Lie type (terminology I won’t even try to explain)! These were all known by the early 1960s, together with a small number of so-called sporadic finite simple groups, notably including the five Mathieu groups, named after their discoverer 19th-century French mathematician Émile Léonard Mathieu. These are called sporadic as they are not obviously part of any of the infinite families.

At the turn of the 20th century, British mathematician William Burnside conjectured that all the non-abelian finite simple groups must have even order. It was only proved true in 1962–1963, by Austrian-American mathematician Walter Feit and American mathematician John Griggs Thompson. Their proof, which covers over 250 pages, helped give impetus to the project to classify all the finite simple groups.

American mathematician Daniel Gorenstein was the organiser of the coordinated effort. During the 1960s and 1970s, as work proceeded, further sporadic simple groups were discovered, bringing the total of such groups to 26 (apart from the five Mathieu groups, they were all discovered after 1965). Perhaps the most remarkable of these sporadic groups, and the last to be found, is that known as the ‘Monster’, discovered by American mathematician Robert Griess and announced in 1980. It is enormous having order

808,017,424,794,512,875,886,459,904,961,710,757,005,754,368,000,000,000≃ 8 × 1053.

The monster group contains 20 sporadic groups (including itself) as sub-quotients.

The classification theorem of finite simple groups (or simply CFSG) states that there are no more. That is, the only finite simple groups are the known infinite families and the 26 sporadic groups. It is difficult to give a single date as to when this theorem was proved. The proof involves tens of thousands of pages in several hundred different research papers written by many tens of authors, where these papers were mostly published between 1955 and 2004. Indeed, in his book (mentioned above), Robert Wilson makes the following statement.

There has been much debate about whether CFSG deserves to be called a theorem, and this debate has contributed to the philosophical arguments about what a theorem is, what a proof is, what mathematics is (or are) and how we recognise them when we see them.

…

So what of the CFSG? Has it indeed been proved? Certainly the process of collating the various parts of the proof, filling in the gaps and correcting errors, has taken longer than anyone expected when the imminent completion of the proof was announced around 1980. The project by Gorenstein, Lyons and Solomon to write down the whole [the so-called second generation] proof is still in progress; six of a projected eleven volumes have been published so far.

I’m afraid I will have to leave the final topic of this book there. This brief account only just scratches the surface of what is a huge topic, with many implications for other parts of group theory. However, before finishing I must just mention one other book, namely the Atlas of Finite Groups, by John Horton Conway, Robert Turner Curtis, Simon Phillips Norton, Richard Alan Parker and Robert Arnott Wilson.

Answers to Questions for the Reader

Sets and Relations

Balls in the Bag Probabilities

In Section 2.2, I made a claim about a ‘balls in the bag’ probability question. This is closely related to something known as Bertrand’s box paradox, after the 19th-century French mathematician Joseph Louis François Bertrand. Suppose the two balls are labelled and . We supposed that the probability that is white and the probability that is white are both equal to (i.e. 0.5 or 50%, whichever you prefer).

So there are four cases to consider, each with probability 1/4:

  • and are both black;
  • is black and is white;
  • is white and is black;
  • and are both white.

When you draw out a ball I assume that it is equally likely to be or . That is, there are eight possible events that could occur when you draw out a ball, each with probability 1/8:

  1. and are both black, and you draw out ;
  2. and are both black, and you draw out ;
  3. is black and is white, and you draw out ;
  4. is black and is white, and you draw out ;
  5. is white and is black, and you draw out ;
  6. is white and is black, and you draw out ;
  7. and are both white, and you draw out ;
  8. and are both white, and you draw out .

Since the ball you draw out is actually black, clearly what has occurred is one of events 1, 2, 3 and 6 from the above list, all of which are equally probable (probability 1/4). But what about the other ball? Well, if events 1 or 2 have occurred (total probability 1/2), then the remaining ball is black. If events 3 or 6 have occurred (total probability 1/2) then the remaining ball is white, i.e. I have proved the required result.

There are many other examples of simple probability calculations which give non-obvious results. Perhaps the most well-known is the so-called Monty Hall problem, which has been very widely discussed.

The Definition of an Equivalence Relation

In Section 2.5, I gave an argument suggesting that we can simplify the definition of an equivalence relation to be one which just satisfies symmetry and transitivity, since reflexivity can be deduced from the other two properties. Why is this argument wrong?

In the argument I gave, I started by saying ‘Choose any element , and let be any other element in for which ’. However, it’s incorrect to say this, since there may not be such an element . That is, the element may not be related to any other element of the set, in which case a suitable wouldn’t exist. In this case will not be true, and so reflexivity does not hold. That is, even if we assume symmetry and transitivity we also need to assume the reflexive property.

A Flawed Induction Argument

Later in the same chapter (in Section 3.5), I gave the following induction argument.

Suppose the statement is ‘Every group of people have the same name’. To prove that is true for every we need to show that (a) is true, and (b) if is true then is true. Now is clearly true since one person clearly has the same name as themselves. Now suppose is true, i.e. we know that any group of people always have the same name. Now consider any group of people, and suppose they line up in order. We know that the first people have the same name (since is true), and also that the last people have the same name. Thus all people must have the same name.

So where is the mistake? The problem comes in moving from to . There won’t be any overlap between the set of the first people and the set of the last people. So we can’t conclude that any set of two people will have the same name (not surprisingly, perhaps)!

The Hamming Code Has Minimum Distance Three

I claimed without proof in Section 6.9.2 that the Hamming Code has minimum distance three, and I promised to explain why this is true.

First observe that if I specify the data bits for a codeword, then the check bits are a fixed function of the data bits. The check bits are those bits for which the value of is one of 1, 2, 4, 8, …, i.e. the numbers whose binary representations contain a single one. The binary representation of for a data bit , by contrast, will always contain at least two ones. Now, for any data bit , the positions of the ones in the value of will determine which check bits are computed as a function of that data bit. So, the number of ones in the value of will be equal to the number of check bits depending on data bit .

So if I change a data bit (from one to zero or from zero to one) then the number of check bits that will change will equal the number of ones in the binary representation of . But we said that this is at least two for any data bit. So changing one data bit will involve changing at least two check bits. This establishes that the minimum distance of the code is three.

Periods of LFSR Sequences of States

I stated in Section 7.4.1 that the sum of the periods of the possible sequences of LFSR states always adds to , where is the number of possible symbols and is the length of the register. I suggested you prove this as a simple exercise.

This is actually very simple to show. Every state of the register occurs in precisely one possible periodic sequence of states, and it can only occur once in a period of such a sequence. Hence, the sum of the periods of the state sequences is equal to the number of possible states, which is simply .

Further Reading

The main problem I had in putting together this final part of the book was in deciding what to leave out—there are so many excellent books to recommend. Indeed, looking through these books reminded me that this small effort rather pales into insignificance by comparison. Nonetheless, I still feel that this volume attempts to do something that no other book I am aware of achieves. In any event, I hope you have found it helpful—and perhaps even enjoyable! I have certainly had fun writing it; after all, as author I get to include all the material I enjoy and leave out the bits I don’t.

I have divided my suggestions for further reading into four main categories, the first three of which list recommended books covering mathematics itself (and mathematicians), abstract algebra and applications. The final category is online resources—there are some really excellent online resources for mathematics, and I list some of those I found most useful.

Mathematics and Mathematicians

These books give personal views on the nature of mathematics, and also descriptions of some of the more famous mathematicians.

  • A D Aczel, ‘Fermat’s Last Theorem’, Viking (1996), describes the history and influence of a ‘theorem’ that the 17th-century mathematician Pierre de Fermat claimed to have a proof for, but did not write down. Attempts to prove this theorem, that forms part of number theory, have had huge impacts in the development of mathematics across a wide range of fields. In 1993, Andrew Wiles gave a proof, which—after some repair work—is now generally accepted as having resolved the problem, i.e. it is now a theorem without the quotation marks!
  • M Aigner and G M Ziegler, ‘Proofs from the Book’, Springer (2001), 2nd edition. This book contains a collection of particularly beautiful proofs of theorems, and was inspired by the late, great Paul Erdős, who talked about ‘The Book’ as something maintained by God for perfect proofs.
  • E T Bell, ‘Men of Mathematics’, Touchstone Books (1986), contains a series of short biographies of major mathematicians, originally published in 1937. The accounts are not always 100% reliable, but are eminently readable and bring the people to life. Of course, the title is somewhat sexist in that it suggests, deliberately or accidentally, that mathematics is for men only. One woman is mentioned, however, namely Sonja Kowalewski.
  • D Debakcsy, ‘A History of Women in Mathematics’, Pen & Sword Books (2023), provides brief portraits of major women mathematicians from antiquity to the present. It is something of a counterpoint to E T Bell’s ‘Men of Mathematics’, and shows the breadth of mathematical results achieved by women over the centuries despite the many obstacles placed in their way.
  • G H Hardy, ‘A Mathematician’s Apology’, Lector House (1940), is a personal view of mathematics, written by one of the greats of the first half of the 20th century and originally published in 1940. He defends the idea that mathematics is something beautiful and worth pursuing for its own sake, and not just for its potential applications. I think he would be surprised to learn how much mathematics viewed as useless but beautiful in 1940 has turned out to be useful!
  • R Kanigel, ‘The Man Who Knew Infinity’, Scribners (1992), is an immensely readable life of the mathematical genius Srinivasa Ramanujan and his friendship with G H Hardy. Indeed, you may be more familiar with the 2016 film adaptation, but I would encourage you to explore the book.
  • M Kline, ‘Mathematics: The Loss of Certainty’, Oxford University Press (1980), is vast in its scope, covering the development of rigorous mathematics over almost 3000 years. It culminates in a review of the state of mathematical foundations, which suffered what seemed then a major disaster in the early 20th century. A gross simplification might say that efforts to prove the consistency of mathematics using mathematics itself was shown to be impossible.
  • L M Osen, ‘Women in Mathematics’, MIT Press (1974), is further evidence of the rich, but often ignored, contributions made by women to mathematics. The book contains eight biographies of women, along with summaries of their mathematical contributions.
  • B Wardaugh, ‘The Book of Wonders’, William Collins (2020), is an entertaining and illuminating history of Euclid’s Elements, one of the first (if not the first) treatises to attempt to give a rigorous treatment to mathematics, involving theorems and proofs. Euclid’s Elements have had a profound influence on the development of mathematics since it was first written some 2300 years ago.

Abstract Algebra

The books listed here all cover much of the ground I cover in this book, although typically with a much broader and deeper scope, and in a more textbook-like fashion.

  • G Birkhoff and S Mac Lane, ‘A Survey of Modern Algebra’, A K Peters (1997), 4th edition, is a classic text on abstract algebra, and remains an excellent introduction, albeit one that is not to be taken lightly. It served as the default textbook on abstract algebra for a generation or more, as exemplified by its unlikely appearance in a 1964 short story, ‘The Mathenauts’ by Norman Kagan.
  • A Meijer, ‘Algebra for Cryptologists’, Springer (2016), is perhaps the book that is closest to this one in scope. It aims to provide a rigorous introduction to the mathematics necessary to understand modern cryptography. However, it is a ‘proper’ mathematics textbook aimed at readers already happy with the theorem–proof style, and is much more comprehensive in its scope than this book.
  • C W Norman, ‘Undergraduate Algebra: A First Course’, Oxford University Press (1986) is a textbook aimed at introducing abstract algebra to undergraduates. It is rather more gentle in its approach than Birkhoff and Mac Lane.
  • R A Wilson, ‘The Finite Simple Groups’, Springer (2009), provides an introduction to the finite simple groups. Written in the wake of the classification of all finite simple groups, it provides very detailed information about all these groups. It is a mathematically sophisticated text, but excellent if you want to learn much more about these groups.

Applications

Throughout this book, interspersed with my introductions to groups, rings and fields, I have described some key applications, focussing mainly on those relating to computing and digital communications. There are so many relevant books—the following are my personal favourites:

  • T Beth, D Jungnickel and H Lenz, ‘Design Theory’, Bibliographisches Institut Mannheim (1985), provides a comprehensive account of the theory of combinatorial designs, including difference sets. An updated 2nd edition in two volumes was published in 1999.
  • R Hill, ‘A First Course in Coding Theory’, Oxford University Press (1986), does what it says on the tin. This is an easy to read and thorough introduction to mathematical coding theory, a subject built on abstract algebra that only emerged in the mid-20th century but has grown to be vitally important in today’s world of ubiquitous digital communications.
  • K M Martin, ‘Everyday Cryptography: Fundamental Principles and Applications’, Oxford University Press (2017), provides a first introduction to the uses and abuses of cryptography. It is not so much concerned with the underlying mathematics, although this is not ignored, but the main focus is on what cryptography can be used for.
  • S Golomb, ‘Shift Register Sequences’, Holden-Day (1967), is the original classic text on shift register sequences, written by the man who played a major role in developing the theory. The presentation now seems rather dated, but it is a very readable and entertaining book.
  • M Goresky and A Klapper, ‘Algebraic Shift Register Sequences’, Cambridge University Press (2012), is a comprehensive and modern account of the subject. It includes a detailed appendix providing the necessary mathematical background.
  • D R Hughes and F C Piper, ‘Design Theory’, Cambridge University Press (1985), gives a highly accessible introduction to block designs, including difference sets. Whilst it is much less comprehensive than Beth, Jungnickel and Lenz, it nevertheless covers the fundamentals of the subject.
  • D Knuth, ‘The Art of Computer Programming, Volumes 1, 2, 3, 4A and 4B’, Addison-Wesley, 1997–2023, is a monumental work, covering a vast range of computer algorithms. It is both comprehensive and rigorous from a mathematical perspective; indeed, it covers much of the material in this book, albeit in a much more condensed form. The books are wonderful, albeit not always an easy read.
  • A Pott, P V Kumar, T Helleseth and D Jungnickel (eds), ‘Difference Sets, Sequences and their Correlation Properties’, Kluwer Academic (1999), contains a series of chapters by leading experts in their field. The topics addressed relate closely to several of the applications introduced in this book.
  • E S Selmer, ‘Linear Recurrence Relations Over Finite Fields’, Department of Mathematics, University of Bergen (1966), covers much of the same ground as Golomb’s book, but from a mathematical rather than an engineering perspective. Despite never being published in the normal way, it served as a key reference for many years, and remains an excellent resource. It is rather a shame that the University of Bergen has not made an electronic version available.
  • T M Thompson, ‘From Error-correcting Codes Through Sphere Packings to Simple Groups’, Mathematical Association of America (1983), is an immensely readable account of a range of topics which also relate closely to subjects introduced in this book.
  • D Welsh, ‘Codes and Cryptography’, Oxford University Press (1988), now looks a little dated, but it is an excellent and very accessible introduction to coding theory and cryptography, focussing on areas of interest from a mathematical perspective.

Online Resources

Finally, I would like to mention a few online resources that I found especially useful when writing this book. There are, of course, many more.

  • A personal favourite is the Combinatorial Objects Server (http://combos.org/). This site enables you to play with combinatorial objects, such as permutations with particular properties.
  • MacTutor (https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/) is an excellent free online resource containing biographies of more than 3000 mathematicians, and much else besides. I have used this resource extensively in providing much of the biographical information in this book.
  • The Mathematics Stack Exchange (https://math.stackexchange.com) is one of 183 online ‘question and answer’ communities, and enables anyone to ask a mathematical question and receive detailed and informative answers from the mathematical community. I thoroughly recommend it—often the question you want to ask has been asked and answered already.
  • I already mentioned the splendid Online Encyclopaedia of Integer Sequences (the OEIS)—available at https://oeis.org/. It is difficult not to get sucked into endless rabbit holes when exploring this terrific resource.
  • ProofWiki (https://proofwiki.org) is a freely accessible repository of proofs of a very wide range of mathematical results, as well as containing a huge collection of definitions of mathematical concepts.

Note

  1. 1 The story was originally published in the July 1964 issue of Worlds of If, and has since appeared in at least two short story collections, including Mathenauts: Tales of Mathematical Wonder, edited by Rudy Rucker and published in 1987 by Arbor House. In the envisaged far future, only mathematicians can travel through space as Mathenauts. A quote involving one of the lead characters, Ed Goldwasser, is as follows ‘He touched a knob and set a widget, and checked in his copy of Birkhoff and MacLane’.
